(2005) focus on another aspect of evaluation--considering the entire list together. This would allow us to consider aspects of a set of recommendations, such as diversification between items in the same list. Our suggested metrics consider only single items, and thus could not be used to evaluate entire lists. It would be interesting to see more evaluation metrics that provide observations over complete lists. Celma and Herrera (2008) suggest looking at topological properties of the recommendation graph--the graph that connects recommended items. They explain how by looking at the recommendation graph one may understand properties such as the novelty of recommendations. It is still unclear how these properties correlate with the true goal of the recommender system, may it be to optimize revenue or to recommend useful items.

As described above, the goal of the offline evaluation is to filter algorithms so that only the most promising need undergo expensive online tests. Thus, the data used for the offline evaluation should match as closely as possible the data the designer expects the recommender system to face when deployed online. Care must be exercised to ensure that there is no bias in the distributions of users, items and ratings selected. For example, in cases where data from an existing system (perhaps a system without a recommender) is available, the experimenter may be tempted to pre-filter the data by excluding items or users with low counts, in order to reduce the costs of experimentation. In doing so, the experimenter should be mindful that this involves a trade-off, since this introduces a systematic bias in the data. If necessary, randomly sampling users and items may be a preferable method for reducing data, although this can also introduce other biases into the experiment (e.g., this could tend to favor algorithms that work better with more sparse data). Offline evaluation must also approximate the interaction that occurs when a system is deployed: the system generates predictions or recommendations, and users respond by rating items or engaging with the recommendations presented to them. Historical records provide observations of these responses, but evaluating an algorithm on information already available to it would not reproduce this interaction. Instead, some observed interactions are withheld from the algorithm, which uses the remaining data to generate its outputs. The withheld observations then provide evidence against which these outputs can be evaluated, allowing the experimenter to simulate aspects of online use without requiring new user interactions. The choice of which interactions to withhold should therefore reflect the target application as closely as possible. A withholding procedure defines the information available to the algorithm and the responses it is expected to anticipate; a mismatch between this procedure and deployment can make the resulting evaluation less informative about online performance. This principle applies both to recommendation tasks, where selected items with which a user has interacted are hidden and the algorithm is assessed on its ability to recommend them, and to ratings prediction tasks, where selected ratings are hidden and the algorithm is assessed on its estimates of those values. In either case, the evaluation should represent the circumstances under which the system will make recommendations or predictions and users will subsequently respond.

As described above, the goal of the offline evaluation is to filter algorithms so that only the most promising need undergo expensive online tests. Thus, the data used for the offline evaluation should match as closely as possible the data the designer expects the recommender system to face when deployed online. Care must be exercised to ensure that there is no bias in the distributions of users, items and ratings selected. For example, in cases where data from an existing system (perhaps a system without a recommender) is available, the experimenter may be tempted to pre-filter the data by excluding items or users with low counts, in order to reduce the costs of experimentation. In doing so, the experimenter should be mindful that this involves a trade-off, since this introduces a systematic bias in the data. If necessary, randomly sampling users and items may be a preferable method for reducing data, although this can also introduce other biases into the experiment (e.g., this could tend to favor algorithms that work better with more sparse data). In order to evaluate algorithms offline, it is necessary to simulate the online process where the system makes predictions or recommendations, and the user corrects the predictions or uses the recommendations. This is usually done by recording historical user data, and then hiding some of these interactions in order to simulate the knowledge of how a user will rate an item, or which recommendations a user will act upon. There are a number of ways to choose the ratings/selected items to be hidden. Once again, it is preferable that this choice be done in a manner that simulates the target application as closely as possible. We discuss these concerns explicitly for the case of selecting used items for hiding in the evaluation of recommendation tasks, and note that the same considerations apply when selecting ratings to hide for evaluation of ratings prediction tasks.

Our goal is to simulate sets of past user selections that are representative of what the system will face when deployed. Ideally, if we have access to time-stamps for user selections, we can randomly sample test users, randomly sample a time just prior to a user action, hide all selections (of all users) after that instant, and then attempt to recommend items to that user. This protocol requires changing the set of given information prior to each recommendation, which can be computationally quite expensive. A cheaper alternative is to sample a set of test users, then sample a single test time, and hide all items after the sampled test time for each test user. This simulates a situation where the recommender system is "trained" as of the test time, and then makes recommendations without taking into account any new data that arrives after the test time. Another alternative is to sample a test time for each test user, and hide the test user's items after that time, without maintaining time consistency across users. This effectively assumes that it is the sequence in which items are selected, and not the absolute times when they are selected that is important. A final alternative is to ignore time; We sample a set of test users, then sample the number n a of items to hide for each user a, then sample n a items to hide. This assumes that the temporal aspects of user selections are unimportant. All three of the latter alternatives partition the data into a single training set and single test set. It is important to select an alternative that is most appropriate for the domain and task of interest, rather than the most convenient one. A further concern is that evaluation protocols often fix the number of rated items available for each test user, or the number withheld for testing. Although this makes experimental conditions easier to control, it can yield a sample of recommendation tasks that does not reflect actual user behavior. Users may differ in how much information they provide and in how their selections accumulate, and an algorithm's performance may depend on these differences. An evaluation conducted under a fixed profile size therefore estimates performance under that particular condition, rather than necessarily estimating performance in deployment. If the distribution of user histories encountered online differs from the distribution imposed by the experiment, the resulting estimates may be biased and may even favor an algorithm that performs less well in practice. The choice of how much information to retain or hide should consequently be guided by the behavior the evaluation is intended to simulate. The partitioning schemes discussed above use held-out test sets: some observations are reserved for evaluation, while the remaining observations provide the information from which recommendations are computed. Cross-validation instead constructs multiple partitions, using different portions of the data for testing and combining the resulting performance estimates. This can be useful when the available data are too limited for a single partition to support a reliable decision. For recommender systems, however, a held-out approach is generally preferable, since the available data typically suffice to compare algorithms without repeatedly repartitioning the observations. Moreover, cross-validation results are not independent: the partitions reuse observations, and their training sets overlap. Combining these results as though they were independent can therefore lead to misleading assessments of uncertainty or statistical significance. A suitably constructed held-out evaluation usually provides sufficient evidence for algorithm selection while avoiding these complications.

This protocol is useful for diagnosing algorithms and identifying in which cases they work best. However, when we wish to make decisions on the algorithm that we will use in our application, we must ask ourselves whether we are truly interested in presenting recommendations for users who have rated exactly n items, or are expected to rate exactly n items more. If that is not the case, then results computed using these protocol have biases that make them difficult to use in predicting the outcome of using the algorithms online. In the case of recommender systems, the held-out approach usually yields enough data to make reliable decisions. Many evaluation metrics have been used to rank recommendation algorithms, some measuring similar features, but some measuring drastically different quantities. For example, methods such as the Root of the Mean Square Error (RMSE) measure the distance between predicted preferences and true preferences over items, while the Recall method computes the portion of favored items that were suggested. Clearly, it is unlikely that a single algorithm would outperform all others over all possible methods. Therefore, we should expect different metrics to provide different rankings of algorithms. As such, selecting the proper evaluation metric to use has a crucial influence on the selection of the recommender system algorithm that will be selected for deployment. This survey reviews existing evaluation metrics, suggesting an approach for deciding which evaluation metric is most appropriate for a given application. We categorize previously suggested recommender systems into three major groups, each corresponding to a different task. The first obvious task is to recommend a set of good (interesting, useful) items to the user. In this task it is assumed that all good items are interchangeable. A second, less discussed, although highly important task is utility optimization. For example, many e-commerce websites use a recommender system, hoping to increase their revenues. In this case, the task is to present a set of recommendations that will optimize the retailer revenue. Finally, a very common task is the prediction of user opinion (e.g., rating) over a set of items. While this may not be an explicit act of recommendation, much research in recommender systems focuses on this task, and so we address it here. For each such task we review a family of common evaluation metrics that measure the performance of algorithms on that task. We discuss the properties of each such metric, and why it is most appropriate for a given task. The choice of an evaluation metric is not a neutral step in comparing recommender systems. A metric that does not match the task can favor an algorithm for the wrong reasons, leading researchers to select a method that appears strongest under one measure but performs differently under another. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate this problem: changing the metric can change the relative ordering of algorithms, producing inconsistent rankings. The results make clear that claims about which algorithm is best depend on how performance is measured. To help researchers design sound offline experiments, the paper examines the choices involved in constructing and assessing evaluations. It offers guidance on data splitting and on what measurements to collect, and explains how to test whether observed differences are statistically significant. The authors also identify common methodological pitfalls that can undermine statistical validity, even when an experiment appears carefully controlled. Together, these recommendations provide a framework for interpreting results with appropriate caution and making comparisons that reflect the intended task. The investigation first establishes background on recommender systems and organizes them by task, then reviews evaluation protocols and the metrics used to measure performance. It illustrates the consequences of misapplying metrics through concrete examples, before turning to related work and placing the analysis within the broader research literature. This structure connects the choice of measure to the design and interpretation of an experiment, showing why rigorous evaluation is essential to reliable conclusions about recommender algorithms.

The sign test is an attractive choice due to its simplicity, and lack of assumptions over the distribution of cases. Still this test may lead to mislabeling of significant results as insignificant when the number of test points is small. In these cases, the more sophisticated Wilcoxon signed rank test can be used (Demšar, 2006). As mentioned in Section 4.2, cross-validation can be used to increase the amount of data, and thus the significance of results, but in this case the results obtained on the cross-validated test sets are no longer independent, and care must be exercised to ensure that our decisions account for this (Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004). Also, model-based approaches (e.g., Goutte and Gaussier, 2005) may be useful when the amount of data is small, but once again, care must be exercised to ensure that the model assumptions are reasonable for the application at hand. A further complication arises when experimenters compare several algorithm variants with the same baseline, applying a significance test to each comparison. Even if all variants are equivalent to the baseline, repeated testing increases the chance of at least one false positive: with ten tests at \(p=0.05\), the probability of spuriously rejecting a null hypothesis reaches 40%, rather than the nominal 5%. Selecting a variant on the basis of such a result amounts to tuning to the test set; the apparent improvement may reflect the repeated search rather than a genuine difference in performance. One way to limit this effect is to partition the test data into development and evaluation subsets. The development subset guides algorithm selection, while the evaluation subset is reserved to validate the selected choice through significance testing. A related, more difficult problem occurs when ranking numerous algorithms, since the many pairwise comparisons also threaten the validity of the conclusions. In that setting, methods such as the Bonferroni correction or the Friedman test can be used to maintain valid statistical inference across comparisons.

For example, an experimenter might try out several variants of a novel recommender algorithm and compare them to a baseline algorithm until they find one that passes a sign test at the p = 0.05 level and therefore infer that their algorithm improves upon the baseline with 95% confidence. However, this is not a valid inference. Suppose the experimenter evaluated ten different variants all of which are statistically the same as the baseline. If the probability that any one of these trials passes the sign test mistakenly is p = 0.05, the probability that at least one of the ten trials passes the sign test mistakenly is 1 − (1 − 0.05) 20 = 0.40. This risk is colloquially known as "tuning to the test set" and can be avoided by separating the test set users into two groups--a development (or tuning) set, and an evaluation set. The choice of algorithm is done based on the development test, and the validity of the choice is measured by running a significance test on the evaluation set. A similar concern exists when ranking a number of algorithms, but is more difficult to circumvent. Suppose the best of N + 1 algorithms is chosen on the development test set. We can have a confidence 1 − p that the chosen algorithm is indeed the best, if it outperforms the N other algorithms on the evaluation set with significance 1 − (1 − p) 1/N . This is known as the Bonferroni correction, and should be used when pair-wise significant tests are used multiple times. Alternatively, the Friedman test for ranking can be used (Demšar, 2006).

The main appeal of our approach is that it deals with three difficulties at once: unboundedness, dependence, and high dimensionality. Existing tools typically address only one of these at a time, and they usually pay for it with restrictive assumptions. McDiarmid's inequality, for example, requires bounded differences, which rules out heavy-tailed or unbounded losses and many of the variables that arise in practice. Symmetrization techniques rely on independence, since the ghost-sample argument breaks down once observations influence one another. Neither tool, taken alone, gives a usable bound when the data are unbounded, dependent, and indexed by a high dimensional parameter. Combining separate arguments to cover all three requirements tends to be cumbersome, and each added layer brings further technical conditions that are hard to verify. Other lines of work improve particular properties but remain tied to special settings. Chaining techniques sharpen the dependence of a bound on the complexity of the function class, yet they are generally developed for independent observations. Ratio-type results can give tighter control when the variance is small relative to the deviation, but they too usually need independence or iid data, and they do not extend readily to general dependent settings. Our approach instead builds on the mixingale framework. Mixingales are more general than martingale-based methods, because they require only that conditional expectations of future observations given the distant past become small, rather than requiring an exact martingale difference structure. Working in this framework lets us obtain a closed-form inequality without any boundedness assumption, so that the dependence, the unbounded tails, and the dimension of the parameter space all enter the bound explicitly through a single, simple argument. Typical uniform deviation results deal with infinite-dimensional function spaces. Our formulation is for a somewhat less general situation where the functions are parameterized, and we formulated uniform convergence on a high dimensional parameter space. Although it may be possible to formulate uniform convergence on function spaces directly for dependent data (see, e.g., Yu, 1994 for beta-mixing and Vidyasagar, 2005 for alpha-mixing), we choose the parametric covering framework which is less abstract and easier to understand, and demonstrates the convergence rates more clearly. The result of such a formulation is that a reader with an elementary background on probability and real analysis can follow the development easily, and arrive at such advanced results as the convergence rates with high dimensional variable selection. Although the formulation is deliberately elementary, the results are powerful enough to handle such complicated dependent situations as the sign prediction for an ARX process with GARCH error in Section 5.

In comparison, our method addresses the three aspects (unboundedness, dependence, high dimensionality) simultaneously with a relative simple approach. While the additional references can sometimes handle one aspect better, they typically do not address the other aspects in the same time. For example, McDiarmid (1998, e.g., Theorem 3.8) can potentially handle data that are dependent 'in multi-dimensions' (such as random graph or spatial dependence), while our method only addresses 'one-dimensional' dependence (i.e., a time series). On the other hand, McDiarmid's method also requires bounded differences which would require some kind of boundedness (e.g., bounded summands in the case of an iid average) while we do not need this assumption. In addition, we note that the 'bad set' term bounding the probability of a large variance will often require applying a large deviation inequality again, while our triplex inequality is one in closed form. Many of these additional references do not treat dependence to the same degree of generality as the current paper. For example, traditional treatments with symmetrization and Rademaker average such as Meir and Zhang (2003) are suitable only for iid data. Ratio-type results such as Bercu, Gassiat, Rio (2002) can relax the assumption on the 'unboundedness' while proving exponential concentration for iid data, but it is not clear how this can be extended to general dependent situations. The chaining technique described in, for example, van de Geer (2000, Section 3.2) and Bousquet, Boucheron and Lugosi (2003, Section 5) may be used to improve the convergence rate by a log n factor in the finite dimensional case. However, most applications of this technique are for independent data or martingales. Our dependence term, on the other hand, is put in the framework of mixingale, which is more general than martingales as discussed in Remark 4. A second experiment applies the DMOZ topic ontology to the problem of website categorization from brief webpage descriptions, with classification targets spanning either 575 intermediate-level (L2) leaf topics or 7100 fine-grained (L3) leaf topics. This scale of classification presents a formidable computational challenge, since conventional multiclass systems require O(Ml) memory proportional to both the number of classes M and the feature dimension l--a requirement that becomes prohibitively expensive as ontology size increases. To overcome this computational barrier, the researchers employ joint hashing of features and labels, producing an efficient shared representation that circumvents the scaling limitations inherent in conventional approaches. By projecting both feature vectors and class labels into a common lower-dimensional hash space, this method maintains the discriminative capacity required for accurate categorization while dramatically reducing memory requirements. The joint hashing strategy substantially improves both memory efficiency and practical feasibility compared to feature-only hashing or naive multiclass baselines. To evaluate the approach comprehensively, the researchers assess performance across multiple classification algorithms and taxonomic levels. The evaluation employs both K Nearest Neighbor (KNN) and Kmeans clustering, comparing results at the L2 and L3 hierarchy levels to understand how joint hashing performs across different algorithmic paradigms on the DMOZ categorization task. The big drawback with string kernels using suffix arrays/trees is that they require large amounts of working memory. Approximately a factor of 50 additional storage is required for processing and analysis. Moreover, updates to a weighted combination are costly. This makes it virtually impossible to apply (4) to millions of documents. Even for modest document lengths this would require Terabytes of RAM. Hashing offers a way out of this predicament. A document is typically a very sparse object: out of the full space of possible terms, only a small number take non-zero values. Hashing exploits this by touching only those non-zero entries, so the reduction in dimensionality can be carried out in a single pass over the document. Each term is mapped directly to a coordinate of the lower-dimensional feature vector, and no auxiliary structure such as a suffix array or tree needs to be built along the way. The resulting vector can be stored as the output of a preprocessing step, which means the source document itself can be discarded once the vector has been computed. Nothing about the original text has to remain in memory while the kernel is later evaluated. A useful property of this construction is that the hash function spreads the features uniformly across the coordinates of the resulting feature vector, so no region of the space is systematically overloaded. The same idea can be used in an analogous fashion to obtain reliable estimates for TF/IDF reweighting, without having to keep exact per-term statistics around for the whole collection. The overall consequence is that the preprocessing stage is about as memory efficient as the kernel computation phase itself. Instead of paying a factor of 50 in additional storage, we keep only a compact vector per document, which makes it realistic to handle millions of documents rather than requiring terabytes of RAM.

Errors in conditional independence (CI) testing and V-structure identification can undermine the RAI algorithm at multiple stages. A mistaken CI result may lead to an incorrect edge removal, while a misidentified V-structure can prompt an erroneous edge orientation. Because later decisions build on the graph produced by earlier stages, these mistakes can propagate, leaving the algorithm to assess or orient edges using an already distorted structure. Constraint-based algorithms are especially vulnerable when limited data must support tests with oversized conditioning sets. Such sets may include nodes introduced through earlier errors, and the resulting dimensionality problems can make dependence difficult to estimate reliably. As these inaccuracies accumulate, the inferred graph becomes less faithful to the underlying structure, which in turn weakens the resulting model's ability to support accurate inference. Although CI-testing in the PC algorithm is more stable than V-structure identification (Spirtes et al., 2000), it is difficult to say whether this is also the case in the RAI algorithm. Being recursive, the RAI algorithm might be more unstable. However, CI test errors are practically less likely to occur, since by alternating between CI testing and edge direction the algorithm uses knowledge about parent-child relations before CI testing of higher orders. This knowledge permits avoiding some of the tests and decreases the size of conditions sets of some other tests (see Lemma 1). In addition, graph decomposition promotes decisions about well-founded orders of node presentation for subsequent CI tests, contrary to the common arbitrary order of presentation (see, e.g., the PC algorithm). Both mechanisms enhance stability and provide some means of error correction, as will be demonstrated shortly.

Similarly to Spirtes et al. (2000), we use the notion of stability informally to measure the number of errors in the output of a stage of the algorithm due to errors in the input to this stage. Similarly to the PC algorithm, the main sources of errors of the RAI algorithm are CI-testing and the identification of V-structures. Removal of an edge due to an erroneous CI test may lead to failure in correctly removing other edges, which are not in the true graph and also cause to orientation errors. Failure to remove an edge due to an erroneous CI test may prevent, or wrongly cause, orientation of edges. Missing or wrongly identifying a V-structure affect the orientation of other edges in the graph during the inductive stage and subsequent stages. Many CI test errors (i.e., deciding that (in)dependence exists where it does not) in CB algorithms are the result of unnecessary large condition sets given a limited database size (Spirtes et al., 2000). Large condition sets are more likely to be inaccurate, since they are more likely to include unnecessary and erroneous nodes (erroneous due to errors in earlier stages of the algorithm). These sets may also cause poorer estimation of the criterion that measures dependence (e.g., CMI or χ 2 ) due to the curse-of-dimensionality, as typically there are only too few instances representing some of the combinations of node states. Either way, these condition sets are responsible for many wrong decisions about whether dependence between two nodes exists or not. Consequently, these errors cause structural inaccuracies and hence also poor inference ability. Although CI-testing in the PC algorithm is more stable than V-structure identification (Spirtes et al., 2000), it is difficult to say whether this is also the case in the RAI algorithm. Being recursive, the RAI algorithm might be more unstable. However, CI test errors are practically less likely to occur, since by alternating between CI testing and edge direction the algorithm uses knowledge about parent-child relations before CI testing of higher orders. This knowledge permits avoiding some of the tests and decreases the size of conditions sets of some other tests (see Lemma 1). Both mechanisms enhance stability and provide some means of error correction, as will be demonstrated shortly.

Most CB algorithms, such as Inductive Causation (IC) (Pearl, 2000), PC (Spirtes et al., 2000) and Three Phase Dependency Analysis (TPDA) (Cheng et al., 1997), construct a DAG in two consecutive stages. The first stage is learning associations between variables for constructing an undirected structure. This requires a number of CI tests growing exponentially with the number of nodes. This complexity is reduced in the PC algorithm to polynomial complexity by fixing the maximal number of parents a node can have and in the TPDA algorithm by measuring the strengths of the independences computed while CI testing along with making a strong assumption about the underlying graph (Cheng et al., 1997). The TPDA algorithm does not take direct steps to restrict the size of the condition set employed in CI testing in order to mitigate the curse-of-dimensionality. In the second stage, most CB algorithms direct edges by employing orientation rules in two consecutive steps: finding and directing V-structures and directing additional edges inductively (Pearl, 2000). Edge direction (orientation) is unstable. This means that small errors in the input to the stage (i.e., CI testing) yield large errors in the output (Spirtes et al., 2000). Errors in CI testing are usually the result of large condition sets. These sets, selected based on previous CI test results, are more likely to be incorrect due to their size, and they also lead, for a small sample size, to poorer estimation of dependences due to the curse-of-dimensionality. Thus, we usually start learning using CI tests of low order (i.e., using small condition sets), which are the most reliable tests (Spirtes et al., 2000). We further note that the division of learning in CB algorithms into two consecutive stages is mainly for simplicity, since no directionality constraints have to be propagated during the first stage. However, errors in CI testing is a main reason for the instability of CB algorithms, which we set out to tackle in this research. The Recursive Autonomy Identification (RAI) algorithm addresses this instability by learning Bayesian network structure through a sequence of conditional independence (CI) tests, edge orientations, and recursive decompositions. Rather than treating these operations as isolated stages, RAI uses the results of each step to identify autonomous sub-structures and continue learning within them. This recursive process lets the algorithm refine the network while limiting how errors in one part of the structure affect the rest. RAI also orders CI tests by their reliability, beginning with tests that use smaller condition sets, and reduces condition set sizes as learning proceeds. These choices target the sources of error described above: large sets are harder to estimate accurately, especially with limited data, and can make edge orientation unstable. By prioritizing more reliable tests and keeping the conditioning burden smaller, the algorithm aims to improve both computational efficiency and the accuracy of the learned structure. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world databases compared RAI with eight other structure-learning algorithms, including the PC algorithm, greedy hill-climbing with tabu search, and naive Bayesian approaches. Across the reported comparisons, RAI achieved superior structural correctness and complexity, along with better runtime and classification accuracy. These results indicate that recursive decomposition and reliability-guided testing can improve the practical performance of Bayesian network structure learning.

When we look at the learning methods known to be consistent, we can separate them into two general types. In the first of these we have methods that are defined in a local manner, for example, the k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) classifier (Stone, 1977; Devroye et al., 1996). The k-NN classifier guesses the class of a point x based on its nearest neighbors in the training set, thus, this classifier behaves in a 'local' way: only close-by points affect the estimate. More generally, by a locallybehaving method we mean one that, given a training set S n and a point x at which to estimate the value of y, in some way treats the close-by part of the training set as the most important. A second type of consistent learning method is defined in a global manner, for example, support vector machines (see Vapnik, 1998; Steinwart, 2002, for a description and proof of consistency, respectively). It is not clear from the definition of support vector machines whether they behave locally or not: The separating hyperplane is determined based on the entire training set S n , and furthermore does not depend on the specific point x at which we classify, perhaps leading us to expect that support vector machines do not behave locally. Thus, on an intuitive level we might think that some consistent methods behave locally and some do not. However, this intuitive reasoning overlooks a fundamental requirement imposed by consistency itself. For a learning method to achieve consistency--to converge to the true underlying relationship as the training set grows infinitely large--it must necessarily concentrate its modeling capacity where the data is most informative. Methods defined in global terms, such as support vector machines, support vector regression, and boosting algorithms, cannot rely on distant points to shape their local predictions without sacrificing their ability to adapt to the true structure. The mathematical properties that guarantee consistency force these seemingly global methods to behave locally in practice: the separating hyperplane in SVMs must be increasingly determined by points near the decision boundary, the regression function must be shaped primarily by neighboring observations, and the ensemble in boosting must focus on difficult nearby instances. This principle is not merely an intuitive observation but a necessity emerging from the statistical requirements of convergence. The same logic extends across all consistent estimation methods within both classification and regression domains. Support vector regression, kernel ridge regression, orthogonal series estimation, and artificial neural networks--despite their formal global definitions and dependence on the entire training set--must fundamentally operate as local methods when properly regularized to achieve consistency. The weights assigned by these methods to training examples necessarily diminish with distance from the point of estimation, whether this localization emerges explicitly through bandwidth selection in kernel methods, implicitly through the capacity constraints in neural networks, or through the regularization parameters in ridge-type estimators. Thus, the apparent dichotomy between locally-defined and globally-defined consistent methods dissolves upon closer examination: all methods that achieve statistical consistency must exhibit local behavior as a prerequisite for their success, making localization not a choice of definition but an inevitable consequence of the fundamental goal of learning from finite data.

In the area of regression, our results show that neural network estimators, orthogonal series estimators, etc., must behave locally if they are consistent, again, despite their being defined in a way that does not indicate such behavior.

The concept of localizability in support vector machines carries significant theoretical and practical importance, as it characterizes a fundamental property of learning methods: the ability to achieve consistent results when restricting computation to subsets of nearby training data. This property proves crucial for understanding the interplay between theoretical consistency guarantees and practical applicability, since many real-world scenarios benefit from considering only local information rather than processing the entire training set. Localizability thus directly connects asymptotic learning guarantees with finite-sample computational efficiency, serving as a bridge between idealized theoretical frameworks and implementable algorithms that must operate within computational constraints. Beyond its theoretical significance, localizability offers distinct practical advantages when implementing local learning strategies. While alternative frameworks for examining local learning behavior exist--particularly those that evaluate the influence of distant training points through reweighting rather than removal--localizability provides a more direct approach to designing and analyzing local learning algorithms. By focusing on which training examples actually contribute to decisions in localized regions of the input space, practitioners can develop methods that exploit this structure for computational gains without sacrificing performance guarantees. This direct relevance to practical algorithm design makes localizability a particularly valuable framework for extending machine learning approaches beyond the constraints of global methods. Previous work related to localizability has been done in the context of learning methods that work by minimizing a loss function: We can 'localize' the loss function by re-weighting it so that close-by points are more influential; this has been investigated in the context of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM; Vapnik, 1998) (Bottou and Vapnik, 1992; Vapnik and Bottou, 1993), as well as in the specific case of linear regression (see, e.g., Cleveland and Loader, 1995, and references therein); this approach has also lead to various applications (Atkeson et al., 1997). In this paper we differ from these approaches in that we work in a more general context: Our approach is applicable to all learning methods, and not just those that are based on minimizing a loss function that can be re-weighted. Another difference is that we consider consistency in the sense of asymptotically arriving at the lowest possible loss achievable by any measurable function, and not in the sense of minimizing the loss within a set of finite VC dimension.

Aside from this main motivation for investigating localizability, another reason is that it allows us to answer questions such as, "What might happen if we localize a support vector machine?" That is, we can apply a support vector machine (or some other useful method) to only the closeby part of the training set, perhaps motivated by the fact that training on this smaller set is more computationally efficient, at least if all we need is to generate estimates at a small number of points. If support vector machines are localizable, then we in fact know that such an approach can be consistent; and if they are not localizable, then we may end up with a non-consistent method with poor performance. Thus, localizability can have practical applications. Note that one can consider other ways to define local behaviour than localizability. In one such approach, we can evaluate the behavior of a method when altering the far-off part of the training set, as opposed to removing it (which is what we do with localizability). Work along those lines (Zakai and Ritov, 2008) arrives at similar conclusions to the ones presented here. In 1997 the decision was taken to redesign WEKA from scratch and to rebuild it in Java. The earlier system had come to depend on several different graphical libraries, and keeping them all working together was becoming steadily harder to sustain. Java looked like a way out of that bind, and the case for it was strengthened by the experience of one member of the team, who had already used the language successfully to prototype machine learning algorithms. Java's inherent portability was an obvious attraction, since the same code could run on different platforms without the repeated adaptation the old arrangement demanded. The team also already had repositories of code for reading and processing data in WEKA's own format, which gave them a solid base of existing work to carry across into the new environment instead of starting from nothing. Development gathered pace when the system's creators taught a machine learning course at the University of Calgary in 1997. Teaching the course gave the work a concrete purpose and a practical deadline, and it pushed the new platform toward being something that students could actually use. The result was a functioning system, initially called JAWS, that by the end of 1998 brought together a diverse collection of classification methods, analytical tools, and filtering capabilities. It was renamed WEKA in 1999, the same year that attribute selection functionality was added, extending the toolkit beyond learning and preprocessing to include the choice of which attributes a model should be built from. Work began on the first edition of the Data Mining book in 1997, based on earlier notes for Witten's courses at the University of Waikato, and a proposal was submitted to Morgan Kaufmann late that year. It finally appeared in 1999 (though for reasons that are not clear to us the official publication date is 2000). WEKA was seen as an important adjunct to the book, and the original title, Practical machine learning, was changed to Data Mining: Practical machine learning tools and techniques with Java to reflect this. The term "data mining" was prepended primarily for marketing reasons. The WEKA software described in that edition was command-line oriented and the book makes no mention of a graphical user interface, for which design began in 1999. By the time the second edition appeared in 2005 the interactive versions of WEKA--the Explorer, Experimenter, and Knowledge Flow interface--were mature and well-tested pieces of software.

Because of dependencies on other libraries, mainly related to the graphical user interfaces, the software became increasingly unwieldy and hard to maintain. In 1997 work began on reimplementing WEKA from scratch in Java into what we now term WEKA 3. One of the authors, Eibe Frank, had earlier decided to adopt Java to implement algorithm prototypes, abandoning C++ because Java development was rapid and debugging was dramatically simplified. This positive experience, the promise of platform independence through virtual machine technology, and the fact that, as part of the research code, classes for reading WEKA's standard ARFF file format into appropriate data structures already existed, led to the decision to re-write WEKA in Java. WEKA's sustained success depended on maintaining a small, stable core development team, supported by New Zealand government research funding from the Foundation for Research, Science and Technology between 1993 and 2007. This continuity provided a basis for developing and maintaining the software over an extended period, with accumulated knowledge of the framework informing subsequent work. The development effort combined long-term academic staff with full-time research programmers and students participating through contractual or study-based arrangements. These different forms of involvement allowed contributions to individual methods and components to proceed alongside the continuing work of maintaining the system as a whole. The project also benefited from contributions from the wider community, including algorithm implementations and patches to the framework. Such contributions extended the development effort beyond the core team, bringing additional methods into consideration and helping to address problems in existing code. Incorporating them nevertheless required attention to how each change fitted into the software: an implementation had to be assessed in relation to the existing framework, while a patch had to be considered for its effects on other components. Community participation therefore complemented the continuity provided by the core developers, with the inclusion of contributed work remaining a matter of careful review. The project has always had a policy of maintaining close control of what became part of the software. Only a handful of developers have ever had write access to the source code repository. The drawback of this policy is reduced functionality; the advantages are improved code quality, ease of maintenance, and greater coherence for both developer and end user. When new algorithm implementations were considered for inclusion, we generally insisted on a backing publication describing the new method. In a few cases we have rejected submitted code, despite publication, when our experiments revealed that the method did not appear to improve on what was already present in WEKA.

The problem of learning from multiple tasks has been the subject of a number of recently published papers. In Evgeniou et al. (2005) a batch multitask learning problem is defined as a regularized optimization problem and the notion of multitask kernel is introduced. More specifically, they consider a regularized functional that encodes multitask relations over tasks, thus biasing the solution of the problem towards functions that lie close to each other. Argyriou et al. (2007, 2008) build on this formalization to simultaneously learn a multitask classifier and the underlying spectral dependencies among tasks. A similar model but under cluster-based assumptions is investigated in Jacob et al. (2009). A different approach is discussed in Ando and Zhang (2005) where a structural risk minimization method is presented and multitask relations are established by enforcing predictive functions for the different tasks to belong to the same hypothesis set. Complexity results for multitask learning under statistical assumptions are also given in Maurer (2006). Online multitask learning has also been studied under several interaction protocols. In settings based on prediction with expert advice, a single task is addressed at each timestep, and the learner selects a prediction for that task using the advice available to it. The sequence of interactions therefore determines which task receives feedback at a given step, while information accumulated across tasks can inform subsequent predictions. In simultaneous protocols, by contrast, the learner must select actions for all tasks at every step. These selections may be subject to joint constraints, so that the admissibility of an action for one task depends on the actions chosen for the others. The protocol thus determines both how feedback is obtained and how decisions across tasks are coupled. A central distinction among these approaches concerns the mechanism used to relate the tasks. Some methods employ a common loss function that aggregates task-specific losses and gives priority to particular tasks, making their relative importance explicit in the learning objective. Other methods exploit cross-task information through regularization, encouraging related predictors to share structure so that experience on one task can accelerate learning on another. These mechanisms address different aspects of the problem: a shared loss specifies how performance across tasks is evaluated, whereas regularization specifies how information is transferred among their predictors. The analysis can therefore be extended to combine the two, yielding an approach in which a common loss expresses task priorities and a regularization term incorporates relations across tasks.

Regret bounds are given under the assumption that the set of best experts for the K tasks is small, as a way to formalize task similarity. Whereas these studies consider a multitask protocol in which a single task is acted upon at each time step (what we call in this paper the adversarially chosen task protocol), the work of Lugosi et al. (2009) investigates the problem where an action for each task must be chosen at every step. The relatedness among tasks is captured by imposing restrictions on the joint action chosen at each step. Online linear multitask algorithms for the simultaneous task setting have been studied in Dekel et al. (2007), where the separate learning tasks are collectively dealt with through a common multitask loss. Their approach, however, is fundamentally different from the one considered here. In fact, using a common loss function has more the effect of prioritizing certain tasks over the others, whereas our regularized approach hopes to benefit from the information provided by each task to speed up the learning process for the other ones. Nonetheless, it is not difficult to extend our analysis to consider a more sophisticated notion of multitask loss (see Remark 12 in Section 6.2), thus effectively obtaining a shared loss regularized multitask algorithm.

Contemporary machine learning increasingly confronts problems where multiple related classification tasks must be learned simultaneously. While training independent classifiers for each task remains a straightforward approach, doing so fails to capture and exploit the inherent connections between related objectives. To address this limitation, we introduce a matrix-based multitask extension of the p-norm Perceptron algorithm that unifies the learning of K tasks within a single framework. This algorithmic innovation achieves a performance improvement factor of K relative to the baseline strategy of maintaining K independent classifiers, providing both theoretical justification and practical motivation for adopting a multitask perspective. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on text categorization problems, examining its effectiveness on topic detection and spam filtering tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed multitask Perceptron algorithm consistently outperforms standard baseline methods across these benchmark tasks. The improvements are particularly pronounced when the classification tasks are naturally related, underscoring the value of the multitask learning framework. These empirical findings establish the significant practical potential of our algorithm for real-world applications involving multiple interconnected learning objectives. This work is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce notation and formally define the adversarially chosen task protocol. The multitask Perceptron algorithm is presented in Section 3 where we also discuss the role of the multitask feature map and show (Section 4) that it can be used to turn online classifiers into multitask classifiers. We detail the matrix-based approach to the simultaneous multitask learning framework in Section 5. Section 6 is devoted to the theoretical analysis of a general potential-based algorithm for this setup. We conclude the paper with a number of experiments establishing the empirical effectiveness of our algorithms (Section 7).

On the experimental side, we give evidence that our multitask algorithms provide a significant advantage over common baselines. The work presented in this paper is motivated by the analysis of functional brain imaging signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG). EEG is measured across time and typically at multiple scalp locations, providing a spatio-temporal data set of the underlying neural activity. In addition, these measurements are often taken over multiple repetitions or trials, where trials may differ in the type of stimulus presented, the task given to the subject, or the subject's response. Analysis of these signals is often expressed as a single-trial classification problem. The goal for the classifier is to determine from the EEG data which stimulus was presented or how the subject responded. Many of these classification techniques were originally developed in the context of Brain Computer Interfaces (BCI) but are now more widely used to interpret activity associated with neural processing. In its original setting, a brain-computer interface extracts command signals from neural activity recorded trial by trial. For severely paralyzed individuals, such a system can provide a means of controlling a computer and so of communicating with the world. The same machinery has also been proposed for healthy users, where decoding the operator's neural state can support efficiency gains in cognitively intensive occupations. In both cases, the central technical problem is the one described above: given a single trial of multichannel recordings, decide which of several conditions it came from. Linear discriminant methods have proven especially well suited to this problem, because they yield a compact, interpretable mapping from high-dimensional spatio-temporal data to a single decision variable. Discriminant analysis, however, is more than a engineering tool for building working interfaces. It also serves as a research framework for understanding how patterns of neural activity relate to behavioral outcomes. By identifying the features in the neural data that best distinguish between experimental conditions, the approach improves the quality of the brain measurements themselves, since components of the signal that do not carry condition-related information can be suppressed. The learned discriminant weights also indicate where on the scalp, and in which temporal windows, condition-specific neural responses arise. Because the discriminant output is available for every trial, it can further be compared against behavior, showing how variations in performance correspond to variations in the underlying neural signal. In this sense, discriminant analysis is an important addition to the quantitative methods available in neuroscience research, and it motivates the developments presented in the remainder of this paper.

We now present an incomplete set of rules that constitutes an exact context-based feature grammar (CBFG) for a context-sensitive language L. We do not list every rule, since the omitted ones follow the same pattern as those shown and add nothing to the argument. The fragment is enough to show how the grammar works and why it is exact. To show that L is not context-free, we intersect it with a suitable regular language. Context-free languages are closed under intersection with regular languages, so if L were context-free, the intersection would be too. The intersection turns out to be an instance of the MIX language, the set of strings over {a, b, c} containing equal numbers of each symbol, which is known not to be context-free. L therefore cannot be context-free either, and the grammar below defines a language outside that class. The exactness of the grammar comes from the contexts we chose for each sublanguage. We selected them so that the sublanguages stay distinct from one another: no string is assigned to two sublanguages through a shared context, and so no feature is attributed to a string that does not properly have it. This lets us reason about each sublanguage separately. We also need every substring to receive the right features. When we derive any substring, the union of all its possible derivations generates every correct feature and nothing else. No derivation introduces an incorrect feature, and no correct feature is missed, because some derivation always supplies it. Together these two properties make the grammar exact, so the feature set it computes for a substring matches the contexts in which that substring can actually occur in L. Note that the MIX language on its own is not definable by an exact CBFG: it is only when other parts of the language can distributionally define the appropriate partial structures that we can get context sensitive languages. Far from being a limitation of this formalism (a bug), we argue this is a feature: it is only in rather exceptional circumstances that we will get properly context sensitive languages. This formalism thus potentially accounts not just for the existence of non context-free natural languages but also for their rarity.

A central aim of this paper is to connect established techniques for grammar learning with the representational frameworks required for natural language processing. We study learnable models for structured context-free languages, where a grammar must capture not only which strings belong to a language but also the structure that makes those strings composable. This setting makes representation a central concern: the form in which grammatical information is expressed determines what a learner can infer from examples and how that information can be used in subsequent processing. Our approach rests on reformulating the learning problem in a more effective representational space. By choosing a representation aligned with the structure of the language, a task that appears computationally difficult can become manageable. This illustrates a broader principle in machine learning: progress may come not from making the same problem-solving procedure more powerful, but from finding a representation in which the relevant structure is easier to learn. To make this principle concrete, we introduce a rich grammatical formalism, which we call Contextual Binary Feature Grammars (CBFG). The contributions of this paper are as follows: we present in Section 3 a rich grammatical formalism, which we call Contextual Binary Feature Grammars (CBFG). This grammar formalism is defined using a set of contexts which play the role of features with a strict semantics attached to these features. Though not completely original, since it is closely related to a number of other formalisms such as Range Concatenation Grammars (Boullier, 2000), it is of independent interest. We consider then the case when the contextual features assigned to a string correspond to the contexts that the string can occur in, in the language defined by the grammar. When this property holds, we call it an exact CBFG. The crucial point here is that for languages that can be defined by an exact CBFG, the underlying structure of the representation relies on intrinsic properties of the language easily observable on samples by looking at context sets.

This is the objective of the approach introduced in this article: for the first time, we can bridge the gap between theoretically well founded grammatical inference methods and the sorts of structured representations required for modeling natural languages. There is a certain lack of flexibility associated with the composite likelihood framework as each likelihood object is either selected or not for the entire sample X (1) , . . . , X (n) . There is no allowance for some objects to be selected more frequently than others. For example, available computational resources may allow the computation of the log-likelihood for 20% of the samples, and the pseudo likelihood for the remaining 80%. In the case of composite likelihood if we select the full likelihood component (or the pseudo likelihood or any other likelihood object) then this component is applied to all samples indiscriminately. The stochastic composite likelihood addresses this limitation by moving the selection of likelihood components from the level of the whole data set to the level of the individual sample. Rather than committing to one component for all of X^(1), ..., X^(n), each sample is assigned a component through a random mechanism, so that a given component is applied to some samples and not to others. The simplest version is non-coordinated selection, in which the assignment for each sample is drawn independently of the others. This is easy to implement and gives the practitioner direct control over how often each component is used, for example computing the full log-likelihood on roughly 20% of the samples and the pseudo likelihood on the remaining 80%. Its weakness is that independent draws offer no protection against waste: the same component may be assigned to a given sample more than once, so that computation is spent redundantly while other components are left unused. Coordinated selection removes this problem by drawing the assignments jointly, so that once a component has been assigned to a sample, it is not assigned to that sample again. The available budget is then spread across distinct components, and each sample contributes distinct information. The stochastic formulation also has a practical advantage over the discrete alternative. If one tried to decide which component should be used on which sample by explicit discrete selection, the problem would become a hard combinatorial optimization, since the number of possible assignments grows rapidly with the sample size and the number of components, and no convenient structure is available to exploit. Parameterizing the selection probabilities continuously avoids this difficulty. The selection mechanism is described by a set of continuous parameters, and the objective can be optimized over them with standard iterative procedures rather than by search over discrete configurations. A continuous parameterization also makes the behavior of the optimization amenable to analysis, so that questions of convergence can be posed and answered with familiar tools. In this sense, the stochastic approach gains both the flexibility that the composite likelihood framework lacks and a formulation that remains tractable to optimize.

Training an SVM requires solving a quadratic optimization problem of dimensionality dependent on the cardinality of the training set. The resulting linear SVM discriminant depends on a subset of elements from the training set, known as support vectors (SVs). In a distributed setting, two broad approaches have been proposed to preserve the advantages of SVM classification. Incremental methods train classifiers across networked nodes and a fusion center, exchanging support vectors so that each participant can incorporate information learned elsewhere. Through repeated updates, these methods can move toward the performance of a classifier trained centrally. That process generally requires multiple exchanges to converge, however, and performance guarantees hold only under specific conditions. Parallel methods instead divide the training data into subsets, train partial SVMs on those subsets, and combine the resulting classifiers at a central processor. This avoids the same iterative exchange of support vectors, but the combined classifier is not guaranteed to converge to the centralized solution for arbitrary data partitions. More generally, distributed systems can approximate centralized classifier performance, but cannot ensure it without continued support-vector updates or data partitions favorable to the combination process.

Web-based information extraction often relies on limited training data, which restricts the robustness of Markov Random Field (MRF) models. With relatively few labeled examples, a model may struggle to resolve ambiguous tokens from their local context alone, producing inconsistent predictions across related instances. Researchers have addressed this limitation by introducing long-range associative dependencies between repeated occurrences of a token. These dependencies encourage consistent labeling, allowing evidence available in one occurrence to inform predictions for others through collective inference. Prior approaches to collective inference can be divided into two broad categories according to how they represent these associative dependencies. The first defines separate potentials over inter-instance edges, connecting token occurrences across otherwise distinct extraction instances. Each potential expresses a preference for compatible labels at the endpoints of its edge, supplementing the dependencies within each instance. Because these additional connections complicate inference in the resulting model, such approaches employ approximation algorithms, including Loopy Belief Propagation and Gibbs sampling, to infer labels collectively. The second category defines potentials over cliques of repeated token occurrences, expressing their labeling preferences jointly rather than through separate inter-instance edges. This representation allows an associative potential to evaluate the labels assigned across a group of repetitions as a whole. Inference in these models has been pursued through local search methods, such as Iterative Conditional Mode fitting, as well as two-stage algorithms. Although the two categories share the goal of improving extraction through consistent labeling, they differ in both the form of their associative potentials and the procedures used to accommodate those potentials during inference. These differences motivate a common representation in which the underlying extraction components and their associative dependencies can be treated within a single framework. This paper unifies various collective extraction tasks with different forms of associative potentials under a single framework. We do this by employing a cluster graph representation of the collective model. Figure 1(e) illustrates the cluster graph for our toy example. The cluster graph comprises of one cluster per MRF-instance, and one cluster per clique with its corresponding associative potential. As in the traditional collective extraction models, we assume that a clique comprises of all the occurrences of a particular token. We emphasize that instead of clusters for chain models, the framework can also define clusters for any tractable component, such as a bipartite matching or an alignment, but since our interest is in IE tasks, we shall focus on chain models. Collective inference in our model then simply corresponds to message passing in this cluster graph. This view of collective inference offers several advantages over earlier approaches. First, it allows us to plug in and study various clique potentials cleanly under the same cluster message passing umbrella. Second, it allows us to exploit special properties of the associative potentials to design combinatorial algorithms that are both more accurate and more efficient than existing algorithms. Specifically, we show that most associative potentials used in practice are symmetric clique potentials. Symmetric clique potentials are invariant under any permutation of their arguments. So the value of a symmetric potential depends only on the counts of its distinct arguments, and not their position in the clique. For example in Figure 1(d), the clique potential on 'Iraq' would give a low score if its end vertices had different labels, regardless of which 'Iraq' vertex gets what label. We present three families of symmetric clique potentials that capture label associativity in different ways-- MAX , SUM (which subsumes the popular Potts potential), and MAJORITY . The most crucial component of the collective inference problem is then to efficiently compute outgoing messages from clique clusters governed by symmetric potentials. We denote this sub-problem as clique inference.

However these setups are characterized by limited training data, which restricts the robustness of the resulting MRFs during deployment. One promising way to increase the robustness of MRFs during deployment is to strengthen the first-order dependencies of the model with extra long-range dependencies , resulting in more robust labelings. The goal of this paper is to exploit long-range dependencies in a principled manner. There has been a lot of work on capturing long-range dependencies between labels of nonadjacent words. This typically includes dependencies of the form--if a token repeats in a document, then the labels of the repetitions should ideally be the same (Sutton and McCallum, 2004; Bunescu and Mooney, 2004; Krishnan and Manning, 2006; Finkel et al., 2005). In Figure 1(d), we show an example where the extra dotted edges join unigram recurrences. Such long-range dependencies are termed associative since they introduce positive couplings between labels of token pairs. Apart from textual tokens, associative dependencies have also been exploited while labeling documents (Lu and Getoor, 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 1998), image pixels (Taskar et al., 2004), and annotating Web documents (Kulkarni et al., 2009). Coupling records solely through shared unigrams captures only a limited range of the regularities that can support collective labeling. Richer properties can establish associations between records even when their surface vocabularies differ, provided that those properties reflect conventions relevant to the labeling task. The choice of properties is therefore crucial: useful properties should take consistent values within an individual domain, while allowing those values to vary across domains. Such properties offer a basis for agreement among records without requiring every domain to exhibit the same textual patterns. This distinction accommodates differences in formatting and authoring style across domains. A convention that supports a particular labeling in one domain may be expressed differently in another, yet the records within each domain can still conform to a common pattern. The same symmetric potentials used for unigram cliques can consequently be applied to cliques defined by richer property values, rewarding associativity among records that share those values. The resulting coupling promotes conformance to domain-specific regularities, making the stability of the associations within a domain more important than the persistence of any particular property value across domains. Now assume that we have an array of such conformance-promoting properties, and a basic MRF trained on some labeled domains. An effective way of deploying this MRF on a previously unseen domain is by labeling the records in the new domain collectively while encouraging the individual labelings to agree on our set of properties. If the properties continue to remain associative in the unseen domain, then collective inference can be expected to correct a significant number of errors. This provides us with an inference-only approach, in contrast to many existing solutions for domain adaptation which require model re-training (Blei et al., 2002; Blitzer et al., 2006; Mann and McCallum, 2007).

Our goal is to empirically demonstrate that cluster message passing is indeed a more accurate and efficient framework for doing collective inference. Once this is established, it would necessitate the design of fast and accurate message computation algorithms that work for symmetric clique potentials. This would justify our design and analysis of the various clique inference algorithms presented in this paper. After illustrating the effectiveness of cluster message passing, we will show that the extension of collective inference to capture richer associative properties leads to significant boosts in domain adaptation tasks. Keeping these goals in mind, we present results of three different experiments--clique inference, collective inference, and the extension to general Markovian properties. We begin our empirical evaluation in Section 7.1 by assessing the performance of clique inference algorithms across both computational speed and accuracy of maximum a posteriori (MAP) assignments. Our experiments span a range of symmetric clique potential types, comparing the α-pass algorithm against established alternatives including iterative conditional maximization and linear programming-based methods. The results demonstrate that α-pass achieves MAP accuracy that is comparable to these competing approaches while exhibiting substantially higher computational efficiency; across all tested potential configurations, α-pass completes inference significantly faster than either baseline method. This finding validates our earlier emphasis on the necessity of developing fast and accurate algorithms for message computation on symmetric clique potentials. We extend this evaluation in Section 7.2 to examine collective inference by comparing message passing on cluster graphs against alternative frameworks for joint inference. Specifically, we benchmark the cluster message passing approach against belief propagation algorithms applied to Potts potentials and stacking-based methods designed for linear MAJORITY potentials. These experiments provide direct empirical validation of the accuracy and computational advantages of cluster message passing within the collective inference setting, establishing strong evidence that this framework indeed offers both improved performance and efficiency for joint inference tasks. The results thus justify the algorithmic development presented in this paper and set the stage for investigating how incorporating richer associative properties can further enhance inference accuracy in domain adaptation scenarios.

Probabilistic graphical models (Pearl, 1988) are a framework for representing a complex joint distribution over a set of n random variables X = {X 1 . . . X n }. A qualitative graph encodes probabilistic independencies between the variables and implies a decomposition of the joint distribution into a product of local terms: P( X ) = ∏ ψ i (C i ), Z i where C i are subsets of X defined by the cliques of the graph structure and ψ i (C i ) are the quantitative parameters (potential functions) that define the distribution. Computing marginal probabilities and likelihood in graphical models are critical tasks needed both for making predictions and to facilitate learning. Obtaining exact answers to these inference queries is often infeasible even for relatively modest problems. Thus, there is a growing need for inference methods that are both efficient and can provide reasonable approximate computations. Despite few theoretical guarantees, the Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP, Pearl, 1988) algorithm has gained significant popularity in the last two decades due to impressive empirical success, and is now being used in a wide range of applications ranging from transmission decoding to image segmentation (Murphy and Weiss, 1999; McEliece et al., 1998; Shental et al., 2003). Recently there has been an explosion in practical and theoretical interest in propagation based inference methods, and a range of improvements to the convergence behavior and approximation quality of the basic algorithms have been suggested (Wainwright et al., 2003; Wiegerinck and Heskes, 2003; Elidan et al., 2006; Meshi et al., 2009). FastInf provides a framework for approximate inference in large-scale discrete graphical models. It implements propagation-based methods alongside alternatives including mean-field inference and Gibbs sampling, and its flexible representation supports both Markov random fields and template-based probabilistic relational models. This range of representations and algorithms allows the same library to address different model structures and inference needs. FastInf also supports learning model parameters through maximum-likelihood estimation with regularization, and uses the Expectation Maximization algorithm when data are missing. Its methods have been applied to challenging problems, including inference over large protein-protein networks, protein design, and object localization in images.

Spectral techniques use singular values and their associated singular vectors to reveal significant correlations in data. They are fundamental tools in machine learning, statistics, and signal processing, where high-dimensional observations often admit a more compact representation. Low-rank matrix approximation is a central example: retaining the dominant singular components captures the principal relationships encoded by a matrix while discarding less significant variation. Matrix completion poses a related but distinct question: can a low-rank matrix be recovered when only a small subset of its entries is observed? A breakthrough in this direction established that a rank-r matrix can be reconstructed exactly from a small random subset of its entries, provided that its structure is not excessively concentrated in particular rows or columns. Candès and Recht first established this result through an analysis of a convex relaxation, replacing rank minimization with nuclear-norm minimization subject to agreement with the observed entries. Candès and Tao subsequently refined the theoretical guarantees, further clarifying the conditions under which exact recovery is possible. These developments quickly prompted the design of iterative algorithms for solving the resulting convex optimization problem, turning the recovery theory into practical computational methods. In an alternative line of work, Keshavan, Montanari, and Oh (2010) attacked the same problem using a combination of spectral techniques and manifold optimization: We will refer to their algorithm as O PT S PACE . O PT S PACE is intrinsically of low complexity, the most complex operation being computing r singular values (and the corresponding singular vectors) of a sparse m × n matrix. The performance guarantees proved by Keshavan et al. (2010) are comparable with the information theoretic lower bound: roughly nr max{r, log n} random entries are needed to reconstruct M exactly (here we assume m of order n). A related approach was also developed by Lee and Bresler (2009), although without performance guarantees for matrix completion.
