The conditions on the loss function and regularizer required by output perturbation and objective perturbation are somewhat different. As Theorem 6 shows, output perturbation requires strong convexity in the regularizer and convexity as well as a bounded derivative condition in the loss function. The last condition can be replaced by a Lipschitz condition instead. However, the other two conditions appear to be required, unless we impose some further restrictions on the loss and regularizer. Objective perturbation on the other hand, requires strong convexity of the regularizer, convexity, differentiability, and bounded double derivatives in the loss function. Sometimes, it is possible to construct a differentiable approximation to the loss function, even if the loss function is not itself differentiable, as shown in Section 3.4.2. Our experimental as well as theoretical results indicate that in general, objective perturbation provides more accurate solutions than output perturbation. Thus, if the loss function satisfies the conditions of Theorem 9, we recommend using objective perturbation. In some situations, such as for SVMs, it is possible that objective perturbation does not directly apply, but applies to an approximation of the target loss function. In our experiments, the loss of statistical efficiency due to such approximation has been small compared to the loss of efficiency due to privacy, and we suspect that this is the case for many practical situations as well. Several challenges in private machine learning remain unresolved. In particular, our methods do not address regularized empirical risk minimization when the regularizer is not strongly convex, as in the case of L1-regularization. Strong convexity plays an important role in controlling the effect of changes in the training data on the solution. Without this property, an individual training point may significantly affect the optimizer, making it difficult to obtain both privacy and an accurate solution. Whether useful private solutions can be obtained under alternative assumptions, and how far the sensitivity of these problems imposes inherent limitations, remain open questions. One direction for future work is therefore to extend objective perturbation beyond strongly convex regularization to a broader class of convex optimization problems. Such an extension would require identifying conditions under which perturbing the objective provides a privacy guarantee while preserving the utility of the resulting solution. This question is relevant not only to empirical risk minimization, but also to convex optimization problems arising throughout machine learning, economics, and communications. Since these problems often involve sensitive data, understanding which features of the objective or feasible set permit accurate private optimization would broaden the applicability of the approach. A second direction is to develop more statistically efficient methods for privacy-preserving kernel-based classification. Linearization offers a way to bring kernel methods within the scope of private linear classification, but its usefulness is limited by the dimension of the required projection. Obtaining an accurate approximation may require a high-dimensional representation, whereas differential privacy constrains the accuracy attainable in such a representation. Improving this tradeoff, or developing methods that avoid the limitations of the current linearization approach, is an important open problem. It also motivates a closer examination of the statistical efficiency achievable for private classification even in the linear setting. A final question is to provide better upper and lower bounds on the sample requirement of privacy-preserving linear classification. The main open question here is to provide a computationally efficient algorithm for linear classification which has better statistical efficiency. Privacy-preserving machine learning is the endeavor of designing private analogues of widely used machine learning algorithms. We believe the present study is a starting point for further study of the differential privacy model in this relatively new subfield of machine learning. The work of Dwork et al. (2006b) set up a framework for assessing the privacy risks associated with publishing the results of data analyses. Demanding high privacy requires sacrificing utility, which in the context of classification and prediction is excess loss or regret. In this paper we demonstrate the privacyutility tradeoff for ERM, which is but one corner of the machine learning world. Applying these privacy concepts to other machine learning problems will lead to new and interesting tradeoffs and towards a set of tools for practical privacy-preserving learning and inference. We hope that our work provides a benchmark of the current price of privacy, and inspires improvements in future work.

The conditions on the loss function and regularizer required by output perturbation and objective perturbation are somewhat different. As Theorem 6 shows, output perturbation requires strong convexity in the regularizer and convexity as well as a bounded derivative condition in the loss function. The last condition can be replaced by a Lipschitz condition instead. However, the other two conditions appear to be required, unless we impose some further restrictions on the loss and regularizer. Objective perturbation on the other hand, requires strong convexity of the regularizer, convexity, differentiability, and bounded double derivatives in the loss function. Sometimes, it is possible to construct a differentiable approximation to the loss function, even if the loss function is not itself differentiable, as shown in Section 3.4.2. Our experimental as well as theoretical results indicate that in general, objective perturbation provides more accurate solutions than output perturbation. Thus, if the loss function satisfies the conditions of Theorem 9, we recommend using objective perturbation. In some situations, such as for SVMs, it is possible that objective perturbation does not directly apply, but applies to an approximation of the target loss function. In our experiments, the loss of statistical efficiency due to such approximation has been small compared to the loss of efficiency due to privacy, and we suspect that this is the case for many practical situations as well. Finally, our work does not address the question of finding private solutions to regularized ERM when the regularizer is not strongly convex. For example, neither the output perturbation, nor the objective perturbation method work for L 1 -regularized ERM. However, in L 1 -regularized ERM, one can find a data set in which a change in one training point can significantly change the solution. As a result, it is possible that such problems are inherently difficult to solve privately. An open question in this work is to extend objective perturbation methods to more general convex optimization problems. Currently, the objective perturbation method applies to strongly convex regularization functions and differentiable losses. Convex optimization problems appear in many contexts within and without machine learning: density estimation, resource allocation for communication systems and networking, social welfare optimization in economics, and elsewhere. In some cases these algorithms will also operate on sensitive or private data. Extending the ideas and analysis here to those settings would provide a rigorous foundation for privacy analysis. A second open question is to find a better solution for privacy-preserving classification with kernels. Our current method is based on a reduction to the linear case, using the algorithm of Rahimi and Recht (2008b); however, this method can be statistically inefficient, and require a lot of training data, particularly when coupled with our privacy mechanism. The reason is that the algorithm of Rahimi and Recht (2008b) requires the dimension D of the projected space to be very high for good performance. However, most differentially-private algorithms perform worse as the dimensionality of the data grows. Is there a better linearization method, which is possibly data-dependent, that will provide a more statistically efficient solution to privacy-preserving learning with kernels? A final question is to provide better upper and lower bounds on the sample requirement of privacy-preserving linear classification. The main open question here is to provide a computationally efficient algorithm for linear classification which has better statistical efficiency. A fundamental question in word sense disambiguation is how to measure similarity between word senses. The answer depends in part on the lexical resource used: WordNet organizes senses around semantic relations, whereas VerbNet foregrounds shared syntactic behavior and argument structure. A metric based on either resource alone may therefore capture one kind of resemblance while missing another. We propose instead to define similarity through combinations of lexical and syntactic context, so that relatedness reflects how senses are used as well as how they are described. We evaluated K-means and hierarchical agglomerative clustering as ways to group the senses, but neither produced adequate groupings. Many senses had too little similarity to any others to form meaningful clusters and consequently remained as singletons. This problem persisted when we varied the clustering parameters and similarity thresholds: changing the settings did not prevent substantial numbers of senses from standing alone. These results motivate a method that can leave such senses unclustered while forming cohesive groups from those that are sufficiently similar. We thus need a clustering method that gives tight clusters of word senses, and does not attempt to cluster those word senses which are not similar to any other word sense in the corpus. We do this using a "foreground-background" clustering algorithm as proposed by Kandylas et al. (2007). This algorithm gives highly cohesive clusters of word senses (the foreground) and puts all the remaining word senses in the background. The parameters that it takes as input are the % of data points to put in background (i.e., what would be the singleton clusters) and a similarity threshold which impacts the number of foreground clusters. We experimented with putting 20% and 33% data points in background and adjusted the similarity threshold to give us 50 − 100 foreground clusters. The results reported below have 20% background and 50 − 100 foreground clusters.

Finding a good similarity metric between different word senses is perhaps one of the biggest challenges that we faced. It is also the part of this section that is specific to the problem of word sense disambiguation. There are many ways in which word senses can be judged as similar, including having similar "meanings" or similar syntactic usages. Human annotated lexicons such as Levin classes (Levin, 1993), hypernyms or synonyms according to W ORD N ET (Miller, 1990; Lin, 1999), or V ERB N ET classes (Kipper et al., 2000; Schuler, 2006) capture different aspects of this similarity, as does I NFO M AP (http://infomap.stanford.edu) (Raina et al., 2006), which gives distributional similarity score for words in the corpus. We choose instead to define a similarity metric based, as described below on combinations of many different aspects of the lexical and syntactic context of the word. One might think of doing K-means clustering of the word senses based on their features, but this works poorly, as it assigns all the word senses to some cluster, while in reality, there are in practice many word senses that are not sufficiently similar to any other word sense, either semantically or syntactically and hence many word senses occur in "singleton" clusters. K-means and perhaps surprisingly, hierarchical agglomerative clustering, even after extensive use of different 'K' or thresholds, failed to give reasonable clusters. We thus need a clustering method that gives tight clusters of word senses, and does not attempt to cluster those word senses which are not similar to any other word sense in the corpus. We do this using a "foreground-background" clustering algorithm as proposed by Kandylas et al. (2007). This algorithm gives highly cohesive clusters of word senses (the foreground) and puts all the remaining word senses in the background. The parameters that it takes as input are the % of data points to put in background (i.e., what would be the singleton clusters) and a similarity threshold which impacts the number of foreground clusters. We experimented with putting 20% and 33% data points in background and adjusted the similarity threshold to give us 50 − 100 foreground clusters. The results reported below have 20% background and 50 − 100 foreground clusters.

Weka is widely regarded as the leading machine learning toolkit, and it is the natural point of comparison for any new package in this area. We do not present Waffles as a competitor to Weka. Weka already serves a large community of users well, and it would be neither practical nor useful to duplicate everything it offers. Our aim is instead for Waffles to complement it, covering areas where Weka provides little support and giving practitioners a wider set of tools to choose from. Users who rely on Weka for much of their work may therefore find Waffles a useful addition to their toolbox rather than a replacement for it. A primary strength of Waffles is its extensive range of unsupervised algorithms. This is most evident in dimensionality reduction, where Waffles implements principal component analysis (PCA), isomap, locally linear embedding, and manifold sculpting. Most of these techniques, apart from the more established ones, are not available in Weka. Waffles also implements a number of clustering algorithms and several transduction algorithms, which extend the range of problems the toolkit can address. Together, these capabilities give users of machine learning systems options that are otherwise hard to find in a single package, and they are the main reason we see the two toolkits as complementary. Waffles provides some of the most-common supervised learning techniques, such as decision trees, multi-layer neural networks, k-nearest neighbor, naive Bayes, and some less-common algorithms, such as Mean-margin trees (Gashler et al., 2008). Waffles' collection of supervised algorithms is much smaller than that of Weka, which implements more than 50 classification algorithms. Waffles, however, provides an interface that offers several advantages in many situations. For example, Weka requires the user to set up filters that convert data to types that each algorithm can handle. Waffles automatically handles type conversion when an algorithm receives a type that it is not implicitly designed to handle, while still permitting advanced users to specify custom filters. The Waffles algorithms also implicitly handle multi-dimensional labels. As some algorithm-specific examples, the Waffles implementation of multi-layer perceptron provides the ability to use a diversity of activation functions, and also supplies methods for training recurrent networks. The k-nearest neighbor algorithm automatically supports acceleration structures and sparse training data, so it is suitable for use with problems that require high scalability, such as document classification.

Generalized linear models provide a powerful and widely applicable framework for modeling relationships between covariates and response variables, yet they rely on two restrictive structural assumptions that limit their applicability to many real-world phenomena. First, the linear predictor assumption posits that all covariates influence the response through a linear combination of their values, an assumption that fails to capture the complex, sometimes nonlinear associations present in heterogeneous datasets. Second, the assumption of mean-variance independence--that the variability in responses remains constant across the covariate space--is frequently violated in practice, where heteroscedasticity emerges naturally as the conditional variance of responses changes with covariate values. These constraints, while enabling analytical tractability and interpretability, often force practitioners to accept suboptimal model fit or resort to ad-hoc transformations. To address these limitations, we propose a regression algorithm that relaxes both assumptions by modeling the conditional response distribution as a mixture of local generalized linear models, each governing a distinct region of the covariate space where data exhibit similar patterns. Within each region, the familiar GLM framework remains intact, preserving interpretability and computational efficiency; across regions, however, the algorithm constructs piecewise nonlinear mean functions by allowing the local GLM parameters to vary. This localization strategy simultaneously addresses heteroscedasticity, as the within-region variance component of each GLM can adapt to its region's characteristics, while the between-region variation in model parameters produces heterogeneous conditional variance across the entire covariate space. The method thus retains the practical advantages of generalized linear models--their flexibility in accommodating different response distributions, their statistical interpretability, and their computational scalability--while extending them to capture the complex dependencies present in real data. Implementing this approach raises a fundamental question: how many local regions should the model contain, and how should their parameters be determined? In principle, these structural choices could be fixed in advance based on domain expertise or held constant across analyses, but doing so sacrifices the adaptability that makes the approach valuable. Ideally, the data themselves should dictate both the number of local GLM components and their functional form, scaling the model's complexity in proportion to the actual signal present. A dataset exhibiting simple, smooth conditional relationships might be well-captured by just a few local models, while patterns showing complex heterogeneity or multiple modes may require substantially more components to represent accurately. The algorithmic challenge, then, is to develop an automated framework that discovers this optimal regional decomposition and functional specification without manual tuning or arbitrary structural constraints. Finally, we use a Bayesian nonparametric mixture model to let the data determine both the number and form of the local mean functions. This is critical for modeling arbitrary response distributions: complex response functions can be constructed with many local functions, while simple response functions need only a small number. Unlike frequentist nonparametric regression methods, for example, those that create a mean function for each data point, the Bayesian nonparametric approach uses only as complex a model as the data require. Moreover, it produces a generative model. It can be used to infer properties other than the mean function, such as the conditional variance or response quantiles. Thus, we develop Dirichlet process mixtures of generalized linear models (DP-GLMs), a regression tool that can model many response types and many response shapes. DP-GLMs generalize several existing Bayesian nonparametric regression models (Müller et al., 1996; Shahbaba and Neal, 2009) to a variety of response distributions. We derive Gibbs sampling algorithms for fitting and predicting with DP-GLMs. We investigate some asymptotic properties, including weak consistency of the joint density estimate and consistency of the regression estimate. We study DP-GLMs with several types of data. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the current research on Bayesian nonparametric regression and discuss how the DP-GLM extends this field. In Section 3, we review Dirichlet process mixture models and generalized linear models. In Section 4, we construct the DP-GLM and derive algorithms for posterior computation. In Section 5 we give general conditions for weak consistency of the joint density model and consistency of the regression estimate; we give several models where the conditions hold. In Section 6 we study the DP-GLM and other methods on three data sets; our study illustrates that the DP-GLM provides a powerful nonparametric regression model that can be used in many types of data analysis.

Generalized linear models (GLMs) extend linear regression to many types of response variables (McCullagh and Nelder, 1989). In their canonical form, a GLM assumes that the conditional mean of the response is a linear function of the covariates, and that the response distribution is in an exponential family. Many classical regression and classification methods are GLMs, including logistic regression, multinomial regression, and Poisson regression. The GLM framework makes two assumptions about the relationship between the covariates and the response. First, the covariates enter the distribution of the response through a linear function; a non-linear function may be applied to the output of the linear function, but only one that does not depend on the covariates. Second, the variance of the response cannot depend on the covariates. Both these assumptions can be limiting--there are many applications where we would like the response to be a non-linear function of the covariates or where our uncertainty around the response might depend on the covariates. In this paper, we develop a general regression algorithm that relaxes both of these assumptions. Our method captures arbitrarily shaped response functions and heteroscedasticity, that is, the property of the response distribution where both its mean and variance change with the covariates, while still retaining the flexibility of GLMs. Our idea is to model the mean function m(x) by a mixture of simpler "local" response distributions f i (m i (x)), each one applicable in a region of the covariates that exhibits similar response patterns. To handle multiple types of responses, each local regression is a GLM. This means that each m i (x) is a linear function, but a non-linear mean function arises when we marginalize out the uncertainty about which local response distribution is in play. (See Figure 1 for an example with one covariate and a continuous response function.) Furthermore, our method captures heteroscedasticity: the variance of the response function can vary across mixture components and, consequently, varies as a function of the covariates. One advantage of the DP-GLM is that it provides a strategy for handling common problems in predictive modeling. Many models, such as GLMs and Gaussian processes, make assumptions about data dispersion and homoscedasticity. Overdispersion occurs in single parameter GLMs when the data variance is larger than the variance predicted by the model mean. Mukhopadhyay and Gelfand (1997) have successfully used DP mixtures over GLM intercept parameters to create classes of models that include overdispersion. The DP-GLM retains this property, but is not limited to linearity in the covariates. Standard GLMs, however, maintain a fundamental homoscedasticity assumption--that the response variance remains constant across the covariate space. This assumption becomes severely limiting when applied to real-world data exhibiting heteroscedasticity, where the variance of the response changes systematically with the covariates. Under such conditions, traditional GLMs perform poorly, producing biased estimates and inefficient inference. The inability to model varying dispersion substantially constrains the model's capacity to capture the complex patterns of variability frequently observed in practice, highlighting the need for more adaptive approaches. The DP-GLM overcomes this limitation by employing mixtures of generalized linear models to explicitly model how variance changes across different clusters or regions of the covariate space, extending the earlier DP mixture framework beyond intercept parameters to encompass full heteroscedastic structure. The approach maintains smoothly transitioning posterior distributions, avoiding the abrupt discontinuities that plague simpler extensions. When compared against both standard homoscedastic methods and heteroscedastic modifications of traditional models, the DP-GLM demonstrates superior robustness and produces smooth, stable estimates of the mean function. In contrast, alternative heteroscedastic approaches often lack this robustness or generate non-smooth, unstable fits, making the DP-GLM a compelling framework for practical applications where both mean structure and variance heterogeneity require careful modeling.

Figure 21 shows that the proposed algorithm outperforms both Floyd--Warshall and the algorithm of Karger et al. on uniform graphs of practical size. Despite its higher asymptotic cost, the proposed method therefore offers a computational advantage over the range of graph sizes considered in these experiments. This comparison illustrates the importance of distinguishing asymptotic growth from performance at the sizes encountered in practice. Memory constraints prevented us from extending the experiments to larger graphs, however, so the results do not establish whether the observed advantage persists as the graph size increases. All three algorithms have a worst-case complexity of Θ(N³), although the literature contains more elaborate approaches with improved worst-case bounds. These improvements do not yield truly subcubic performance: they do not establish a running time of O(N³⁻ε) for any fixed ε > 0. Thus, the practical gains demonstrated in Figure 21 should be distinguished from an improvement in the worst-case complexity of the all-pairs shortest-path problem. The possibility of such an improvement is also relevant to the inference problems considered here, through the relationship between shortest-path computation and min-sum matrix multiplication. It should also be noted that the transformations given in Aho et al. (1983) apply in both directions, that is, solutions to the all-pairs shortest-path problem can be used to solve min-sum matrix multiplication. Thus any subcubic solution to the all-pairs shortest-path problem can be applied to the inference problems in graphical models presented in Section 4. However, the transformation of Aho et al. (1983) introduces a very high computational overhead (namely, solving min-sum matrix multiplication for an N × N matrix requires solving all-pairs shortest-path in a graph with 3N nodes), and moreover it violates the assumptions on the graph distribution required for fast inference given in Karger et al. (1993). In practice, we were unable to produce an implementation of min-sum matrix multiplication based on this transformation that was faster than the naı̈ve solution.

There has been previous work on speeding-up message-passing algorithms by exploiting different types of structure in certain graphical models. For example, Kersting et al. (2009) study the case where different cliques share the same potential function. In Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher (2006), fast message-passing algorithms are provided for cases in which the potential of a 2-clique is only dependent on the difference of the latent variables (which is common in some computer vision applications); they also show how the algorithm can be made faster if the graphical model is a bipartite graph. In Kumar and Torr (2006), the authors provide faster algorithms for the case in which the potentials are truncated, whereas in Petersen et al. (2008) the authors offer speed-ups for models that are specifically grid-like. Another direction for improving message-passing algorithms is to use informed scheduling, selecting the order in which messages are computed according to their expected contribution to inference. Such strategies concern the allocation and ordering of updates, whereas our methods concern the computations required to perform an update. The two approaches are therefore orthogonal: a scheduling strategy may determine which message to compute next, while our techniques may reduce the work involved in computing that message. This distinction allows improvements in scheduling to be considered alongside the factorization and sorting strategies studied here. The approach of Park and Darwiche is more directly related to ours, since it applies the same type of factorization to sum-product algorithms. Their work is complementary to our treatment of max-product algorithms: both exploit a decomposition of the relevant expressions, but the operation used to combine contributions differs. Consequently, the shared factorization provides a connection between the approaches without making their computational procedures interchangeable. Our focus is on exploiting this structure in maximization, including the opportunities it creates for using sorting to organize the computation. Kjærulff also exploits factorization within the cliques of a junction tree, demonstrating that the internal structure of clique computations can be useful even when inference is organized around the same junction-tree representation. However, the type of factorization used there differs from the one considered in this work, so the resulting methods address distinct computational structure. These connections place our approach among methods that improve inference by examining the operations within message updates. To understand the computational implications of our particular factorization, we next relate the resulting maximization problem to an established algebraic problem. In Section 4, we shall see that our algorithm is closely related to a well-studied problem known as 'tropical matrix multiplication' (Kerr, 1970). The worst-case complexity of this problem has been studied in relation to the all-pairs shortest-path problem (Alon et al., 1997; Karger et al., 1993).

We have briefly discussed the application of our algorithm to the all-pairs shortest-path problem, and also mentioned that a variety of other problems are related to max-product matrix multiplication via a series of subcubic transformations (Williams and Williams, 2010). To our knowledge, of all these problems only all-pairs shortest-paths has received significant attention in terms of expected-case analysis. The analysis in question centers around two types of model: the uniform model, where edge weights are sampled from a uniform distribution, and the endpoint-independent model, which essentially makes an assumption on the independence of outgoing edge weights from each vertex (Moffat and Takaoka, 1987), which seems very similar to our assumption of independent order statistics. It remains to be seen whether this analysis can lead to better solutions to the problems discussed here, and indeed if the analysis applied to uniform models can be applied in our setting to uniform matrices. An important property of our algorithm is that its running time depends only on the order statistics of the input data, and not on the values themselves. Two matrices whose entries differ wildly in magnitude, but which induce the same orderings within each row and column, will therefore be processed in the same expected time. The price of this generality is the independence assumption on which our analysis rests. We believe the assumption is broad enough to cover a wide range of practical inputs, but it is also a blunt instrument. In specialized settings, such as data with a very high dynamic range or factors that are scaled very differently from one another, the structure of the values may carry information that the order statistics alone discard. A stronger, more tailored assumption in these cases could plausibly be exploited to obtain tighter bounds on the expected running time. This points to two promising directions for future work. The first is the design of faster algorithms that build explicitly on stronger assumptions about the input, trading some of the generality of the present method for speed on the classes of problems where those assumptions hold. The second is to adapt the method to support probabilistic early termination. Rather than running until the maximum is guaranteed to have been found, a user could specify either an acceptable probability of error or a maximum runtime. Given such a budget, the algorithm would then report the probability that it had already identified the maximum within those constraints. Because our analysis already describes how quickly the search is expected to converge, we regard this as a natural extension, and one that would make the method more useful in settings where an approximate answer obtained quickly is preferable to an exact one obtained late.

We have briefly discussed the application of our algorithm to the all-pairs shortest-path problem, and also mentioned that a variety of other problems are related to max-product matrix multiplication via a series of subcubic transformations (Williams and Williams, 2010). To our knowledge, of all these problems only all-pairs shortest-paths has received significant attention in terms of expected-case analysis. The analysis in question centers around two types of model: the uniform model, where edge weights are sampled from a uniform distribution, and the endpoint-independent model, which essentially makes an assumption on the independence of outgoing edge weights from each vertex (Moffat and Takaoka, 1987), which seems very similar to our assumption of independent order statistics. It remains to be seen whether this analysis can lead to better solutions to the problems discussed here, and indeed if the analysis applied to uniform models can be applied in our setting to uniform matrices. It is interesting to consider the fact that our algorithm's running time is purely a function of the input data's order statistics, and in fact does not depend on the data itself. While it is pleasing that our assumption of independent order statistics appears to be a weak one, and is satisfied in a wide variety of applications, it ignores the fact that stronger assumptions may be reasonable in many cases. In factors with a high dynamic range, or when different factors have different scales, it may be possible to identify the maximum value very quickly, as we attempted to do in Section 7.5.1. Deriving faster algorithms that make stronger assumptions about the input data remains a promising avenue for future work. Our algorithm may also lead to faster solutions for approximately passing a single message. While the stopping criterion of our algorithm guarantees that the maximum value is found, it is possible to terminate the algorithm earlier and state that the maximum has probably been found. A direction for future work would be to adapt our algorithm to determine the probability that the maximum has been found after a certain number of steps; we could then allow the user to specify an error probability, or a desired running time, and our algorithm could be adapted accordingly.

We consider the problem of designing a measurement policy that identifies the alternative maximizing some objective, where each measurement is noisy and the budget for measurements is limited. This problem arises across a wide range of stochastic search applications. In a simulated system, for example, we may wish to tune a set of parameters, such as buffer sizes or routing thresholds, so that the long-run performance of the simulation is as good as possible, yet every run of the simulator is expensive and returns only a noisy estimate. In drug discovery, we must choose among a large set of candidate compounds, where each laboratory test is costly and its outcome is uncertain. In product design, we may want to select the combination of features that a customer population will respond to most favorably, with each trial providing only a noisy signal of that response. In many of these settings the decision is not a single discrete choice but a vector of continuous parameters, so that the set of alternatives, once discretized, may be very large and have many dimensions. Measurement policies for this kind of problem have been studied extensively under the heading of ranking and selection, but most of this work assumes that beliefs about the alternatives are independent, so that a measurement of one alternative tells us nothing about any other. Frazier et al. (2009) introduced a knowledge-gradient policy that accounts for correlated beliefs, in which an observation of one alternative updates our beliefs about similar alternatives. This is a natural fit for the settings above, where nearby parameter settings, structurally similar compounds, or related feature bundles should perform similarly. Our work builds on that approach. As in Frazier et al. (2009), we propose a knowledge-gradient policy that exploits the correlations in our belief structure, and we assume that these correlations are known. This paper makes the following contributions. First, we propose a version of the knowledge gradient policy that exploits aggregation structure and similarity between alternatives, without requiring that we specify an explicit covariance matrix for our belief. Instead, we develop a belief structure based on the weighted estimates given in (1). We estimate the weights using a Bayesian model adapted from frequentist estimates proposed by George et al. (2008). In addition to eliminating the difficulty of specifying an a priori covariance matrix, this avoids the computational challenge of working with large covariance matrices. Second, we show that a learning policy based on this method is optimal in the limit, that is, eventually it always discovers the best alternative. Our method requires that a family of aggregation functions be provided, but otherwise does not make any specific assumptions about the structure of the function or set of alternatives.

Finding the maximum of an unknown function from noisy measurements has long been studied through stochastic approximation, beginning with the methods of Robbins and Monro (1951). These methods seek the function's maximizer by repeatedly sampling and updating an estimate. In many settings, however, they require a large number of measurements. That can be a serious limitation when each measurement is costly, making it important to understand how efficiently an optimization method can identify the best choice. The present work is rooted in the ranking and selection literature, which began with Bechhofer (1954). In that framework, a decision-maker chooses the highest-value alternative from a finite collection, learning each alternative's value through sampling. This focus on a final choice connects the problem to offline optimization, such as simulation, where performance is judged by the quality of the answer returned after sampling ends. Online learning and multi-armed bandits address a related but distinct objective: they assess a sequence of decisions as it is made, as in dynamic pricing, and measure the losses accumulated along the way. These different goals lead to different notions of regret. Cumulative regret captures the cost of decisions throughout an online process, while terminal regret measures how far the final selected alternative falls below the best one. The online-learning literature has developed theoretical bounds for cumulative regret and for average regret, its per-decision counterpart. Those guarantees characterize performance during sequential decision-making; for offline optimization, the central question is instead how quickly terminal regret can be reduced. General-purpose online-to-batch conversion techniques have been developed, starting with Littlestone (1989), for transforming online-learning methods with bounds on cumulative regret into methods with bounds on terminal regret (for a summary and literature review see Shalev-Shwartz, 2007, Appendix B). While these techniques are easy to apply and immediately produce methods with theoretical bounds on the rate at which terminal regret converges to zero, methods created in this way may not have the best achievable bounds on terminal regret: Bubeck et al. (2009b) shows that improving the upper bound on the cumulative regret of an online learning method causes a corresponding lower bound on the terminal regret to get worse. This is indicative of a larger difference between what is required in the two types of problems. Furthermore, as as example of the difference between cumulative and terminal performance, Bubeck et al. (2009b) notes that with finitely many unrelated arms, achieving optimal cumulative regret requires sampling suboptimal arms no more than a logarithmic number of times, while achieving optimal terminal regret requires sampling every arm a linear number of times. Despite the difference between cumulative and terminal value, a number of methods have been developed that are often applied to both online learning and R&S problems in practice, as well as to more complex problems in reinforcement learning and Markov decision processes. These heuristics include Boltzmann exploration, interval estimation, upper confidence bound policies, and hybrid exploration-exploitation policies such as epsilon-greedy. See Powell and Frazier (2008) for a review of these. Other policies include the Explicit Explore or Exploit (E 3 ) algorithm of Kearns and Singh (2002) and R-MAX of Brafman and Tennenholtz (2003).

We introduce a method for analyzing deep networks that combines kernel methods and descriptive statistics in order to quantify the layer-wise evolution of the representation in deep networks. Our method abstracts deep networks as a sequence of deeper and deeper kernels subsuming the mapping performed by more and more layers. The kernel framework expresses the relation between the representation built in the deep network and the learning problem. Applied to properly trained deep neural networks, this analytical framework shows that successive layers progressively reduce the complexity of the input data distribution. Viewed through the corresponding kernels, the representations become simpler while retaining distinctions relevant to the learning problem. This progression culminates in final-layer representations that reconcile simplicity with predictive accuracy: the reduction in complexity preserves the structure needed to discriminate among the target outputs. Layer-wise analysis thus connects the transformations performed within the network to the quality of the representation ultimately used for prediction. The analysis further indicates that network architecture supports efficient use of representational capacity by regulating the rate at which information is discriminated across depth. The allocation of this process among layers shapes how the network simplifies the distribution while preserving task-relevant distinctions, making the trajectory of representation development central to understanding its behavior. From this perspective, regularization mechanisms can be understood within a common framework that relates their effects to the evolution of complexity and discrimination throughout the network. These findings provide a unified account of how deep networks arrive at representations that are both simple and accurate.

Our method abstracts deep networks as a sequence of deeper and deeper kernels subsuming the mapping performed by more and more layers. The kernel framework expresses the relation between the representation built in the deep network and the learning problem. Our analysis is able to detect and quantify the progressive and layer-wise transformation of the input performed by the deep network. In particular, we find that properly trained deep networks progressively simplify the statistics of complex data distributions, building in their last layers representations that are both simple and accurate. The analysis also corroborates the hypothesis that a suitable structure for the deep network allows to make efficient use of its representational power by controlling the rate of discrimination at each layer of the deep network. This observation provides a new unified view on the role and effect of regularizers in deep networks.

A useful representation should make the learning task amenable to models that are both simple and accurate. If the representation captures the structure relevant to the target, a comparatively simple model can express the desired decision rule without sacrificing predictive performance. The challenge is that simplicity is not an intrinsic property of a model: what counts as simple depends on the knowledge brought to the task. Visual recognition illustrates this dependence. People often recognize objects with ease, while basic algorithms may struggle with the same images. This difference does not mean that the task itself is inherently simple; people bring prior knowledge about images, such as the expectation that modest changes in appearance need not change an object's identity. A measure of representation quality must therefore account for the prior knowledge that makes some patterns easier to learn than others. We propose to model such prior knowledge through kernel operators, which measure similarity between pairs of data points. Different kernels encode different assumptions about which transformations or variations should preserve similarity, and thus represent different invariances. The feature map induced by a kernel implicitly incorporates these assumptions into the representation, allowing linear models to be built on top of it. This gives a concrete setting in which to examine representations through the accuracy and simplicity of the models they support. A second technical difficulty comes from the fact that accuracy and simplicity are not always measurable in practice: accuracy of a model can only be estimated up to a certain precision from the finite data set and estimating the simplicity depends on whether we consider, for example, the number of parameters of a model, its entropy or its algorithmic complexity. For these reasons, we need to restrict ourselves to a class of models whose simplicity and accuracy can be easily measured and that are expressive enough to solve the learning problem. We choose to use the kernel principal component analysis (kernel PCA, Schölkopf et al., 1998) as a basis for building measurably simple models of the learning problem. Our method consists of projecting the input distribution on the d first components (in terms of variance) of the kernel feature space and fitting a linear model on this low-rank representation. The number of components d controls the simplicity of the model. When d is small, the model is simple. When d is large, the model is complex. The accuracy can in turn be obtained by measuring the prediction error e(d) of a linear predictor on top of the d-component kernel representation. We refer to the parameter d as the dimensionality of the model and e(d) as the prediction error obtained with the d-component model. The curve e(d) gives a complete picture of how good a representation is with respect to the learning problem. Figure 2 gives some examples of curves e(d) and explains how these curves can be interpreted.

In this section, we are interested in quantifying how good a representation is with respect to the learning problem. The representation is good when it is possible to build models of the learning problem on top of it that are both simple and accurate. A first technical difficulty is to quantify how simple a model is. Indeed, the notion of simplicity is highly subjective (Bousquet et al., 2004) and typically depends on which prior knowledge on the learning problem is taken for granted. For example, visual recognition tasks are very simple for humans, but very complex for simple learning algorithms such as a local learning machine. The notion of simplicity encoded by the Gaussian kernel is meaningful for a wide range of learning problems, however, it does not explain how simple more intelligent systems perceive problems such as vision and speech. Indeed, domain-specific regularities such as invariance to translation, scale or occlusion can not be modeled efficiently by a Gaussian kernel. Consequently, observing the learning problem become simpler as we build deeper and deeper kernels highlights the capacity of deep networks to model the regularities of the input distribution. To make the comparison across dimensionalities fair, the scale parameter σ of the Gaussian kernel must be chosen in a principled way rather than fixed once for all experiments. For each number of kernel principal components d, we select the value of σ that minimizes the error metric e(d). Because the optimum is computed separately for every d, this procedure yields a different best parameter for each dimensionality: a small number of components generally favors a different bandwidth than a larger one, since the kernel must trade off the smoothness of the representation against the amount of structure it can retain in the available directions. Selecting σ this way ensures that any remaining error reflects a limitation of the Gaussian kernel itself, and not a poorly tuned hyperparameter. The effect is easiest to see on a family of binary classification problems that are distorted by increasing amounts. In the original, undistorted problem, the two classes are arranged so that they can be separated along a single direction in the kernel feature space, and one kernel principal component is therefore enough to solve the task. As the distortion grows, the class boundary becomes more convoluted, and the visualizations show that the classes no longer line up along one axis. The more distorted versions require two, three, or more components before the classes can be separated well, so the representation needed to solve the problem becomes steadily less compact. This progression suggests that Gaussian kernels become progressively less suited to problems as they move away from the simple regularities the kernel assumes, and it motivates building deeper kernels that can absorb such distortions and make the problem easy again.

Robust decision-making for autonomous agents requires evaluating actions in terms of both their immediate effects and their consequences for future behavior. An action that offers a favorable short-term outcome may lead to a state in which subsequent opportunities are limited, whereas an initially less rewarding action may support better outcomes over time. This evaluation must also account for uncertainty, since the consequences of an action cannot generally be predicted with certainty. Probabilistic models provide a framework for representing such uncertainty by specifying the probabilities of possible outcomes conditional on the current system state and the selected action. These models allow an agent to compare alternative courses of action by considering the range of states they may produce and the value of the decisions available thereafter. The quality of the resulting decisions, however, depends on how accurately the model represents the environment. When predicted outcome probabilities differ substantially from those governing actual behavior, an agent may favor actions whose apparent advantages do not materialize or overlook alternatives that would better serve its objective. This limitation is particularly relevant when the available models are crude approximations of reality: reasoning carefully within an inaccurate model can still yield suboptimal decisions. Learning methods can mitigate this problem by using accumulated experience to progressively refine the agent's representation of action consequences. As observations reveal discrepancies between predictions and outcomes, the model can be revised to support more reliable evaluations and improve future decision quality. Sequential decision-making thus involves not only acting on the basis of available knowledge, but also acquiring the knowledge needed to make better choices over time. In the past few decades, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as an elegant and popular technique to handle sequential decision problems when the model is unknown (Sutton and Barto, 1998). Reinforcement learning is a general technique that allows an agent to learn the best way to behave, that is, such as to maximize expected return, from repeated interactions in the environment. A fundamental problem in RL is that of exploration-exploitation: namely, how should the agent chooses actions during the learning phase, in order to both maximize its knowledge of the model as needed to better achieve the objective later (i.e., explore), and maximize current achievement of the objective based on what is already known about the domain (i.e., exploit). Under some (reasonably general) conditions on the exploratory behavior, it has been shown that RL eventually learns the optimal action-select behavior. However, these conditions do not specify how to choose actions such as to maximize utilities throughout the life of the agent, including during the learning phase, as well as beyond.

Robust decision-making is a core component of many autonomous agents. This generally requires that an agent evaluate a set of possible actions, and choose the best one for its current situation. In many problems, actions have long-term consequences that must be considered by the agent; it is not useful to simply choose the action that looks the best in the immediate situation. Instead, the agent must choose its actions by carefully trading off their short-term and long-term costs and benefits. To do so, the agent must be able to predict the consequences of its actions, in so far as it is useful to determine future actions. In applications where it is not possible to predict exactly the outcomes of an action, the agent must also consider the uncertainty over possible future events. Probabilistic models of sequential decision-making take into account such uncertainty by specifying the chance (probability) that any future outcome will occur, given any current configuration (state) of the system, and action taken by the agent. However, if the model used does not perfectly fit the real problem, the agent risks making poor decisions. This is currently an important limitation in practical deployment of autonomous decision-making agents, since available models are often crude and incomplete approximations of reality. Clearly, learning methods can play an important role in improving the model as experience is acquired, such that the agent's future decisions are also improved. Jaulmes et al. (2005) have for their part considered active learning in partially observable domains where information gathering actions are provided by oracles that reveal the underlying state. The key assumption of this approach, which is not used in other model-free approaches, concerns the existence of this oracle (or human) which is able to correctly identify the state following each transition. This makes it much easier to know how to update the prior. In the same vein than Jaulmes and colleagues, Doshi et al. (2008) developed an approach for active learning in POMDPs that can robustly determine a near-optimal policy. To achieve that, they introduced meta-queries (questions about action) and a risk-averse action selection criterion that allows agents to behave robustly even with uncertain knowledge of the POMDP model. Finally, Doshi-Velez (2010) proposed a Bayesian learning framework for the case of POMDPs where the number of states is not known a priori, thus allowing the number of states to grow gradually as the agent explores the world, while simultaneously updating a posterior over the parameters. Hutter's AIXI framework offers an alternative to BAPOMDPs for sequential decision-making under uncertainty by considering a broader class of possible environment models. Rather than restricting uncertainty to the parameters of a particular model family, AIXI allows models drawn from any computable distribution, with their prior weights determined by Kolmogorov complexity. This formulation favours simpler explanations of the agent's observations while retaining the capacity to represent increasingly complex environments. Its generality, however, comes at the cost of incomputable inference, so the framework does not directly provide an implementable solution. Further algorithmic development grounded in Monte-Carlo Planning is therefore needed to approximate its decision-making principles and enable practical comparisons with BAPOMDP approaches. Recent theoretical advances in reinforcement learning exploration have also clarified the relationship between Bayesian methods and approaches based on PAC-MDP guarantees. These perspectives place different emphasis on uncertainty: Bayesian methods guide decisions through a posterior over possible environments, whereas PAC-MDP analyses seek to bound the experience required for near-optimal behaviour with high probability. Asmuth et al. contributed a Bayesian analysis of sampling approaches, helping to explain how sampled models can support exploration and how such procedures relate to formal performance guarantees. Kolter and Ng, in turn, presented an algorithm for efficient near-Bayesian exploration, addressing the difficulty of obtaining effective exploratory behaviour without carrying out full Bayesian planning. Together, these developments provide a firmer theoretical basis for examining how tractable exploration strategies approximate Bayesian decision-making.

Recent results in Monte-Carlo Planning provide a good basis for this (Silver and Veness, 2010; Veness et al., 2011). A number of useful theoretical results have also been published recently. For the specific case of exploration in reinforcement learning, Asmuth et al. (2009) presented a fully Bayesian analysis of the performance of a sampling approach. Subsequently, Kolter and Ng (2009) clarified the relation between Bayesian and PAC-MDP approaches and presented a simple algorithm for efficiently achieving near-Bayesian exploration.

From the theoretical analysis, we are able to derive simple algorithms for belief tracking and (near-)optimal decision-making in this model. We illustrate performance of these algorithms in a collection of synthetic POMDP domains. Results in the Follow problem showed that our approach is able to learn the motion patterns of two (simulated) individuals. This suggests interesting applications in human-robot interaction, where we often lack good models of human behavior and where it is imperative that an agent be able to learn quickly, lest the human user lose interest (this is in contrast to robot navigation tasks, for which we often have access to more precise dynamical models and/or high-fidelity simulators). For their part, results of RockSample problem shows how one should take into account prior knowledge on agent's sensors when this knowledge is available. Despite these encouraging results, the BAPOMDP model has a number of limitations that deserve mention. The most obvious is that the model, as formulated here, is restricted to discrete domains: the states, actions and observations are assumed to be finite, and the Dirichlet-based parameterization of the unknown transition and observation functions relies on this assumption. This restriction is not fundamental, however. The overall framework of maintaining a posterior over models while planning in the joint space of states and model parameters is not tied to discreteness, and approximate algorithms, such as those based on sampling and particle-based belief tracking, can in principle be extended to continuous cases, though we have not explored this direction empirically. Even within the discrete setting, the size of the augmented state space grows quickly, which is one reason that we rely on approximate planning rather than exact solutions. A second limitation is that the model requires the user to specify a prior over the unknown parameters. This requirement is standard in Bayesian reinforcement learning, and it is part of what makes the approach principled, but it can be challenging in practice, particularly in large domains where it is unclear how to encode meaningful domain knowledge into a prior over many parameters. In addition, the prior must place sufficient weight on the correct model; if the true dynamics lie in a region of the parameter space to which the prior assigns very little probability, the posterior will take much longer to concentrate around them. Our empirical evaluation nonetheless suggests that the approach is reasonably robust, as it performed well across a variety of priors. The experiments also clarify the role that the prior plays: its influence is most pronounced when data is scarce, at the early stages of learning, but it becomes negligible as the agent accumulates experience and the observed data dominates the posterior.

From the theoretical analysis, we are able to derive simple algorithms for belief tracking and (near-)optimal decision-making in this model. We illustrate performance of these algorithms in a collection of synthetic POMDP domains. Results in the Follow problem showed that our approach is able to learn the motion patterns of two (simulated) individuals. This suggests interesting applications in human-robot interaction, where we often lack good models of human behavior and where it is imperative that an agent be able to learn quickly, lest the human user lose interest (this is in contrast to robot navigation tasks, for which we often have access to more precise dynamical models and/or high-fidelity simulators). For their part, results of RockSample problem shows how one should take into account prior knowledge on agent's sensors when this knowledge is available. While the BAPOMDP model provides a rich model for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, it has a number of important limitations. First, the model and theoretical analysis are limited to discrete domains. It is worth noting however that the approximate algorithms extend quite easily to the continuous case (Ross et al., 2008b), at least for some families of dynamical systems. Other related references for the continuous case are available in the control literature, as described in Section 7. Another limitation is the fact that the model requires specification of a prior. This is standard in the Bayesian RL framework. The main concern is to ensure that the prior assigns some weight to the correct model. Our empirical evaluation shows good performance for a range of priors; though the issue of choosing good priors in large domains remains a challenge in general. Our empirical results also confirm standard Bayesian intuition, whereby the influence of the prior is particularly important for any inference and decision-making performed when only a small amount of data has been observed, but the influence becomes negligible as large amounts of data are acquired.

A key aspect of reinforcement learning is the issue of exploration. This corresponds to the question of determining how the agent should choose actions while learning about the task. This is in contrast to the phase called exploitation, through which actions are selected so as to maximize expected reward with respect to the current value function estimate. The issues of value function estimation and exploration are assumed to be orthogonal in much of the MDP literature. However in many applications, where data is expensive or difficult to acquire, it is important to consider the rewards accumulated during the learning phase, and to try to take this cost-of-learning into account in the optimization of the policy. In practical reinforcement learning, the trade-off between exploration and exploitation is commonly managed through heuristics such as ε-greedy action selection and Boltzmann strategies. An ε-greedy strategy usually selects an action with the highest estimated value, but occasionally chooses an action at random, while a Boltzmann strategy assigns action probabilities according to their estimated values and a temperature parameter. These methods provide simple ways to vary the amount of exploration as learning proceeds. However, their exploratory choices are not explicitly directed toward resolving uncertainty that matters for policy improvement. Consequently, the agent may spend costly interactions revisiting well-understood actions rather than acquiring the information needed to distinguish promising alternatives. Theoretical advances have established that exploration can instead be organized to provide guarantees on learning performance. Under suitable assumptions, an agent can attain near-optimal performance within a polynomial amount of time, or accumulate low regret relative to an optimal policy during its interactions with the environment. These guarantees address complementary aspects of the cost of learning: the time required to obtain a good policy and the reward forgone before and while that policy is learned. By relating action selection to uncertainty about the task, such approaches give exploration a more specific purpose than random deviations from current preferences. Although theoretical guarantees do not by themselves ensure practical effectiveness, in some cases they have led to algorithms with reasonably good empirical performance, suggesting that principled exploration can also be useful in applied reinforcement learning.

Because the optimal value function of a Bayesian adaptive MDP is intractable to compute exactly in all but the smallest problems, a number of approximate algorithms have been proposed. One of the earliest is due to Dearden and colleagues, who maintain a Dirichlet distribution over the unknown transition parameters and use it to reason about uncertainty in the value of each action. Rather than computing a single point estimate of the Q-value, their approach computes a distribution over Q-values. This is done by sampling: MDPs are drawn from the current Dirichlet posterior, each sampled MDP is solved, and the resulting Q-values are collected to form an empirical picture of how good each action might be. The spread of this distribution then informs action selection, so that actions whose values are uncertain can be favoured when the potential gain from learning more is high. Strens takes a related but distinct view by fully representing the posterior over the process parameters and using it directly to drive behaviour. The key appeal of this approach is that it yields goal-directed exploration without resorting to ad hoc exploration heuristics. Because the agent's choices are always conditioned on its current beliefs about the process, exploratory actions are taken only to the extent that they are justified by what remains unknown. As the posterior concentrates with experience, the agent shifts from exploration to exploitation, and this transition occurs automatically rather than being imposed through a hand-tuned schedule or an exploration bonus. In this sense the method embodies the Bayesian ideal that the balance between gathering information and exploiting it should emerge from the model itself. Duff pursues a different strategy, one that focuses on the policy rather than on the value function. His proposal is to represent the optimal policy of the Bayesian adaptive MDP compactly using a Finite-State Controller. The internal state of the controller acts as a bounded summary of the agent's history, standing in for the potentially unbounded set of belief states that an exact solution would have to track. With the policy parameterized in this way, the search for a good solution becomes an optimization problem over the controller's parameters, and Duff finds the best controller through gradient descent. This trades the guarantee of exact optimality for tractability, since the quality of the result depends on the size and structure of the controller, but it offers a way to obtain a usable policy without enumerating the full space of beliefs. For their part, Wang et al. (2005) present an online planning algorithm that estimates the optimal value function of the BAMDP (Equation 1) using Monte-Carlo sampling. This algorithm is essentially an adaptation of the Sparse Sampling algorithm (Kearns et al., 1999) to BAMDPs. However instead of growing the tree evenly by looking at all actions at each level of the tree, the tree is grown stochastically. Actions are sampled according to their likelihood of being optimal, according to their Q-value distributions (as defined by the Dirichlet posteriors); next states are sampled according to the Dirichlet posterior on the model. This approach requires multiple sampling and solving of MDPs from the Dirichlet distributions to find which action has highest Q-value at each state node in the tree. This can be very time consuming, and so far the approach has only been applied to small MDPs. Castro and Precup (2007) present a similar approach to Wang et al. However their approach differs on two main points. First, instead of maintaining only the posterior over models, they also maintain Q-value estimates using a standard Q-Learning method. Planning is done by growing a stochastic tree as in Wang et al. (but sampling actions uniformly instead) and solving for the value estimates in that tree using Linear Programming (LP), instead of dynamic programming. In this case, the stochastic tree represents sampled constraints, which the value estimates in the tree must satisfy. The Q-value estimates maintained by Q-Learning are used as value estimates for the fringe nodes (thus as value constraints on the fringe nodes in the LP). Finally, Poupart et al. (2006) proposed an approximate offline algorithm to solve the BAMDP. Their algorithm, called Beetle, is an extension of the Perseus algorithm (Spaan and Vlassis, 2005) to the BAMDP model. Essentially, at the beginning, hyperstates (s, φ) are sampled from random interactions with the BAMDP model. An equivalent continuous POMDP (over the space of states and transition functions) is solved instead of the BAMDP (assuming (s, φ) is a belief state in that POMDP). The value function is represented by a set of α-functions over the continuous space of transition functions. Each α-function is constructed as a linear combination of basis functions; the sampled hyperstates can serve as the set of basis functions. Dynamic programming is used to incrementally construct the set of α-functions. At each iteration, updates are only performed at the sampled hyperstates, similarly to Perseus (Spaan and Vlassis, 2005) and other Point-Based POMDP algorithms (Pineau et al., 2003).

Within ILP, no significant attention has been paid to the problem of parameter screening or optimisation. Reports in the literature rarely contain any discussion of sensitive parameters of the system or their values. Of 100 experimental studies reported in papers presented between 1998 and 2008 to the principal conference in the area, none attempt any form of screening for relevant parameters. 17 describe settings for some pre-selected parameters--usually one--from performance estimates obtained during an enumerative search over some small set of possible values (that is, effectively using the wrapper approach of Kohavi and John, 1995). 38 reports, however, mention values assigned to some parameters, without elucidating how these values were reached (on occasions, these were just the default values provided by the system). The work in Srinivasan (2001b) can be seen as addressing the question of optimal values for several input parameters somewhat indirectly by first constructing an "operating characteristic curve" that describes the performance of an ILP system across a range of values for the relevant parameters. While no method is proposed for identifying the parameters themselves, the characteristic curve provides a way of optimally selecting amongst models, provided model goodness is restricted to a specific class (that of cost functions that are linear in the error-rates). . Since each model is obtained from a particular combination of values for relevant parameters, we are able to identify the values that resulted in the best model for the task. The procedure is somewhat reminiscent of putting the cart before the horse though, requiring us to identify all models on the characteristic curve first. Parameter optimisation has received more attention in other areas of machine learning, although the methods developed there are not always applicable to ILP. Gradient-based methods are useful when the objective function has a mathematical form that permits the calculation of derivatives with respect to the parameters being adjusted. In an ILP system, however, the relationship between parameter settings and performance is generally available only through running the system and evaluating the resulting models. The objective function lacks a closed-form expression from which the required gradients can be obtained, so methods that depend on such an expression cannot be adapted directly. An alternative is the "wrapper" approach, in which parameter selection is treated as a search problem and candidate settings are evaluated using the learning system itself. Discretising the range of each parameter into k levels yields a k-level full-factorial design whose combinations define the search space. Heuristic search can then be used to explore this space without evaluating every combination, with observed performance guiding the choice of subsequent settings. Exhaustive search provides an upper bound on the performance attainable within the specified design, since it identifies the best of all the combinations considered. This bound is restricted to the chosen parameter levels, however, and obtaining it requires evaluating the entire design. A related approach to parameter optimisation for mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) systems is described by Baz et al., who combine a sampling design with machine learning models to guide parameter selection. Their procedure uses exhaustive enumeration of the combinations specified by the design to obtain performance observations, followed by regression-based parameter screening. The regression models relate the observed performance to the parameter settings and provide a basis for identifying which parameters merit attention when selecting values. This combination of designed evaluations and statistical modelling extends the role of experimentation beyond comparing individual configurations: it also seeks to explain which aspects of those configurations affect performance, thereby connecting parameter optimisation with the broader problem of parameter screening. The problem of screening and tuning of parameters to optimise a system's performance has been studied extensively in areas of industrial engineering, using results obtained from the design and analysis of experiments. It is our intention in this paper to investigate the application of techniques developed in these areas to ILP, and we summarise some of the relevant ideas next.

Bengio (2000) is most closely related to the optimisation goals of this paper, in that it presents a methodology to optimise several parameters (Bengio and the following papers call them hyperparameters, to avoid confusion with the statistical term), based on the computation of the gradient of a model selection criterion expressed in terms of the parameters. The main restriction is that this criterion must be a known, continuous and differentiable function of the parameters (almost) everywhere. While Bengio assumes a training criterion that is quadratic in the parameters, Keerthi et al. (2006) present a fast method for computing the gradient of a validation function with respect to parameters for a range of SVM models. Their method only needs a single linear system of equations to be solved. Unfortunately, it is not possible to directly adapt these methods to ILP systems. In almost all ILP settings, the training criterion cannot be even expressed in closed form, let alone being a differentiable and continuous function of the parameters. That is, what can be done at best is to treat the ILP system is a black box (as we have done in the previous section) and empirically observe variations in its response to changes in the values of the parameters. Methods have been developed that use such empirically observed responses to direct the assignment of values to relevant parameters. The seminal work in Kohavi and John (1995) introduced the "wrapper" approach to parameter optimisation, in which responses from a ML system are used to direct a heuristic search through combinations of possible values for the parameters. For tractability, these values are discretised a priori, and approach essentially performs a sub-optimal search through a finite space of what are called k-level full-factorial designs in this paper (the k refers to the number of discrete values: more on such designs in the next section). In this paper, we use a exhaustive search through such a space as a baseline for comparison against a gradient-based optimisation method. The results from the exhaustive search clearly represent an upper-bound on the results achievable by any heuristic search through the same space. The work described in Baz et al. (2007) is concerned with determining parameter values that minimise the computation time of mixed integer linear programming (MILP) systems. As with the ILP systems we consider here, the MILP solvers have many parameters, with no clear relationships known amongst them; and the objective function cannot be expressed as a closed form function of these parameters. Their approach is to select an initial set of values for the hyperparameters using some sampling design. The response of the MILP solver is then obtained, from which a ML system is used to construct a model relating the response to parameter values. This model is then used to suggest new values for some subset of the parameters. For example, if the model used is a regression tree, then the parameters used in the top 2 levels of the tree (the choice of 2 is arbitrary, but no method is proposed for automating this choice) are selected and additional sets of values obtained for the parameters (the exact procedure of how this is done is not elaborated upon). The set that results in the best performance is returned. This work can be seen as a case of exhaustive enumeration of responses in a k-level full factorial design, followed by a single stage of ad hoc non-linear regression-based parameter screening and optimisation.
