In high-dimensional settings, the number of candidate variables can greatly exceed the number of observations, and many candidates may carry overlapping or redundant information. The central task is therefore to distinguish the small subset that is truly informative from variables that add little to the analysis. Choosing too sparse a model can omit relevant variables and underfit; choosing too many can overfit, making the selected model sensitive to the particular sample and obscuring the underlying relationships. Penalized regression methods, including the lasso and SCAD, address this problem by shrinking coefficients and, in many cases, setting some to zero. Their tuning parameters govern the strength of this penalty and thus the sparsity of the resulting model. A substantial body of research has examined how the rates at which these parameters are chosen affect consistency and performance, clarifying conditions under which a method can recover the informative variables. Yet these results often describe the behavior of a method under suitable tuning choices without resolving how to choose the parameter in practice. Classical selection criteria such as cross-validation, BIC, and other information-based methods have been adapted to penalized regression. They provide useful ways to compare candidate models, but their objectives generally emphasize prediction error or the probability assigned to a model, rather than whether the selected variables are the informative ones. This leaves a gap between choosing a model that performs well by those criteria and choosing a tuning parameter that reliably identifies a stable set of relevant variables. This article proposes a tuning parameter selection criterion based on variable selection stability. The key idea is that if multiple samples are available from the same distribution, a good variable selection method should yield similar sets of informative variables that do not vary much from one sample to another. The similarity between two informative variable sets is measured by Cohen's kappa coefficient (Cohen, 1960), which adjusts the actual variable selection agreement relative to the possible agreement by chance. Similar stability measures have been studied in the context of cluster analysis (Ben-Hur et al., 2002; Wang, 2010) and variable selection (Meinshausen and Bühlmann, 2010). Whereas the stability selection method (Meinshausen and Bühlmann, 2010) also follows the idea of variable selection stability, it mainly focuses on selecting the informative variables as opposed to selecting the tuning parameters for any given variable selection methods. The effectiveness of the proposed selection criterion is demonstrated in a variety of simulated examples and a real application. More importantly, its asymptotic selection consistency is established, showing that the variable selection method with the selected tuning parameter would recover the truly informative variable set with probability tending to one. The rest of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews the penalized regression models. Section 3 presents the idea of variable selection stability as well as the proposed kappa selection criterion. Section 4 establishes the asymptotic selection consistency of the kappa selection criterion. Simulation studies are given in Section 5, followed by a real application in Section 6. A brief discussion is provided in Section 7, and the Appendix is devoted to the technical proofs.

The rapid advance of technology has led to an increasing demand for modern statistical techniques to analyze data with complex structure such as the high-dimensional data. In high-dimensional data analysis, it is generally believed that only a small number of variables are truly informative while others are redundant. An underfitted model excludes truly informative variables and may lead to severe estimation bias in model fitting, whereas an overfitted model includes the redundant uninformative variables, increases the estimation variance and hinders the model interpretation. Therefore, identifying the truly informative variables is regarded as the primary goal of the highdimensional data analysis as well as its many real applications such as health studies (Fan and Li, 2006). Among other variable selection methods, penalized regression models have been popularly used, which penalize the model fitting with various regularization terms to encourage model sparsity, such as the lasso regression (Tibshirani, 1996), the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD, Fan and Li, 2001), the adaptive lasso (Zou, 2006), and the truncated l 1 -norm regression (Shen et al., 2012). In the penalized regression models, tuning parameters are often employed to balance the trade-off between model fitting and model sparsity, which largely affects the numerical performance and the asymptotic behavior of the penalized regression models. For example, Zhao and Yu (2006) showed that, under the irrepresentable condition, the lasso regression is selection consistent when the tuning parameter converges to 0 at a rate slower than O(n −1/2 ). Analogous results on the choice of tuning parameters have also been established for the SCAD, the adaptive lasso, and the truncated l 1 -norm regression. Therefore, it is of crucial importance to select the appropriate tuning parameters so that the performance of the penalized regression models can be optimized. In literature, many classical selection criteria have been applied to the penalized regression models, including cross validation (Stone, 1974), generalized cross validation (Craven and Wahba, 1979), Mallows' C p (Mallows, 1973), AIC (Akaike, 1974) and BIC (Schwarz, 1978). Under certain regularity conditions, Wang et al. (2007) and Wang et al. (2009) established the selection consistency of BIC for the SCAD, and Zhang et al. (2010) showed the selection consistency of generalized information criterion (GIC) for the SCAD. Most of these criteria follow the route of minimizing the estimated prediction error or maximizing the posterior model probability. To the best of our knowledge, few criteria has been developed directly focusing on the selection of the informative variables. The Cuboid detector depends on a set of linear filters for computing the response function of a video clip. The response function has the form of a 2D Gaussian smoothing function (applied in the spatial domain) and a quadrature pair of 1D Gabor filters (applied in the temporal direction). Then the keypoints are detected at the local maxima of the response function. The video batches extracted at each of the keypoints are converted to a descriptor. There are a number of ways to compute descriptors from video batches as discussed by Dollár et al. (2005). Among those, gradient-based descriptors such as histograms of oriented gradients (HOG) and concatenated gradient vectors are the most reliable ones. For more details about the Cuboid feature, please see Dollár et al. (2005). The Harris3D detector extends the Harris corner detector to video by locating interest points in both space and time. It computes spatio-temporal second-moment matrices with Gaussian smoothing, using local changes in image structure and motion to identify points that are distinctive across adjacent frames. At each detected keypoint, histograms of oriented gradients (HOG) and histograms of optical flow (HOF) describe the appearance and motion in its neighbourhood. This combination captures complementary spatial and temporal information about the video. MoSIFT combines SIFT with optical flow to select and describe points that exhibit motion. It constructs Gaussian and optical-flow pyramids from successive video frames, then searches across scales for interest points with sufficient motion. For each selected point, it computes descriptors from both pyramid types, representing visual structure alongside local movement. The resulting MoSIFT descriptor has 256 dimensions.

Then the keypoints are detected at the local maxima of the response function. The video batches extracted at each of the keypoints are converted to a descriptor. There are a number of ways to compute descriptors from video batches as discussed by Dollár et al. (2005). Among those, gradient-based descriptors such as histograms of oriented gradients (HOG) and concatenated gradient vectors are the most reliable ones. For more details about the Cuboid feature, please see Dollár et al. (2005). The Harris3D detector (Laptev, 2005) is an extension of the Harris corner detector (Harris and Stephens, 1988). The author computes a spatio-temporal second-moment matrix at each video point using independent spatial and temporal scale values, a separable Gaussian smoothing function, and space-time gradients. The final locations of space-time interest points are given by the local positive spatio-temporal maxima. Then, at each keypoint, two types of descriptors are calculated, which are HOG and histograms of optical flow (HOF) descriptors. The MoSIFT (Chen and Hauptmann, 2009) is derived from scale invariant feature transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 2004) and optical flow (Lucas et al., 1981). First, a pair of Gaussian pyramids are built from two successive frames, respectively. Then, optical flow pyramids are calculated by each layer of the pair of Gaussian pyramids. Next, a local extreme detected from difference of Gaussian pyramids (DoG) can only become an interest point if it has sufficient motion in the optical flow pyramid. Finally, as the process of the SIFT descriptor calculation, the MoSIFT descriptors are respectively computed from Gaussian pyramid and optical flow pyramid so that each MoSIFT descriptor now has 256 dimensions.

Many successful feature learning algorithms are trained to minimize reconstruction error, yet it remains unclear what such a criterion teaches the model about the distribution that generated the data. Does an auto-encoder implicitly capture the full density of its inputs, or only certain aspects of it, such as the location of the manifold near which the data concentrate? And if something about the density is being learned, can that knowledge be made precise enough to support sampling from the model? This paper takes up these questions. We start from two closely related regularized auto-encoders, the denoising auto-encoder and the contractive auto-encoder, and show how they are connected: training with small corruption noise behaves like penalizing the sensitivity of the reconstruction to the input. We then ask what an auto-encoder actually learns when it minimizes the contractive training criterion, which trades off reconstruction error against a penalty on the derivatives of the learned mapping. The intuition is illustrated by the manifold picture of Figure 1. The contraction penalty pushes the auto-encoder to become insensitive to its input, while the reconstruction term forces it to stay sensitive to the variations that matter for reproducing the data, namely those along the manifold of high density. The representation and reconstruction therefore capture variations on the manifold while largely ignoring variations orthogonal to it. Our main finding makes this intuition quantitative. We show that the auto-encoder estimates the score, the first derivative of the log-density with respect to the input. The score points in the direction of maximum increase in density and corresponds to the local mean, so the reconstruction can be read as a displacement toward regions of higher probability. We further show that the derivative of the reconstruction function carries information about the Hessian of the log-density, and hence about the local curvature of the density around the data. Finally, Section 4 shows how having access to an estimator of the score can be exploited to estimate energy differences, and thus perform approximate MCMC sampling. This is achieved using a Metropolis-Hastings MCMC in which the energy differences between the proposal and the current state are approximated using the denoising auto-encoder. Experiments on artificial data sets show that a denoising auto-encoder can recover a good estimator of the data-generating distribution, when we compare the samples generated by the model with the training samples, projected into various 2-D views for visualization. Some important questions remain concerning many of feature learning algorithms based on reconstruction error. Most importantly, what is their training criterion learning about the input density? Do these algorithms implicitly learn about the whole density or only some aspect? If they capture the essence of the target density, then can we formalize that link and in particular exploit it to sample from the model? The answers may help to establish that these algorithms actually learn implicit density models, which only define a density indirectly, e.g., through the estimation of statistics or through a generative procedure. These are the questions to which this paper contributes. The paper is divided in two main sections, along with detailed appendices with proofs of the theorems. Section 2 makes a direct link between denoising auto-encoders (Vincent et al., 2008) and contractive auto-encoders (Rifai et al., 2011b), justifying the interest in the contractive training criterion studied in the rest of the paper. Section 3 is the main contribution and regards the following question: when minimizing that criterion, what does an auto-encoder learn about the data-generating density? The main answer is that it estimates the score (first derivative of the log-density), i.e., the direction in which density is increasing the most, which also corresponds to the local mean, which is the expected value in a small ball around the current location. When the design matrix consists of orthogonal regressors, Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) demonstrates superior mean squared error performance relative to Group Lasso (GLasso/MKL) and exhibits model selection consistency under general regressor configurations. This superiority arises from ARD's approach to a fundamental challenge in regularized estimation: optimal hyperparameters are typically unknown functions of the true model parameters themselves. In practice, one must substitute these quantities with noisy, data-dependent empirical estimates, which produce objective functions of high sensitivity to noise fluctuations. The resulting instability manifests as poor performance across different data realizations, limiting the practical utility of standard approaches that optimize such noise-sensitive objectives. ARD addresses this challenge through a particular weighting scheme in the hyperparameter estimation procedure that introduces controlled bias into the mean squared error objective. While bias typically increases risk, this approach realizes a critical bias-stability trade-off: the biased estimator achieves substantially lower variance and enhanced robustness against noise compared to unbiased empirical alternatives. This trade-off between deliberately tolerated bias and enhanced estimation stability explains ARD's effectiveness observed in numerical experiments and practical applications, where finite-sample mean squared error performance often favors the stability-oriented biased estimator over solutions optimized for asymptotic properties alone. The mechanism through which ARD weights reshape the hyperparameter estimation landscape illustrates how introducing bias into intermediate estimation steps can paradoxically improve overall prediction accuracy when noise sensitivity poses the primary practical constraint. Remark 17 [PARD: penalized version of ARD] Note that, when one considers sparsity inducing performance, the use of a penalized version of ARD, for example, given by PARD, clearly may help in setting more blocks to zero, see Figure 4 (top). In comparison with GLasso, the important point here is that the non convex nature of PARD permits sparsity promotion without adopting too large a value of γ. This makes PARD a slightly perturbed version of ARD. Hence, PARD is able to induce more sparsity than ARD while maintaining similar performance in the reconstruction of the non null blocks. This is illustrated by the Monte Carlo results in Section 4.2. To better understand the role of γ, consider the orthogonal case discussed in Section 5.1, for sake of clarity. Recall the observation in Remark 11 that model selection consistency requires γ = γ n . It is easy to show that the oracle property (Zou, 2006) holds provided γ n n → ∞ and γ n n 2 → 0. However, large γ's tend to introduce excessive shrinkage, for example, see Figure 4 (center). It is well known (Leeb and Pötscher, 2005) that shrinkage estimators that possess the oracle property have unbounded normalized risk (normalized Mean Squared Error for quadratic loss), meaning that they are certainly not optimal in terms of Mean Squared Error. The toolbox architecture is based on a separation of the manifolds, the solvers and the problem descriptions. For basic use, one only needs to pick a manifold from the library, describe the cost function (and possible derivatives) on this manifold and pass it on to a solver. Accompanying tools help the user in common tasks such as numerically checking whether the cost function agrees with its derivatives up to the appropriate order, approximating the Hessian based on the gradient of the cost, etc. Manifolds in Manopt are created through factories that provide the mathematical operations needed to perform optimization on a particular search space. These operations allow algorithms to work with points and tangent vectors while respecting the geometry of the manifold. The resulting manifold structure also supplies conversions from derivatives expressed in the ambient space to their Riemannian counterparts. This interface encapsulates the geometric details, enabling users to describe a cost function in familiar terms and solvers to access the operations required by their algorithms. Solvers form the second component and implement various optimization algorithms through this manifold interface. In addition to computing iterates, they maintain logs that support the inspection of convergence and provide customizable stopping criteria. The third component, an optimization problem, is represented by a structure containing the manifold and the cost function, together with derivative information when available. Passing this structure to a solver brings together the geometry of the search space, the objective to be optimized and the algorithm used to seek a solution, while keeping their respective implementations separate. The extensibility of the toolbox rests on an abstraction layer between problem descriptions and solvers. Rather than depending on a particular manifold or a fixed representation of the cost function, solvers obtain the information they need through a common interface. Consequently, new manifolds, solvers and cost function representations can be incorporated as requirements evolve without requiring corresponding changes throughout the toolbox. This separation also provides a natural place to coordinate evaluations of the objective and its derivatives, whose implementations may share substantial computational work. Computing f (x) typically produces intermediate results which can be reused in order to compute the derivatives of f at x. To prevent redundant computations, Manopt incorporates an (optional) caching system, which becomes useful when transitioning from a proof-of-concept draft of the algorithm to a convincing implementation.

(2007)--and conjugate gradients (both with preconditioning), as well as steepest descent and a couple of derivative-free schemes. More solvers can be added. As the needs grow during the lifecycle of the toolbox and new ways of describing f become necessary (subdifferentials, partial gradients, etc.), it will be sufficient to update this interface. The PC-algorithm (Spirtes et al., 1993, 2000) was designed for learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) under the assumption of causal sufficiency, i.e., no unmeasured common causes and no selection variables. It learns a Markov equivalence class of DAGs that can be uniquely described by a so-called completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) (see Section 2 for a precise definition). The PC-algorithm is widely used in high-dimensional settings (Kalisch et al., 2010; Nagarajan et al., 2010; Stekhoven et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), since it is computationally feasible for sparse graphs with up to thousands of variables, and open-source software is available, for example in TETRAD IV (Spirtes et al., 2000) and the R-package pcalg (Kalisch et al., 2012). Moreover, the PC-algorithm has been shown to be consistent for high-dimensional sparse graphs (Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007; Harris and Drton, 2013). The relevance of the PC-algorithm extends beyond the estimation of CPDAGs under causal sufficiency. Other algorithms for learning directed graphical structures, including FCI, RFCI, and CCD, employ its adjacency search as a foundational step. Improvements to this search therefore have implications for several methods, since the adjacencies identified at this stage provide the basis for subsequent inference. Understanding the behavior of the PC-algorithm is thus important both for its direct application and for the broader class of procedures that rely on it. One limitation of the PC-algorithm is its order-dependence: the output can change when the variables are supplied in a different order, even though the data and other inputs remain unchanged. During adjacency search, decisions about removing edges affect the sets of variables available for subsequent conditional independence tests. Consequently, changing the order in which variables are considered can change the course of the search and the resulting graph. Although this issue has been recognized and attempts have been made to resolve it, it has received relatively little scholarly attention and has generally been regarded as a minor practical concern. In this work, we demonstrate that order-dependence can instead be a substantial problem in high-dimensional applications. Different orderings of the same variables can yield highly variable and inconsistent estimates, making the inferred structure sensitive to an arbitrary feature of the algorithm's input. Such variability complicates the interpretation of individual adjacencies and raises questions about the reproducibility of conclusions drawn from a single estimated graph. To examine the practical extent of this problem, we applied the PC-algorithm to high-dimensional data while varying the ordering of the variables. In particular, we analyzed the yeast gene expression data set of Hughes et al. (2000). We chose these data, despite the existence of larger and newer yeast gene expression data sets, since these data contain both observational and experimental data, obtained under similar conditions. The observational data consist of gene expression levels of 5361 genes for 63 wild-type yeast organisms, and the experimental data consist of gene expression levels of the same 5361 genes for 234 single-gene knockout strains. Hence, these data form a nice test bed for causal inference: algorithms can be applied to the observational data, and their output can be compared to the "gold standard" experimental data. (Please see Section 6 for more detailed information about the data.) First, we considered estimating the skeleton of the CPDAG from the observational data, that is, the undirected graph obtained by discarding all arrowheads in the CPDAG. Figure 1(a) shows the large variability in the estimated skeletons for 25 random orderings of the variables. Each estimated skeleton consists of roughly 5000 edges which can be divided into three groups: about 1500 are highly stable and occur in all orderings, about 1500 are moderately stable and occur in at least 50% of the orderings, and about 2000 are unstable and occur in at most 50% of the orderings. Since the FCI- and CCD-algorithms employ the adjacency search of the PC-algorithm as a first step, their resulting skeletons for these data are also highly order-dependent.

The RFCI-algorithm (Really Fast Causal Inference) is a compromise between two established procedures. It keeps most of the computational efficiency of the PC-algorithm, yet it returns output that can be read causally in the way FCI's output can, without assuming causal sufficiency. It therefore allows for latent confounders and selection variables, while avoiding the many additional conditional independence tests that make FCI expensive on larger graphs. The algorithm has three steps. Step 1 is identical to the initialization of the PC-algorithm: starting from the complete undirected graph, edges are removed whenever a conditional independence is found, and the corresponding separating sets are stored. Because these separating sets feed into every later step, the order in which variables are processed at this stage is the first potential source of order-dependence. Step 2 identifies v-structures. For each unshielded triple (a, b, c), where a and c are both adjacent to b but not to each other, RFCI does not simply consult the stored separating set. It first conducts additional conditional independence tests, checking whether a and b are independent given the separating set of a and c with a removed or b removed, and likewise for b and c. If one of these tests finds independence, the corresponding edge is removed and its separating set is stored, and the removal is handled so that it does not depend on the order in which triples are visited. Otherwise the triple is oriented as a v-structure when b is not in the separating set of a and c, and the pair of conditional dependencies is confirmed. Step 3 then applies the orientation rules familiar from FCI, with modifications for discriminating paths. These modifications again involve extra conditional independence tests along the path, so that the rules remain valid when the skeleton is not guaranteed to be complete. The result is an estimated RFCI-PAG, a partial ancestral graph that may contain slightly more edges than the corresponding FCI output, but is far cheaper to compute. From our results, it immediately follows that RFCI with any of our modifications of the PC-algorithm is correct in the oracle version, in the sense it outputs the true RFCI-PAG. Because of its more involved rules for v-structures and discriminating paths, one needs to make several adaptations to create a fully order-independent algorithm. For example, the additional conditional independence tests conducted for the v-structures are based on the separating sets found in Step 1. As already mentioned before (see Example 2) these separating sets are order-dependent, and therefore also the possible edge deletions based on them are order-dependent, leading to an order-dependent skeleton. To produce an orderindependent skeleton one should use a similar approach to the conservative one for the v-structures to make the additional edge removals order-independent. Nevertheless, we can remove a large amount of the order-dependence in the skeleton by using the stable version for the skeleton as a first step. We refer to this modification as RFCI-stable. Note that this procedure does not produce a fully order-independent skeleton, but as shown in Section 5.2, it reduces the order-dependence considerably. Moreover, we can combine this modification with CPC or MPC on the final skeleton to reduce the order-dependence of the v-structures. We refer to these modifications as CRFCI-stable and MRFCI-stable. Finally, we can again use lists for the orientation rules as in the FCI-algorithm to reduce the order-dependence caused by the orientation rules.

In the presences of latent and selection variables, one can also use the RFCI-algorithm (Colombo et al., 2012). This algorithm can be viewed as a compromise between PC and FCI, in the sense that its computational complexity is of the same order as PC, but its output can be interpreted causally without assuming causal sufficiency (but is slightly less informative than the output from FCI). RFCI works as follows. It starts with the first step of PC. It then has a more involved Step 2 to determine the v-structures (Colombo et al., 2012, Lemma 3.1). In particular, for any unshielded triple (X i , X j , X k ), it conducts additional tests to check if both X i and X j and X j and X k are conditionally dependent given sepset(X i , X j ) \ {X j } found in Step 1. If a conditional independence relationship is detected, the corresponding edge is removed and a minimal separating set is stored. The removal of an edge can create new unshielded triples or destroy some of them. Therefore, the algorithm works with lists to make sure that these actions are order-independent. On the other hand, if both conditional dependencies hold and X j is not in the separating set for (X i , X k ), the triple is oriented as a v-structure. Finally, in Step 3 it uses the ten orientation rules of Zhang (2008) with a modified orientation rule for the discriminating paths, that also involves some additional conditional independence tests. The output of the RFCI-algorithm is an (estimated) RFCI-PAG (Colombo et al., 2012, Definition 3.2). In this paper, we investigated this issue systematically, and resolved the various sources of order-dependence. There are of course many ways in which the order-dependence issues could be resolved, and we designed our modifications to be as simple as possible. Moreover, we made sure that existing high-dimensional consistency results for PC-, FCIand RFCI-algorithms remain valid for their modifications under the same conditions. We showed that our proposed modifications yield improved and more stable estimation in sparse high-dimensional settings for simulated data, while their performances are similar to the performances of the original algorithms in low-dimensional settings. One source of order-dependence deserves particular mention, because it is easy to overlook and affects the final output even when the skeleton and separating sets are estimated correctly. In the orientation phase, an edge may satisfy the conditions of more than one orientation rule at the same time. If the rules demand incompatible orientations, the edge can end up pointing in one direction or the other depending on which rule is applied first. The final graph is then a function of the application sequence rather than of the data alone. In our analysis we used the standard rule sequences from the original algorithms, and we found that this ordering effect can change the estimated edge marks even when all conditional independence decisions are held fixed. Resolving it therefore requires an explicit and well-defined treatment of such conflicts, not just a fixed sequence. The simplifications we propose improve upon earlier approaches to this problem while preserving formal validity, since the modified algorithms retain the soundness and consistency guarantees of their originals under the same conditions. Because the changes are deliberately minimal and act only on how orientation conflicts are handled, they are not tied to a single algorithm. They can be combined with other variants of the PC, FCI and RFCI families, and they can be incorporated into hybrid methods that combine constraint-based and score-based strategies. We therefore expect the stabilizing effect to carry over to a wide range of existing and future causal structure learning procedures, without requiring the rest of those procedures to be redesigned.

(2008), the modifications we propose are much simpler and we made sure that they preserve existing soundness, completeness, and high-dimensional consistency results. Finally, our modifications can be easily used together with other adaptations of constraint-based algorithms, for example hybrid versions of PC with score-based methods (Singh and Valtorta, 1993; Spirtes and Meek, 1995; van Dijk et al., 2003) or the PC ∗ algorithm (Spirtes et al., 2000, Section 5.4.2.3).

To compare the classifiers, we propose two complementary metrics computed over the whole collection of data sets. The first, the Probability of Achieving the Maximum Accuracy (PAMA), measures how often each classifier reaches the highest accuracy among all the classifiers on a data set. The second, P95, measures how often a classifier achieves at least 95% of that maximum accuracy. PAMA rewards a classifier only when it wins outright, while P95 also credits a classifier for coming close to the best result. The two are therefore expected to tell different stories, and reading them together gives a fuller picture of how reliable each method is across problems. The PAMA results (upper part of Table 5) show that elm kernel m, svm C and parRF achieve the highest probabilities, with 13.2%, 10.7% and 9.9% respectively. These values are low in absolute terms, which confirms that no single classifier dominates on most of the data sets: even the best one reaches the top accuracy on only a small fraction of them. The proposed dkp C ranks 13th by this measure, so it is not among the most frequent winners. P95 (middle part of Table 5) gives a more revealing comparison. According to it, parRF t, svm C and rf t maintain consistently strong performance, since they stay close to the maximum accuracy on a large share of the data sets. In contrast, elm kernel w, despite its high PAMA rank, exhibits less stability: it wins often enough to appear near the top of the first ranking, but it also fails to reach 95% of the maximum on many other data sets, which pushes it down in the second. Another interesting measurement is the Percentage of the Maximum Accuracy (PMA) achieved by each classifier, averaged over the whole collection of data sets (the 20 first are shown in the lower part of the Table 5). Again, parRF t is the best achieving 94.1%(±11.3) of the maximum accuracy, followed by other two Random Forests: rf t and rforest R (93.6% and 93.3% respectively). The parameter C directly specifies the regret bound via Corollary 6, providing a natural mechanism for controlling the degree of parallelization achievable within experimental deployments. Yet this parameter's inherently abstract nature creates a significant practical barrier for experimentalists attempting to translate theoretical guarantees into concrete implementation decisions. To overcome this specification challenge, several constructive selection methods have been proposed that ground C in more interpretable quantities. By setting C greater than γ(B_min - 1), where B_min represents a desired minimum batch size, practitioners can derive appropriate parameter values either through direct calculation or via constant factor bounds, thereby rendering the theoretical framework more accessible to practical application. This parameterization's flexibility becomes particularly valuable within two-stage adaptive algorithms that integrate Section 4.5 results with the regret guarantees of Corollary 6, enabling the achievement of substantial parallelism while preserving favorable asymptotic performance bounds. Such algorithms permit conservative initialization with small C values such as γ_1, enforcing nearly sequential behavior when algorithm knowledge remains limited, before adaptively increasing parallelism as the algorithm matures and identifies stable action sets. This progression from sequential to parallel operation represents an effective adaptive strategy, allowing dynamic control of exploration-exploitation tradeoffs while leveraging improved estimates to justify expanding parallelization across successive phases of experimentation. Sample compression schemes serve as a fundamental tool in learning theory, extracting a small set of representative examples that encode the essential information needed to reconstruct a hypothesis while simultaneously providing generalization bounds within the PAC-learning framework. The expressive power of such schemes is intimately constrained by the complexity of the underlying concept class, with the size of any compression scheme provably bounded by the VC-dimension of that class. A particularly intriguing connection emerges between these compression schemes and the Recursive Teaching Dimension (RTD), a teaching-theoretic model that quantifies the labeled examples a teacher must strategically provide to guide a learner toward the correct hypothesis. This relationship is mediated through unlabeled sample compression, where the samples themselves carry no explicit labels yet encode sufficient structural information to delineate the concept class. The precise relationship between RTD and unlabeled sample compression has been established through two complementary construction techniques: the corner-peeling method and the Tail Matching algorithm developed by Kuzmin and Warmuth. Both approaches systematically construct compression schemes achieving the maximum size bound of d for concept classes of VC-dimension d, though through fundamentally different mechanisms. A striking finding reveals that these apparently distinct methods--corner-peeling applied to maximum classes and the Tail Matching algorithm--produce exactly the same unlabeled samples, namely those that correspond precisely to the teaching sets a teacher would select under the RTD model. This convergence between teaching theory and compression theory demonstrates a deep structural alignment between the samples designated as informative by an optimal instructor and those required to minimally represent a concept class. This remarkable relationship between the RTD and sample compression suggests that the open question of whether or not the RTD is linear in the VC-dimension might be related to the long-standing open question of whether or not the best possible size of sample compression schemes is linear in the VC-dimension, cf. (Littlestone and Warmuth, 1996; Floyd and Warmuth, 1995). To this end, we observe that a negative answer to the former question would have implications on potential approaches to settling the second. In particular, if the RTD is not linear in the VC-dimension, then there is no mapping that maps every concept class of VC-dimension d to a superclass that is maximum of VC-dimension O(d). Constructing such a mapping would be one way of proving that the best possible size of sample compression schemes is linear in the VC-dimension.

Sample compression schemes are schemes for "encoding" a set of examples in a small subset of examples. For instance, from the set of examples they process, learning algorithms often extract a subset of particularly "significant" examples in order to represent their hypotheses. This way sample bounds for PAC-learning of a class C can be obtained from the size of a smallest sample compression scheme for C (Littlestone and Warmuth, 1996; Floyd and Warmuth, 1995). Here the size of a scheme is the size of the largest subset resulting from compression of any sample consistent with some concept in C. The relationship between RTD and unlabeled sample compression schemes (in which the compression sets consist only of instances without labels) is established via a recent result by Rubinstein and Rubinstein (2012). They show that, for any maximum class of VCdimension d, a technique called corner-peeling defines unlabeled compression schemes of size d. Like the RTD, corner-peeling is associated with a nesting of subclasses of the underlying concept class. A crucial observation we make in this paper is that every maximum class of VC-dimension d allows corner-peeling with an additional property, which ensures that the resulting unlabeled samples contain exactly those instances a teacher following the RTD model would use. Similarly, we show that the unlabeled compression schemes constructed by Kuzmin and Warmuth's Tail Matching algorithm (Kuzmin and Warmuth, 2007) exactly coincide with the teaching sets used in the RTD model, all of which have size at most d. This remarkable relationship between the RTD and sample compression suggests that the open question of whether or not the RTD is linear in the VC-dimension might be related to the long-standing open question of whether or not the best possible size of sample compression schemes is linear in the VC-dimension, cf. (Littlestone and Warmuth, 1996; Floyd and Warmuth, 1995). To this end, we observe that a negative answer to the former question would have implications on potential approaches to settling the second. In particular, if the RTD is not linear in the VC-dimension, then there is no mapping that maps every concept class of VC-dimension d to a superclass that is maximum of VC-dimension O(d). Constructing such a mapping would be one way of proving that the best possible size of sample compression schemes is linear in the VC-dimension.

We are concerned with the problem of estimating the topology of filamentary data structure. Data sets consisting of points roughly aligned along intersecting or branching filamentary paths embedded in 2 or higher dimensional spaces have become an increasingly common type of data in a variety of scientific areas. For instance, road reconstruction based on GPS traces, localization of earthquakes faults, galaxy reconstruction are all instances of a more general problem of estimating basic topological features of an underlying filamentary structure. The recent paper by Aanjaneya et al. (2012), upon which our work is based, contains further applications, as well as numerous references. To provide a more concrete example, consider Figure 1. The left hand side displays raw data portraying a neuron from the hippocampus of a rat (Gulyás et al., 1999). The data were obtained from NeuroMorpho.Org (Ascoli et al., 2007). The right hand side of the figure shows the output of the metric graph reconstruction obtained using the algorithm analyzed in this paper, originally proposed by Aanjaneya et al. (2012). The reconstruction, which takes the form of a graph, captures perfectly all the topological features of the neuron, namely, the relationship between the edges and vertices, the number of branching points and the degree of each node. Metric graphs provide a geometric framework for describing such filamentary structures: edges represent curves embedded in Euclidean space, while vertices record their endpoints and intersections. This representation connects the geometry of the observed data to the underlying network topology, allowing intersecting and branching paths to be studied within a common framework. When observations are noisy, however, the connectivity of the graph may be difficult to distinguish from apparent connections caused by perturbations of the sampled points. Our aim is to determine when the data contain enough information to recover the underlying graph structure accurately. We study this reconstruction problem from a statistical perspective, establishing the minimum sample size needed for accurate topological recovery and assessing the performance of the algorithm proposed by Aanjaneya et al. (2012). Our analysis provides an upper bound on the reconstruction risk of this algorithm, together with a corresponding lower bound on the risk achievable by any estimator. These matching bounds characterize the statistical difficulty of the problem and show that the existing reconstruction procedure achieves near-optimal performance. Thus, the analysis relates the sample size required for reliable recovery to the fundamental limits imposed by noisy observations.

Furthermore, in our theoretical analysis we characterize explicitly the minimal sample size required for perfect topological reconstruction as a direct function of parameters defining the shape of the metric graph, introduced in Section 2. Finally, we obtain a lower bound on the risk of topological reconstruction, which, in the noiseless case, almost matches the derived upper bound, indicating that the algorithm of Aanjaneya et al. (2012) behaves nearly optimally.

Blackwell's approachability theory and its variants have become a standard and useful tool in analyzing online learning algorithms (Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006) and algorithms for learning in games (Hart and Mas-Colell, 2000, 2001). The first application of Blackwell's approachability to learning in the online setup is due to Blackwell (1956b) himself. Numerous other contributions are summarized in the monograph by Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006). Blackwell's approachability theory enjoys a natural geometric interpretation that allows it to be used in situations where other learning methods (online convex optimization or exponential weights) do not seem to be easily applicable. In some sense, it can be used to go beyond the minimization of the regret to control quantities of a different flavor. Examples of such uses can be found in Mannor et al. (2009), which minimizes the regret together with path constraints, and in Mannor and Shimkin (2008), which minimizes the regret in games whose stage duration is not fixed. Recently, it has been shown by Abernethy et al. (2011) that approachability and low regret learning are equivalent in the sense that efficient reductions exist from one problem to the other. Another recent paper by Rakhlin et al. (2011) showed that approachability can be analyzed from the perspective of learnability using tools from learning theory. The application of approachability theory becomes particularly nuanced in the context of games with partial monitoring, where the fundamental information available to the decision maker departs significantly from the idealized case of complete reward feedback. In such settings, the decision maker does not observe rewards directly but instead receives signals whose informativeness spans a wide spectrum--ranging from sufficiently informative to permit accurate reward estimation, all the way to scenarios where the signals provide virtually no useful information about the underlying payoffs. This partial information structure is further complicated by the inability to determine the actual rewards obtained or the actions selected by opponents, creating an environment of substantial uncertainty in which traditional online learning approaches require careful adaptation. Within this challenging framework, regret minimization remains a viable objective, though the strategies for achieving it must carefully account for the degraded information available to the decision maker. One class of approaches builds on sufficient reward monitoring, leveraging those instances where the signals provide sufficient informativeness to enable estimation of true rewards from partial observations. A complementary direction employs exponential weights policies, which can be configured to achieve vanishing external regret despite variations in signal informativeness, thereby furnishing provable regret guarantees even when the decision maker lacks direct access to actual payoffs and opponent actions.

In partial monitoring the decision maker does not know how much reward was obtained and only gets a (random) signal whose distribution depends on the pair of actions taken by the decision maker and the opponent. There are two extremes of this setup that are well studied. On the one extreme we have the case where the signal includes the reward itself (or a signal that can be used to unbiasedly estimate the reward), which is essentially the celebrated bandits setup. The other extreme is the case where the signal is not informative (i.e., it tells the decision maker nothing about the actual reward obtained); this setting then essentially consists of repeating the same situation over and over again, as no information is gained over time. We consider a setup encompassing these situations and more general ones, in which the signal is indicative of the actual reward, but is not necessarily a sufficient statistic thereof. The difficulty is that the decision maker cannot compute the actual reward obtained nor the actions of the opponent. Regret minimization with partial monitoring (defined in the general sense of Rustichini, 1999) has been studied in several papers in the learning theory community. Piccolboni and Schindelhauer (2001), Mannor and Shimkin (2003), Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2006), Bartók et al. (2010, 2011), Foster and Rakhlin (2012) study games in which an accurate estimation of the rewards (or worst-case rewards) of the decision maker is possible thanks to some statistically sufficient monitoring; in this case, the notion of regret with partial monitoring reduces to the classical notion of regret with full monitoring. A general policy with vanishing external regret with partial monitoring is presented by Lugosi et al. (2008). This policy is based on exponential weights and a specific estimation procedure for the (worst-case) obtained rewards.

The paper is organized in three parts. The first reviews vector-valued approachability theory, establishing the classical framework in which rewards are represented by vectors. The second introduces set-valued approachability, a novel framework that captures reward ambiguity by having the decision maker receive sets rather than vectors. We develop this framework first for linear reward functions in Section 3, then extend it in Section 4 to non-linear concave-convex cases. Set-valued approachability is a distinct concept that cannot be directly reduced to classical vector-valued approachability. At the same time, it recovers familiar results, including characterizations of approachable sets and convergence rates independent of dimension. These foundational results provide tools for the paper's subsequent contributions. The third part studies approachability in repeated games with partial monitoring. The third part studies approachability in repeated games with partial monitoring. Previous general results in this setup suffered from at least one of the following drawbacks. They were either non-constructive (Rustichini, 1999) or were highly inefficient. The latter drawback refers to strategies that relied on some sort of lifting to the space of probability measures on mixed actions (see e.g., Lehrer and Solan, 2007 and Perchet, 2009, 2011a). They then typically required a fine grid of elements in this lifted space, which had to be progressively refined over time. This construction leads to two main issues: on the one hand, the step complexity continuously increases and becomes prohibitive in the number T of past steps. On the other hand, rates of convergence deteriorate and depend on the dimension. Our aim is therefore to devise algorithms that are efficient (as long as the projection onto some convex set can be done efficiently), with a constant step complexity (although it may depend on parameters of the problem at hand), and with rates of convergence independent of the ambient dimension. Our strategies are the first, to our knowledge, satisfying all of these properties in the general approachability framework. They do so because they do not rely on finer and finer grids; as a byproduct, they can also be considered more natural. Section 5 discusses in greater detail all the points mentioned in this paragraph.

We would like to emphasize that this inconsistency should not be viewed as a deficiency of DPMs and PYMs, but is simply due to a misapplication of them. As flexible priors on densities, DPMs are superb, and there are strong results showing that in many cases the posterior on the density converges in L 1 to the true density at the minimax-optimal rate, up to logarithmic factors (Ghosal et al., 1999; Ghosal and Van der Vaart, 2001; Lijoi et al., 2005; Tokdar, 2006; Ghosh and Ghosal, 2006; Tang and Ghosal, 2007; Ghosal and Van der Vaart, 2007; Walker et al., 2007; James, 2008; Wu and Ghosal, 2010; Bhattacharya and Dunson, 2010; Khazaei et al., 2012; Scricciolo, 2012; Pati et al., 2013); for a general overview, see Ghosal (2010). We would also like to stress that we do not intend to discourage the use of DPMs and PYMs for clustering--provided that the model is indeed well-suited to the application. In some situations, however, it may be that a finite mixture model with an unknown number of components is more appropriate--in particular, for cluster sizes that are all the same order of magnitude--and in such cases, one would expect to get better clustering results by using a variable-dimension mixture model (see Section 1.2.1 below) rather than a DPM or PYM. Existing work on posterior consistency of nonparametric mixtures has been primarily focused on the density estimation problem (as mentioned above), although recently, Nguyen (2013) has shown that the DPM posterior on the mixing distribution converges in the Wasserstein metric to the true mixing distribution. These existing results do not necessarily imply consistency for the number of components, since any mixture can be approximated arbitrarily well in these metrics by another mixture with a larger number of components (for instance, by making the weights of the extra components infinitesimally small). There seems to be no prior work on consistency of DPMs or PYMs for the number of components in a finite mixture (aside from Miller and Harrison, 2013, in which we discuss the very special case of a DPM on data from a univariate Gaussian "mixture" with one component of known variance). In the context of finite mixtures with a fixed but overestimated number of components, a related line of theoretical work has examined how the posterior behaves when the model is deliberately overfitted, that is, when it allows more components than the data-generating distribution actually contains. The results in this setting are encouraging: under suitable conditions on the prior, particularly on the concentration of the weight distribution, the superfluous components are predicted to receive vanishingly small posterior weight, so that the fitted mixture effectively empties the extra components rather than splitting genuine clusters among them. Analogous reasoning has been applied to Pitman--Yor process posteriors, where the hope is that the additional atoms permitted by the nonparametric prior will likewise be assigned negligible mass as the sample size grows. Taken at face value, these findings suggest that a nonparametric or overfitted mixture should, in the limit, reveal the true number of components through the components that carry nontrivial weight. The empirical picture, however, is considerably less tidy. Studies applying Dirichlet process mixtures to data drawn from finite mixtures have repeatedly reported that the posterior on the number of clusters tends to overshoot the truth. The source of this overestimation is not a wholesale misrepresentation of the underlying structure; the large, well-supported clusters are typically recovered quite faithfully. Rather, the posterior persistently places appreciable probability on partitions that include a handful of small, spurious clusters, often containing only one or a few observations, alongside the genuine ones. These tiny clusters do little to change the implied density, which is precisely why density-based or Wasserstein-based consistency results are silent about them, but they have a direct and visible effect on any inference about how many components the data contain. There is thus an apparent tension between the theoretical expectation that extra components should be suppressed and the practical observation that they stubbornly survive. Practitioners, confronted with this behavior, have developed a variety of workarounds. One common strategy is to prune the posterior by discarding clusters whose size or weight falls below some threshold, and then counting only those that remain. Another is to summarize the posterior by a single partition, either the maximum a posteriori partition or a posterior mean partition chosen to minimize an expected loss over pairwise co-clustering, and to read off the number of clusters from that point estimate. Each of these heuristics can produce more sensible answers in particular applications, and they are often adopted precisely because the raw posterior on the number of clusters appears untrustworthy. Yet none of them has been shown to be consistent in general: it remains unresolved whether thresholding, MAP selection, or posterior mean partitions recover the true number of components as the sample size tends to infinity, and the thresholds and loss functions involved are typically chosen without principled guidance. This gap between ad hoc practice and theoretical justification motivates a closer examination of what the posterior itself actually does with respect to the number of clusters.

We would like to emphasize that this inconsistency should not be viewed as a deficiency of DPMs and PYMs, but is simply due to a misapplication of them. As flexible priors on densities, DPMs are superb, and there are strong results showing that in many cases the posterior on the density converges in L 1 to the true density at the minimax-optimal rate, up to logarithmic factors (Ghosal et al., 1999; Ghosal and Van der Vaart, 2001; Lijoi et al., 2005; Tokdar, 2006; Ghosh and Ghosal, 2006; Tang and Ghosal, 2007; Ghosal and Van der Vaart, 2007; Walker et al., 2007; James, 2008; Wu and Ghosal, 2010; Bhattacharya and Dunson, 2010; Khazaei et al., 2012; Scricciolo, 2012; Pati et al., 2013); for a general overview, see Ghosal (2010). We would also like to stress that we do not intend to discourage the use of DPMs and PYMs for clustering--provided that the model is indeed well-suited to the application. In some situations, however, it may be that a finite mixture model with an unknown number of components is more appropriate--in particular, for cluster sizes that are all the same order of magnitude--and in such cases, one would expect to get better clustering results by using a variable-dimension mixture model (see Section 1.2.1 below) rather than a DPM or PYM. Existing work on posterior consistency of nonparametric mixtures has been primarily focused on the density estimation problem (as mentioned above), although recently, Nguyen (2013) has shown that the DPM posterior on the mixing distribution converges in the Wasserstein metric to the true mixing distribution. These existing results do not necessarily imply consistency for the number of components, since any mixture can be approximated arbitrarily well in these metrics by another mixture with a larger number of components (for instance, by making the weights of the extra components infinitesimally small). There seems to be no prior work on consistency of DPMs or PYMs for the number of components in a finite mixture (aside from Miller and Harrison, 2013, in which we discuss the very special case of a DPM on data from a univariate Gaussian "mixture" with one component of known variance). In the context of "species sampling", several authors have studied the Pitman--Yor process posterior (Pitman, 1996; Hansen and Pitman, 2000; James, 2008; Jang et al., 2010; Lijoi et al., 2007, 2008), and interestingly, James (2008) and Jang et al. (2010) have shown that on data from a continuous distribution, the posterior of a Pitman--Yor process with σ > 0 is inconsistent in the sense that it does not converge weakly to the true distribution. (In contrast, the Dirichlet process is consistent in this sense.) However, this is very different from our situation--in a species sampling model, the observed data is drawn directly from a discrete measure with a Pitman--Yor process prior, while in a PYM model, the observed data is drawn from a mixture with such a measure as the mixing distribution. Rousseau and Mengersen (2011) proved an interesting result on "overfitted" mixtures, in which data from a finite mixture is modeled by a finite mixture with too many components. In cases where this approximates a DPM, their result implies that the posterior weight of the extra components goes to zero. In a rough sense, this is complementary to our results, which involve showing that there are always some nonempty (but perhaps small) extra clusters. Empirically, many investigators have noticed that the DPM posterior tends to overestimate the number of components (e.g., West et al., 1994; Ji et al., 2010; Argiento et al., 2009; Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Onogi et al., 2011, and others), and such observations are consistent with our theoretical results. This overestimation seems to occur because there are typically a few tiny "extra" clusters, and among researchers using DPMs for clustering, this is an annoyance that is sometimes dealt with by pruning such clusters--that is, by removing them before calculating statistics such as the number of clusters (e.g., West et al., 1994; Fox et al., 2007). It may be possible to obtain consistent estimators in this way, but this remains an open question; Rousseau and Mengersen's (2011) results may be applicable here. Other possibilities are using a maximum a posteriori (MAP) partition or posterior "mean" partition (Dahl, 2006; Huelsenbeck and Andolfatto, 2007; Onogi et al., 2011) to estimate the number of components; again, the consistency of such approaches remains an open question to our knowledge.

In this work we study an approximate EM approach for spike-and-slab sparse coding which does not assume a-posteriori independence and which can model multiple modes. The novel approach can be considered as a variational EM approach but instead of using factored distributions or Gaussians, it is based on posterior distributions truncated to regions of high probability mass (Lücke and Eggert, 2010). Such truncated EM approaches have recently been applied to different models (see e.g., Puertas et al., 2010; Shelton et al., 2011; Dai and Lücke, 2012; Bornschein et al., 2013). In contrast to the previously studied factored variational approaches (Titsias and Lazaro-Gredilla, 2011; Mohamed et al., 2012; Goodfellow et al., 2013), the truncated approach will furthermore take advantage of the fact that in the case of a Gaussian slab and Gaussian noise model, integrals over the continuous latents can be obtained in closed-form (Lücke and Sheikh, 2012). This implies that the posteriors over latent space can be computed exactly if the sums over the binary part are exhaustively evaluated over exponentially many states. This enumeration of the binary part becomes computationally intractable for high-dimensional hidden spaces. However, by applying the truncated variational approach exclusively to the binary part of the hidden space, we can still fully benefit from the analytical tractability of the continuous integrals. The main goal of this paper is to derive and evaluate the truncated EM algorithm for the spike-and-slab sparse coding model, and to compare it systematically against factored variational approaches and other competing methods. We regard such a comparison as essential for the further development of sparse coding applications. Factored variational methods have recently been very successful, both in terms of the quality of the learned representations and in terms of their scaling to large problems. It is therefore important to understand how a method that retains posterior dependencies and multiple modes relates to approaches that give these up in exchange for simplicity. Whether the additional modeling power of a truncated posterior actually pays off, and at what computational cost, cannot be settled by theoretical arguments alone, because the answer depends on the data, on the number of latents, and on the optimization landscape that each approximation induces. We therefore use numerical experiments to assess each method along two main axes. The first is computational efficiency: we compare how the costs of the different algorithms scale with the size of the hidden space and how much computation is required to reach a given level of the objective. The second is the question of potential optimization biases. Any approximate EM scheme optimizes a surrogate of the log-likelihood, and the choice of approximation can systematically push the learned parameters away from the true maximum-likelihood solution. Factored posteriors, for instance, may favor solutions in which the latents are encouraged to be less dependent than the data warrant. By evaluating the methods under conditions where the ground truth is known, as well as on more general data, we can examine whether the recovered generative parameters differ systematically between approaches. This allows us to separate genuine differences in the quality of the solutions from differences that merely reflect how quickly or cheaply each algorithm runs.

Many real-life problems involve dealing with multiple objectives (Coello et al., 2006; Tesauro et al., 2008; Hernandez-del Olmo et al., 2012). For example, in a wireless sensor network the criteria consist of energy consumption and latency, which are conflicting objectives (Gorce et al., 2010). When the system engineer wants to optimize more than one objective, it is not always clear a priori which objectives might be correlated and how they influence each other. As the objectives are conflicting, there usually exists no single optimal solution. In those cases, we are interested in a set of trade-off solutions that balance the objectives. More precisely, we want to obtain the set of best trade-off solutions, i.e., the set of solutions that Pareto dominate all the other solutions but are mutually incomparable. There are, broadly speaking, two methodologically distinct ways of tackling such multi-objective problems. The first, often called the scalarization approach, simplifies the problem by converting it into a single-objective one. The objectives are combined into a single scalar function, typically through a weighted sum or a similar aggregation, governed by a set of adjustable parameters that encode the relative importance of each criterion. Once this transformation has been made, any standard single-objective optimizer can be applied. The strategy is attractive for its simplicity, but it has well-known limitations. When the problem is nonlinear, a scalarized formulation may be unable to recover parts of the set of trade-off solutions, so some of the best compromises remain unreachable no matter how the parameters are set. Moreover, a single run yields only one solution, and there is no guarantee that this solution lies in a useful region of the Pareto front. Obtaining a balanced coverage of the front therefore requires many separate runs, each with a different combination of parameter values, and it is difficult to know in advance which combinations will spread the solutions evenly. The second approach avoids this reduction and instead seeks to identify many optimal alternatives simultaneously within a single run. It does so with algorithms inspired by natural evolution, which maintain a population of candidate solutions rather than a single incumbent. Because the population is improved as a whole, through mechanisms such as selection, recombination and mutation, different members can converge toward different regions of the trade-off surface, and the algorithm can return a diverse approximation of the Pareto front without repeated restarts or manual parameter tuning. This population-based view fits naturally with the goal of finding a set of mutually incomparable solutions, and it has no need for the assumptions that cause scalarization to fail on nonlinear problems. For these reasons, evolutionary methods have demonstrated superior effectiveness on multi-objective problems and have become the dominant choice in practice.

There are two main approaches when dealing with multi-objective problems. The simplest way is to use a scalarization function (Miettinen and Mäkelä, 2002) which transforms the multi-objective problem into a standard single-objective problem. However, this transformation may not be valid when the scalarization function is non-linear. This approach is called a single-policy algorithm, as each run converges to a single solution. In order to find a variety of trade-off solutions, several parameterized scalarization functions are employed and their results are combined. However, the mapping from weight space to objective space is not guaranteed to be isomorphic (Das and Dennis, 1997). This means that it is not obvious how to define the weights in order to get a good coverage of the Pareto front of policies. Another class of algorithms are multi-policy algorithms. In contrast to focusing only on a single solution at a time, a multi-policy algorithm searches for a set of optimal solutions in a single run. Well-known examples of this class are evolutionary multi-objective algorithms, such as SPEA2 (Zitzler et al., 2002) and NSGA-II (Deb et al., 2002), which evolve a population of multi-objective solutions. These evolutionary multi-objective algorithms are amongst the most powerful techniques for solving multi-objective optimization problems.

Pareto Q-learning demonstrates substantial performance gains over conventional single-policy multi-objective reinforcement learning approaches through the adoption of set-based evaluation mechanisms that incorporate various multi-objective indicators. By maintaining and evaluating entire solution sets simultaneously rather than committing to a single policy, this approach captures the fundamental trade-offs inherent in multi-objective optimization problems and enables a more comprehensive exploration of the policy space. The architecture permits flexible integration of different evaluation criteria, each potentially suited to distinct problem configurations and optimization objectives. The Pareto indicator achieves particularly strong empirical performance by according equal treatment to all Pareto-optimal solutions, avoiding the arbitrary preference for specific objectives that characterizes alternative approaches. However, testing across diverse multi-objective environments revealed a critical insight: the greedy selection of locally dominating actions does not guarantee the discovery of globally Pareto-optimal policies. This gap between local action dominance and global solution optimality underscores the complexity of multi-objective reinforcement learning and demonstrates that myopic decision-making at individual states can lead to suboptimal trajectory-level behavior. While alternative indicators may offer advantages for specific problem domains by prioritizing particular policy characteristics, the Pareto indicator's balanced treatment provides a robust general approach. To maintain consistent reward accumulation throughout policy execution, a return vector tracking mechanism was proposed that follows the expected return vectors from initial to terminal states. This mechanism addresses the technical challenge of accurately aggregating multi-objective returns across episodes, ensuring that the reward accounting aligns with true expected performance across all objectives simultaneously. The introduction of such tracking components becomes increasingly important as algorithms scale to larger and more complex environments, where the consistency of value estimates directly influences the reliability of policy evaluation and selection. In Pareto Q-learning, the Q set 's grow according to the size of the Pareto front. Therefore, PQL is primarily designed for episodic environments with a finite number of Pareto optimal policies. To make the algorithm practically applicable for infinite horizon problems with a large value for the discount factor, we have to consider that all states can be revisited during the execution of an optimal policy. Upon revisiting a state, a different action that is optimal w.r.t. other criteria can be chosen. As explained by Mannor and Shimkin (2002), this offers a possibility to steer the average reward vector towards a target set using approaching policies. Alternatively, we could reduce the number of learned policies by using a consistency operator to select the same action during each revisit of some state, similar to the work of Wiering and de Jong (2007) for multi-criteria DP. Currently, PQL is limited to a tabular representation where each state-action pair stores a Q set . In order to make PQL applicable to real-life problems or ergodic environments, these sets should also be represented through function approximation. A possible idea is to fit the elements in each set through a geometric approach, such as for instance ordinal leastsquares. If the environment would consist of two or three objectives, we would be fitting the vectors on a curve or a plane, respectively. In that case, we would be learning the shape of the Pareto front through local interactions that each update parts of this geometric shape. To summarize, we note that PQL (1) can learn the entire Pareto front under the assumption that each state-action pair is sufficiently sampled, (2) while not being biased by the shape of the Pareto front or a specific weight vector. Furthermore, we have seen that (3) the set evaluation mechanisms provide indicative measures to explore the objective space based on local action selections and (4) the learned policies can be tracked throughout the state and action space.

We note that, regardless of the set evaluation mechanisms, PQL obtained better performance than the single-policy MORL algorithms and in the end PO-PQL sampled the entire Pareto front. For a more in-depth analysis of the results, we refer to Section 4.3.1. The current set evaluation mechanisms rely on basic multi-objective indicators to translate the quality of a set of vectors into a scalar value. Based on these indications, local action selection is possible during the learning phase. Currently, we have combined PQL with a cardinality, hypervolume and Pareto indicator. We have seen that the Pareto indicator performed the best on average as it treats every Pareto optimal solution equally. The cardinality and hypervolume set evaluation measures rate the actions also on additional criteria than the Pareto relation to provide a total order. We have seen that in more complex environments, these set evaluation mechanisms bias the action selection too much in order to learn the entire Pareto front. Nevertheless, it could be that the user is not interested in sampling the entire Pareto front but is looking for particular policies that satisfy certain criteria. For instance, other quality indicators such as the spread indicator (Van Veldhuizen and Lamont, 1998) could be used to sample policies that are both Pareto optimal and well-spread in the objective space. This can straightforwardly be incorporated in our framework. In our experiments, we have tested the Pareto Q-learning algorithm on environments with two and three objectives. However, as the algorithm is based on the Pareto relation, it is without problem applicable to environments with a larger number of objectives. Additionally, we also conducted empirical evaluations on a benchmark instance and we compared Pareto Q-learning's performance to several single-policy MORL algorithms. We have seen that selecting actions that are locally dominating does not guarantee that the overall combination of selected actions in each state, i.e., the policy, is globally Pareto optimal. As a solution, we proposed a mechanism that tracks a given return vector, i.e., we can follow a selected expected return consistently from the start state to a terminal state in order to collect the predicted rewards. The idea is that, after the discounted Pareto dominating rewards are propagated and the Q̂ set 's converge to a set of Pareto dominating policies, the user can traverse the tree of Q̂ set 's by applying a preference function. As highlighted in Section 2.1, a deterministic stationary policy suffices for single-objective reinforcement learning. In the case of MORL, White (1982) showed that deterministic non-stationary policies, i.e., policies that do not only condition on the current state but usually also on the time step t, can Pareto dominate the best deterministic stationary policies. As a result, in infinite horizon problems with large values for the discount factor, the number of non-stationary policies increases exponentially and therefore it can lead to an explosion of the sets. In order to make the algorithm practically applicable, Wiering and de Jong (2007) proposed the CON-MODP algorithm which solves the problem of non-stationary policies by introducing a consistency operator, but their work is limited to deterministic transition functions. Building on White's theoretical insights regarding Pareto optimality, researchers subsequently developed algorithms specifically designed to extract deterministic policies located on the convex boundary of the Pareto frontier. Barrett and Narayanan introduced Convex Hull Value Iteration (CHVI), a computational approach that directly identifies extreme-point policies within the decision space. By focusing on these vertices of the convex hull rather than attempting to characterize the entire policy frontier, the method offered a computationally tractable alternative to the combinatorial explosion of non-stationary policies, enabling practitioners to discover the most informative decision points without exhaustive enumeration. Recognizing opportunities to further enhance computational efficiency, Lizotte and colleagues subsequently refined this framework through weighted value-function learning, which substantially reduced the computational requirements for frontier computation while preserving the capacity to recover extreme-point solutions. Their methods were validated empirically on clinical datasets, illustrating the practical utility of these approaches in real-world sequential decision problems. Nevertheless, the resulting batch-based algorithms operate under two fundamental constraints: they necessitate prior knowledge of the environment's transition dynamics and reward structure, and they are restricted to extracting only the subset of extreme-point policies rather than fully characterizing the entire convex frontier.
