In this paper we presented a general framework, rational kernels, for extending kernel methods to the analysis of variable-length sequences and, more generally, of weighted automata. Many sequence kernels had previously been defined and analyzed one at a time, with a specialized algorithm devised for each. Rational kernels are instead defined by weighted transducers, which give a compact representation of the kernel and make a single general algorithm sufficient for its computation. The same algorithm, based on composition of weighted transducers and shortest-distance computation over the appropriate semiring, applies whether the inputs are strings or weighted automata, so that a new kernel does not require a new implementation. This also means that the choice of kernel reduces to the choice of a transducer, a representation that is both easy to describe and amenable to the optimization algorithms available for weighted automata and transducers. Because kernel methods such as support vector machines require kernels that are positive definite symmetric (PDS), we devoted a significant part of our analysis to the conditions under which a rational kernel has this property. We established several characterization results for PDS rational kernels, and we proved closure properties for them under operations such as sum, product, and Kleene closure. These results make it possible to build complex PDS kernels from simpler ones, with the guarantee that the result remains valid for use in learning algorithms. We further described ways of constructing PDS rational kernels directly, from weighted transducers defined over appropriate semirings, or from negative definite kernels. Together, these tools provide both a theoretical basis and a practical recipe for designing sequence kernels that are guaranteed to be well defined. We also gave a study of the relation between rational kernels and several kernels or similarity measures introduced by others. Rational kernels provide a unified framework for the design of computationally efficient kernels for strings or weighted automata. The framework includes in particular pair-HMM string kernels (Durbin et al., 1998; Watkins, 1999), Haussler's convolution kernels for strings, the path kernels of Takimoto and Warmuth (2003), and other classes of string kernels introduced for computational biology. We also showed that the classical edit-distance does not define a negative definite kernel when the alphabet contains more than one symbol, a result that to our knowledge had never been stated or proved and that can guide the study of kernels for strings in computational biology and other similar applications.

In this matrix-based classification approach, each column represents a learned feature property, and the pattern of entries across a row specifies the code assigned to a class. Sejnowski and Rosenberg first introduced the framework; Dietterich and Bakiri later refined it by bringing in error-correcting code theory. Their construction sought to maximize the matrix's capacity to correct errors: the minimum Hamming distance between any two rows determines how many misclassifications can be corrected while still identifying the intended class. That capacity depends not only on the distance between rows but also on the distinctness of the columns. If two columns are identical, or one is the opposite of the other, they encode redundant distinctions and can produce equivalent classification errors. Such columns add no independent protection against mistakes, so the matrix must avoid them to make effective use of its error-correcting capacity. To evaluate the effectiveness of different decoding methods and binary code schemes, we conducted experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets using AdaBoost and SVM classifiers. Our synthetic evaluation focused on comparing the classification accuracy achieved when optimizing over loss functions against the traditional approach of utilizing Hamming-distance matching for decoding. These experiments were designed to isolate the effect of decoding strategy while systematically varying the code architectures employed. The results from this initial phase were illuminating: the loss function optimization approach consistently delivered superior classification accuracy across multiple experimental settings, establishing it as a more principled and effective decoding strategy than the simpler Hamming-distance baseline. Beyond the decoding methodology, we examined whether different binary code architectures themselves contributed meaningfully to classification performance. Surprisingly, the findings indicated that various code schemes--despite their theoretical differences in information-theoretic properties and construction principles--delivered equivalent performance levels in practice. These observations motivated a systematic evaluation of multiple code schemes and decoding approaches on real-world benchmark datasets, allowing us to assess whether the synthetic findings generalize and to quantify the relative contributions of code design and decoding methodology in practical classification scenarios. One might argue that OVA is the first thing thought of when asked to come up with an approach for combining binary classifiers to solve multiclass problems. Although it is simple and obvious, the primary thesis of this paper is that the OVA scheme is extremely powerful, producing results that are often at least as accurate as other methods. This thesis seems quite innocuous and hardly worth writing a paper about, until one realizes that this idea is in opposition to a large body of recent literature on multiclass classification, in which a number of more complicated methods have been developed and their superiority over OVA claimed. These methods can be roughly divided between two different approaches--the "single machine" approaches, which attempt to construct a multiclass classifier by solving a single optimization problem (Weston and Watkins, 1998, Lee et al., 2001a,b, Crammer and Singer, 2001) and the "error correcting" approaches (Dietterich and Bakiri, 1995, Allwein et al., 2000, Crammer and Singer, 2002, Fürnkranz, 2002, Hsu and Lin, 2002), which use ideas from error correcting coding theory to choose a collection of binary classifiers to train and a method for combining the binary classifiers. A substantial portion of this paper is devoted to a detailed review and discussion of this literature. What we find is that although a wide array of more sophisticated methods for multiclass classification exist, experimental evidence of the superiority of these methods over a simple OVA scheme is either lacking or improperly controlled or measured. Several authors have reported that the all-vs-all (AVA) scheme, in which one classifier is trained for every pair of classes, outperforms the one-vs-all (OVA) scheme. We do not find these claims convincing. In the studies we reviewed, the comparisons were typically made on a small number of data sets, with base classifiers whose parameters were not carefully tuned, and the reported differences were rarely accompanied by any statistical test of significance. A gap of a fraction of a percentage point on a single test set can easily arise from chance variation in the sample or from a modest difference in how the underlying classifiers were regularized. Without sufficient experimental rigor, such results cannot support the conclusion that AVA is inherently the better scheme. A deeper issue concerns what one should expect from a sophisticated combination method in the first place. Methods such as error-correcting output codes, and many of the schemes that generalize or extend AVA, are designed to exploit the errors of the individual binary classifiers: if those errors are reasonably independent, a well-designed code or voting rule can correct many of them. Whether this helps depends heavily on the quality of the base classifiers. When the classifiers are weak, their mistakes are numerous and varied, and a sophisticated scheme has real room to improve on a naive one. When the classifiers are strong, as with support vector machines whose regularization and kernel parameters have been carefully tuned, the situation changes. Their errors tend to be highly correlated, since they are driven largely by the same difficult or ambiguous examples, so there is little independence left for a clever combination rule to exploit. In that regime a simple method, such as OVA, should be all that is needed. This account suggests a testable prediction: simple methods for combining strong classifiers should do at least as well as sophisticated methods for combining weak ones. The evidence we present bears this out. In carefully controlled experiments, we find that OVA with well-tuned base classifiers matches or outperforms the more elaborate alternatives, including AVA, whose apparent advantages in earlier work seem to stem from comparing against under-tuned baselines. The lesson is not that sophisticated schemes are never useful, but that their benefit is largely an artifact of weak underlying classifiers, and it disappears once those classifiers are made strong. Establishing this claim requires more than reporting that one scheme beat another on a given data set, and so we turn now to the question of how such comparisons should be made. One possible test for comparing two schemes is McNemar's test (McNemar, 1947, Everitt, 1977) (see Appendix A). A difficulty with McNemar's test is that it is insensitive to the number of points that the two schemes agree on; directly related to this, McNemar's test simply tells whether or not two scores are statistically significantly different (according to the assumptions inherent in the test), but gives no indication of how different they are. For this reason, we advocate and use a simple bootstrap method for computing confidence intervals of the difference in performance between a pair of classifiers. This method is described in Appendix A. 2 Additionally, in order to allow for comparisons by different researchers, we feel that it is crucial to present the actual error rates of various classification schemes, rather than (or in addition to) the relative differences in error between two schemes (see, for example, Dietterich and Bakiri, 1995, Crammer and Singer, 2001, 2002); this is particularly important given that different researchers are often unable to produce identical results using identical methodologies (see Appendix B). In general, we are not stating that an OVA scheme will perform substantially better than other approaches. Instead, we are stating that it will perform just as well as these approaches, and therefore it is often to be preferred due to its computational and conceptual simplicity. In Section 2 we describe support vector machines and regularized least squares classifiers, which are the binary classifiers used throughout this paper. In Section 3, we describe previous work in multiclass classification using binary classifiers. In Section 4, we present a large, carefully controlled and carefully measured set of experiments, as well as analysis of these experiments. In Section 5, we present theoretical arguments that help to indicate why OVA approaches perform well. Finally, in Section 6, we discuss our results and outline open questions. Note that notation which is used in Sections 4 and 5 is introduced in Section 3.2, as this seemed the most natural approach to the presentation.

One possible test for comparing two schemes is McNemar's test (McNemar, 1947, Everitt, 1977) (see Appendix A). For this reason, we advocate and use a simple bootstrap method for computing confidence intervals of the difference in performance between a pair of classifiers. This method is described in Appendix A. 2 Additionally, in order to allow for comparisons by different researchers, we feel that it is crucial to present the actual error rates of various classification schemes, rather than (or in addition to) the relative differences in error between two schemes (see, for example, Dietterich and Bakiri, 1995, Crammer and Singer, 2001, 2002); this is particularly important given that different researchers are often unable to produce identical results using identical methodologies (see Appendix B). In general, we are not stating that an OVA scheme will perform substantially better than other approaches. Instead, we are stating that it will perform just as well as these approaches, and therefore it is often to be preferred due to its computational and conceptual simplicity. In general, semi-supervised learning algorithms use both labeled and unlabeled data to train a classifier. Although a number of methods have been proposed, their effectiveness is not always clear. For example, Vapnik introduced the notion of transductive inference (Vapnik, 1998), which may be regarded as an approach to semi-supervised learning. Although some success has been reported (e.g., see Joachims, 1999), there has also been criticism pointing out that this method may not behave well under some circumstances (Zhang and Oles, 2000). Another popular semi-supervised learning method is co-training (Blum and Mitchell, 1998), which is related to the bootstrap method used in some NLP applications (Yarowsky, 1995) and to EM (Nigam et al., 2000). The basic idea is to label part of unlabeled data using a high precision classifier, and then put the "automaticallylabeled" data into the training data. However, it was pointed out by Pierce and Cardie (2001) that this method may degrade the classification performance when the assumptions of the method are not satisfied (that is when noise is introduced into the labels through non-perfect classification). This phenomenon is also observed in some of our experiments reported in Section 5. A central limitation of existing semi-supervised learning approaches lies in their reliance on unlabeled data to construct smooth function classes, typically through graph-based structures. While such methods aim to leverage the abundance of unlabeled examples, the smoothness assumptions embedded in these constructions often fail to guarantee predictive power on the target task. The learned function classes may be well-smoothed according to the graph structure, yet lack the discriminative capacity needed for effective prediction. This observation motivates a fundamental shift in perspective: rather than attempting to improve semi-supervised learning by refining the smoothness assumptions imposed on individual problems, a more promising direction involves directly learning function classes that inherently possess strong predictive properties. This reorientation suggests considering the structure of predictors across multiple related prediction problems simultaneously. When one observes multiple prediction tasks and their corresponding solutions, the collection of predictors provides an empirical sample from the underlying space of predictor structures. By analyzing this sample, one can identify and extract the common structural patterns that characterize effective predictors. These discovered structures capture regularities shared across problems and represent genuine features of the predictor space rather than assumptions imposed by prior beliefs about smoothness. Such structures, once identified, can be transferred and applied to improve performance on individual prediction tasks. We propose a framework called structural learning, which operationalizes this principle by jointly analyzing multiple prediction problems to discover and exploit common predictive structures. Rather than treating each supervised learning problem in isolation, the approach constructs representations that capture the essential patterns shared across problems. The method learns effective function classes by observing how different prediction tasks relate to one another, thereby obtaining information about the underlying structure of the predictor space that would be inaccessible from a single problem alone. This integrated perspective allows the framework to identify and leverage structural regularities that improve predictive performance beyond what traditional semi-supervised or single-task approaches can achieve. The idea that one can benefit by considering multiple problems together has appeared in the statistical literature. In particular, Bayesian hierarchical modeling is motivated from the same principle. However, the framework developed in this paper is under the frequentist setting, and the most relevant statistical studies are shrinkage methods in multiple-output linear models (see Section 3.4.6 of Hastie et al., 2001). In particular, the algorithm proposed in Section 3 has a form similar to a shrinkage method proposed by Breiman and Friedman (1997). However, the framework presented here (as well as the specific algorithm in Section 3) is more general than the earlier statistical studies. In the machine learning literature, related work is sometime referred to as multi-task learning, for example, see (Baxter, 2000; Ben-David and Schuller, 2003; Caruana, 1997; Evegniou and Pontil, 2004; Micchelli and Ponti, 2005) and references therein. We shall call our procedure structural learning since it is a more accurate description of what our method does in the semi-supervised learning setting. That is, we transfer the predictive structure learned from multiple tasks (on unlabeled data) to the target supervised problem. In the literature, this idea is also referred to as inductive transfer. The success of this approach depends on whether the learned structure is helpful for the target supervised problem. It follows that although this work is motivated by semi-supervised learning, the general structural learning (or multi-task learning) problem considered in the paper is of independent interest. For semi-supervised learning, as we shall show later, the multiple prediction problems needed for structural learning can be generated from unlabeled data. However, the basic framework can also be applied to other applications where we have multiple prediction problems that are not necessarily derived from unlabeled data (as in the earlier statistical and machine learning studies). Because of this, the first part of the paper focuses on the development of a general structural learning paradigm as well as our algorithm. The main implication is that one can reliably learn a good underlying structure if it is shared by multiple prediction problems. In the second part, we shall demonstrate how to apply the idea of learning structure to semi-supervised learning, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in this context. A short version of this paper, mainly reporting some empirical results, appeared in ACL (Ando and Zhang, 2005). This version includes a more complete derivation of the proposed algorithm, with theoretical analysis and several additional experimental results. In Section 2, we formally introduce the structural learning problem under the framework of standard machine learning. We then propose a specific algorithm that finds a common low-dimensional feature space shared by the multi-problems. The algorithm will be studied in Section 3, with theoretical analysis given in Appendix A. Section 4 shows how to apply structural learning in the context of semi-supervised learning. The basic idea is to use unlabeled data to generate auxiliary prediction problems that are useful for discovering important predictive structures. Such structures can then be estimated using the algorithm developed in Section 3. We will also give intuitive justifications on why the structure shared by the artificially created auxiliary problems is helpful for the supervised problem. Experiments are provided in Section 5 to illustrate the effectiveness of the algorithm proposed in Section 3 on several semi-supervised tasks. Section 6 presents a high level summary of the main ideas developed in the paper.

In the first strategy, we regard some observable substructures of the input data X as auxiliary class labels, and try to predict these labels using other parts of the input data. For instance, for the word tagging task mentioned above, at each word position, we can create auxiliary problems by regarding the current word as auxiliary labels, which we want to predict using the surrounding words. We create one binary classification problem for each possible word value, and hence can obtain many auxiliary problems using this idea. More generally, we can construct auxiliary classification problems by masking selected features of the input and training classifiers to predict their values from the remaining, unmasked features. In implementation, we replace the masked values with zeros, withholding the information to be predicted while retaining the other features as inputs to the classifiers. The original, observable values of the masked features provide the corresponding auxiliary labels. Thus, this procedure generates labeled training problems directly from the input data, without requiring separately supplied annotations. These auxiliary problems also naturally satisfy the relevancy requirement for learning feature representations. To predict a masked feature, a classifier must exploit information in the unmasked features that is correlated with the prediction target. Features that support the same prediction therefore share a relationship with the masked feature, providing a basis for identifying correlations among them. By learning representations useful for these auxiliary tasks, we seek to capture groups of features that combine predictive capability with mutual correlation, rather than selecting features solely on the basis of their individual occurrence in the input.

In the actual implementation, we just replace the masked feature values by zero, which has the same effect. The automatic-labeling requirement is satisfied since the auxiliary labels are observable to us. To see why this technique may naturally meet the relevancy requirement, we note that feature components that can predict a certain masked feature are correlated to the masked feature, and thus are correlated among themselves. Therefore this technique helps us to identify correlated features with predictive power.

Ex 3. Predict the prediction of classifier T 1 . The simplest auxiliary task created by following this strategy is the prediction of the class labels proposed by classifier T 1 . When the target task is c-way classification, c binary classification problems are obtained in this manner. For example, suppose that we train a classifier using only one half of content words for the text genre categorization task. Then, one of auxiliary problems will be to predict whether this classifier would propose sports category or not, based on the other half of content words only. A more advanced auxiliary task is to predict the ordered combination of the top-k classes to which classifier T 1 assigns the highest confidence values. Here, the prediction concerns not only which classes appear among the leading candidates, but also their relative order. For example, texts for which sports receives the highest confidence and another genre receives the second highest confidence can be distinguished from texts for which these positions are reversed. Learning to predict such combinations allows the auxiliary classifier to capture finer-grained distinctions within the original classes, since examples assigned the same leading label may exhibit different patterns among the remaining candidates. Each ordered combination can be treated as a separate binary prediction problem, asking whether T 1 would produce that combination, thereby transforming the multi-way classification task into a collection of binary tasks. A second extension is to predict the labels proposed by T 1 together with the ranges in which their confidence values fall. Rather than asking only whether T 1 would propose the sports category, an auxiliary task can ask whether it would propose sports with confidence above a specified threshold. Additional tasks can distinguish confidence ranges associated with the same proposed label, allowing the auxiliary classifier to learn differences between examples that T 1 labels similarly but evaluates with different degrees of confidence. In the text genre setting, these predictions are still made from the other half of the content words, while the labels and confidence values produced by T 1 define the auxiliary targets. This construction thus incorporates information about both the classifier's proposed category and the confidence accompanying that proposal.

Given an arbitrary input space X without any known structure, we argue that it is often possible to learn what a good predictor looks like from multiple prediction problems. The key reason is that in practice, not all predictors are equally good (or equally likely to be observed). In real world applications, one usually observes "smooth" predictors where the smoothness is with respect to a certain intrinsic underlying distance on the input space. In general, if two points are close in this intrinsic distance, then the values that a good predictor produces at these points are also likely to be similar. In particular, completely random predictors are likely to be bad predictors, and are rarely observed in practical applications. Machine learning systems exploit this tendency toward smoothness by explicitly constructing hypothesis spaces that enforce or encourage smooth functions. Methods such as kernel-based approaches and data-manifold techniques are fundamentally predicated on the premise that distance relationships in the input space should translate to similarity in function values. By selecting appropriate distance or similarity metrics, these approaches constrain the learned predictor to respect the geometric structure of the data, penalizing abrupt changes in predictions and promoting consistency across neighboring regions. This structural bias toward smoothness serves as a powerful inductive principle, reducing the complexity of the hypothesis class and guiding learning toward functions that generalize well beyond the training data. Determining the appropriate distance measure in practice, however, remains a fundamental and often intractable challenge. In discrete domains such as natural language processing, where inputs are words or symbolic sequences, the notion of meaningful proximity becomes inherently elusive, and conventional distance metrics frequently fail to capture the semantic or linguistic relationships that should govern predictor smoothness. Even in continuous vector spaces, where distance appears more naturally defined, the underlying assumptions about what constitutes meaningful proximity are difficult to justify rigorously. Consequently, practitioners must inevitably make somewhat arbitrary choices about distance functions, and once such a choice is made, it remains fundamentally unclear whether the smoothness properties enforced by the resulting hypothesis space are truly well-defined and appropriate with respect to that particular distance metric.

For example, kernel methods constrain the smoothness of a function using a certain reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) norm. For such functions (in a RKHS), closeness of two points under a certain metric often implies closeness in predictive values. One may also consider more complicated smoothness conditions that explore the observed data-manifold (e.g. graph-based semi-supervised learning methods mentioned in the introduction). Such a smoothness condition will be useful if it correlates well with predictive ability. In general, a good distance measure on X induces a good hypothesis space which enforces smoothness with respect to the underlying distance. However, in reality, it is often not clear what is the best distance measure in the underlying space. For example, in natural language processing, the space X consists of discrete points such as words, for which no appropriate distance can be easily defined. Even for continuous vector-valued input points, it is difficult to justify that the Euclidean distance is better than something else. Even after a good distance function can be selected, it is not clear whether we can define appropriate smoothness conditions with respect to the distance.

SimpleSVM and LASVM both construct a kernel expansion through an iterative process that adds or removes support vectors. They differ, however, in the optimization performed on the current support vector set. SimpleSVM solves the full SVM quadratic programming problem on this set, seeking optimal coefficients at each iteration. LASVM instead takes steps that improve the dual objective function without requiring an optimal solution at every intermediate stage. These choices lead to different computational requirements and completion procedures: SimpleSVM requires no separate finishing step, whereas LASVM requires a finishing step to complete the optimization. Solving the current problem to optimality does not necessarily produce the most effective progression through the training examples. In SimpleSVM, this strategy discards support vectors too aggressively, limiting the expansion retained as subsequent examples are processed. Consequently, despite optimizing over its current support vector set at each iteration, SimpleSVM cannot achieve competitive accuracy within a single epoch. LASVM's more incremental improvement of the dual objective allows it to defer completion of the optimization until the finishing step. The distinction between these approaches also shapes the operations used to maintain the kernel expansion and their associated computational costs. Each SimpleSVM iteration updates the current kernel expansion using rank 1 matrix updates (Cauwenberghs and Poggio, 2001) whose computational cost grows as the square of the number of support vectors. LASVM performs these updates using SMO direction searches whose cost grows linearly with the number of examples. Rank 1 updates make good sense when one seeks the optimal coefficients. On the other hand, all the kernel values involving support vectors must be stored in memory. The LASVM direction searches are more amenable to caching strategies for kernel values.

When we have access to an abundant source of training examples, the simple way to reduce the complexity of a learning algorithm consists of picking a random subset of training examples and running a regular training algorithm on this subset. Unfortunately this approach renounces the more accurate models that the large training set could afford. This is why we say, by reference to statistical efficiency, that an efficient learning algorithm should at least pay a brief look at every training example. The online LASVM algorithm meets this requirement. A single pass over the training set is enough for it to reach a generalization performance comparable to that of a standard SVM trained to convergence, and it does so after one epoch. Each example is looked at once as it arrives, so the algorithm never has to hold the whole kernel problem in memory. Its memory footprint is substantially smaller than that of a batch solver, which must keep a large set of candidate support vectors and their kernel values available while it iterates. This profile also suits how modern storage systems behave. Disks and network file systems deliver sequential reads far more efficiently than random access, and an algorithm that streams through the data in order takes advantage of this instead of fighting it. Active selection of training examples adds further practical benefits on top of the online procedure. Rather than processing examples in the order they are stored, the learner can choose to process those that are most informative given its current model. Because it concentrates on such examples, the final solution needs fewer support vectors. Fewer support vectors in turn lower both the computational time and the memory demands, since every kernel evaluation during training and prediction scales with the size of the support set. The search for informative examples can also be parallelized. Candidate examples can be scored independently against the current model by several workers at once, while the update of the model itself remains a comparatively small sequential step.

Learning algorithms can often reduce their computational requirements by exploiting differences in how informative individual training examples are, while still achieving competitive performance. This motivates methods that adapt the work devoted to each example rather than treating all examples as equally valuable. For kernel classifiers, a central computational choice is which examples to retain in the active set of support vectors. Changing this set has an immediate effect on the cost of each iteration: adding examples requires additional kernel computations, whereas removing them reduces that cost. The overall trade-off is less straightforward, however, because the active set also shapes the classifier's progress. It therefore remains unclear how changes that make individual iterations cheaper or more expensive affect the total number of iterations needed to reach satisfactory performance. Online kernel algorithms, such as the kernel perceptrons usually produce different classifiers when given different sequences of training examples. Section 3 proposes an online kernel algorithm that converges to the SVM solution after many epochs. The final set of support vectors is intrinsically defined by the SVM QP problem, regardless of the path followed by the online learning process. Intrinsic support vectors provide a benchmark to evaluate the impact of changes in the active set of current support vectors. Augmenting the active set with an example that is not an intrinsic support vector moderately increases the cost of each iteration without clear benefits. Discarding an example that is an intrinsic support vector incurs a much higher cost. Additional iterations will be necessary to recapture the missing support vector. Empirical evidence is presented in Section 3.5.

By suggesting that all examples should not be given equal attention, we first state that all training examples are not equally informative. This question has been asked and answered in various contexts (Fedorov, 1972; Cohn et al., 1990; MacKay, 1992). Our work answers this question by proposing algorithms that exploit these differences and achieve very competitive performances. LASVM is an incremental kernel classifier that combines the sequential incorporation of training examples with the removal of outdated examples from the current kernel expansion. Rather than allowing every incorporated example to remain indefinitely, the method revisits the expansion and discards examples whose contributions are no longer needed. Its optimization procedure reworks sequential methods so that incremental updates can be followed by further refinement toward convergence to a standard SVM solution. Compared with earlier incremental kernel approaches, LASVM offers improved handling of corrupted data together with verified convergence guarantees, giving the procedure both practical robustness and a firm optimization basis. The incremental formulation also offers advantages over batch-based solvers: it reduces computational demands and permits training examples to be processed one at a time. This makes it possible to build and refine the classifier as examples become available, while retaining the ability to attain the performance of conventional SVM training. Experimental evidence shows that LASVM achieves performance parity with a standard SVM after processing all training examples exactly once. The central mechanism is the coordination of updates that introduce examples into the kernel expansion with updates that reconsider the coefficients of examples already present. This is achieved by alternating two kinds of direction searches named PROCESS and REPRO- CESS . Each direction search involves a pair of examples. Direction searches of the PROCESS kind involve at least one example that is not a support vector of the current kernel expansion. They potentially can change the coefficient of this example and make it a support vector. Direction searches of the REPROCESS kind involve two examples that already are support vectors in the current kernel expansion. They potentially can zero the coefficient of one or both support vectors and thus remove them from the kernel expansion.

This section presents a novel online SVM algorithm named LASVM . There are two ways to view this algorithm. LASVM is an online kernel classifier sporting a support vector removal step: vectors collected in the current kernel expansion can be removed during the online process. LASVM also is a reorganization of the SMO sequential direction searches and, as such, converges to the solution of the SVM QP problem. Compared to basic kernel perceptrons (Aizerman et al., 1964; Freund and Schapire, 1998), the LASVM algorithm features a removal step and gracefully handles noisy data. Compared to kernel perceptrons with removal steps (Crammer et al., 2004; Weston et al., 2005), LASVM converges to the known SVM solution. Compared to a traditional SVM solver (Platt, 1999; Chang and Lin, 2001- 2004; Collobert and Bengio, 2001), LASVM brings the computational benefits and the flexibility of online learning algorithms. Experimental evidence indicates that LASVM matches the SVM accuracy after a single sequential pass over the training examples. LASVM can be used in the online setup where one is given a continuous stream of fresh random examples. The online iterations process fresh training examples as they come. LASVM can also be used as a stochastic optimization algorithm in the offline setup where the complete training set is available before hand. Each iteration randomly picks an example from the training set. In practice, the online iterations of LASVM can be organized into epochs, each of which visits the training examples sequentially in a randomly shuffled order. A finishing step is then performed after a predefined number of epochs. This organization accommodates both uses of the algorithm: a single epoch corresponds to online learning, in which each example is processed once, whereas multiple epochs allow LASVM to revisit the available examples and serve as a stochastic optimization method in the offline setting. Random shuffling determines the order of presentation within each epoch while ensuring that all training examples are visited before the next epoch begins. To analyze the convergence properties of the online iterations, we first set aside the finishing step and suppose that the iterations continue indefinitely. This separates the behavior of the iterative procedure from the additional optimization performed at termination. The analysis focuses on the τ-violating pairs that remain at iteration T, namely those pairs whose violation still exceeds the prescribed tolerance. Their persistence characterizes the optimality conditions that have yet to be satisfied, so studying their behavior as the iterations proceed provides a basis for understanding convergence.

The online iterations of LASVM behave much like the iterations of the SMO algorithm. Each PROCESS step admits a new example into the working set, and each REPROCESS step then picks a pair of coefficients that violates the optimality conditions by more than the tolerance τ and updates them, just as SMO would. Repeated iterations therefore exploit the τ-violating pairs one after another, and the objective improves steadily as they do. Once no τ-violating pair remains, the current coefficients form a τ-approximate solution, and the algorithm stops changing them. No further update can be justified at that tolerance, so later iterations leave the coefficients untouched. In practice, LASVM is not run until this condition is reached. It is usually run for a predefined number of epochs. Each epoch makes one sequential pass of online iterations over the training examples, which are randomly shuffled beforehand so that the order of presentation does not bias the solution. After the last epoch, a finishing step tightens the solution by running REPROCESS until the τ-approximate condition is met. This procedure is cheap relative to full batch training, and the empirical results are encouraging. A single epoch already produces a classifier that is nearly equivalent to the complete SVM solution, so additional epochs usually bring little further gain in accuracy. Graphical models and message-passing algorithms defined on graphs comprise a growing field of research. In particular, the belief propagation (or sum-product) algorithm has become a popular means of solving inference problems exactly or approximately. One part of its appeal lies in its optimality for tree-structured graphical models (models which contain no loops). However, its is also widely applied to graphical models with cycles. In these cases it may not converge, and if it does its solution is approximate; however in practice these approximations are often good. Recently, some additional justifications for loopy belief propagation have been developed, including a handful of convergence results for graphs with cycles (Weiss, 2000; Tatikonda and Jordan, 2002; Heskes, 2004). The approximate nature of loopy belief propagation is often a more than acceptable price for performing efficient inference; in fact, it is sometimes desirable to make additional approximations. There may be a number of reasons for this--for example, when exact message representation is computationally intractable, the messages may be approximated stochastically (Koller et al., 1999) or deterministically by discarding low-likelihood states (Coughlan and Ferreira, 2002). For belief propagation involving continuous, non-Gaussian potentials, some form of approximation is required to obtain a finite parameterization for the messages (Sudderth et al., 2003; Isard, 2003; Minka, 2001). Additionally, simplification of complex graphical models through edge removal, quantization of the potential functions, or other forms of distributional approximation may be considered in this framework. Finally, one may wish to approximate the messages and reduce their representation size for another reason--to decrease the communications required for distributed inference applications. In distributed message passing, one may approximate the transmitted message to reduce its representational cost (Ihler et al., 2004a), or discard it entirely if it is deemed "sufficiently similar" to the previously sent version (Chen et al., 2004). Through such means one may significantly reduce the amount of communications required. To understand the consequences of these approximations on graphs with cycles, we compare the resulting loopy belief propagation (BP) messages and beliefs with those produced by exact BP on the same graph. This distinction matters: the goal is to isolate the error introduced by approximating messages, rather than to measure the gap between BP and the true marginals. Even exact BP can be inaccurate on a loopy graph, so conflating these two sources of error would obscure what the approximation itself changes. We use dynamic range to quantify message error and derive conditions under which approximate BP converges, together with bounds on the fixed points it reaches. These results describe how local deviations can propagate around cycles and affect the eventual beliefs. The analysis also extends to approximate BP variants and considers settings in which errors arise independently, making it possible to examine how the guarantees apply across different sources and forms of approximation. As a complementary perspective, we consider KL divergence as an alternative measure of error. It offers more direct intuition about average-case discrepancies between distributions, whereas dynamic range supports guarantees framed around worst-case deviations. The KL-based analysis is therefore less rigorous as a convergence and error guarantee, but helps clarify what approximation may mean in typical rather than extreme cases.

Our experiments reveal serious differences between Laplace's method and EP when used in GPC models. The results corroborate the considerations about the two approximations based on the structure of the posterior given in Section 5. Although only a handful of data sets have been used in the study, we believe the conclusions to be well-founded and generally valid. From the structural properties of the posterior we described why Laplace's method systematically underestimates the mean m. The resulting approximate posterior GP over latent functions will have too small amplitude, although the sign of the mean function will be mostly correct. As an effect Laplace's method gives over-conservative predictive probabilities, and diminished information about the test labels. This effect has been shown empirically on several real world examples. Large resulting discrepancies in the actual posterior probabilities were found, even at the training locations, which renders the predictive class probabilities produced under this approximation grossly inaccurate. Note, the difference becomes less dramatic if we only consider the classification error rates obtained by thresholding p ∗ at 1/2. For this particular task, we have seen the sign of the latent function tends to be correct (at least at the training locations). However, the performance on benchmark data sets also revealed the error rates obtained by Laplace's method to be inferior to EP results. The EP approximation has shown to give results very close to MCMC both in terms of predictive distributions and marginal likelihood estimates. We have shown and explained why the marginal distributions of the posterior can be well approximated by Gaussians. To assess the practical utility of these approximation schemes, we systematically compared Laplace's method and Expectation Propagation as approximate inference techniques for binary Gaussian process classification. Both methods were evaluated on their capacity to compute marginal likelihood values and estimate optimal hyper-parameters, metrics essential for model selection and tuning in real applications. While Laplace's method provides computational simplicity through a closed-form approximation, our experiments revealed that its accuracy limitations become problematic when precise marginal likelihood estimates are required. In contrast, Expectation Propagation maintained consistency with MCMC-derived posteriors across multiple datasets and problem configurations, demonstrating superior reliability for the inferential tasks central to Bayesian model comparison. When benchmarking Gaussian process classifiers against support vector machines as a standard baseline, we observed that SVMs achieved marginally lower test error rates on several benchmark problems. However, this performance advantage did not translate to substantially better predictive distributions; the probabilistic predictions from well-calibrated GPC models proved comparable to SVM decision functions when appropriately interpreted. The critical practical distinction lies in the inherent properties of each approach: while SVMs require careful hyperparameter tuning through cross-validation and offer no principled framework for model selection, Gaussian process classifiers enable fully Bayesian hyperparameter optimization through marginal likelihood maximization. This capability renders GPC computationally efficient for practitioners seeking to avoid the overhead of cross-validation procedures. These findings establish Expectation Propagation as the preferred algorithmic choice for approximate Bayesian inference in Gaussian process classification when computational constraints preclude the use of MCMC sampling. EP delivers both accurate predictive probability estimates and reliable marginal likelihood values necessary for principled hyperparameter selection, substantially outperforming Laplace's method in scenarios demanding inferential precision. Consequently, practitioners implementing approximate GPC should prioritize EP-based approximations and exercise caution against adoption of the Laplace approximation, whose inadequate accuracy undermines the Bayesian model selection advantages that motivate probabilistic classification in the first place.

Recent advances in data acquisition and computational power have stimulated interest in flexible Bayesian models capable of representing complex dependencies in large collections of observations. The expressive power of these models, however, comes with substantial computational demands: exact inference is generally intractable, making approximate methods of polynomial complexity essential. The most widely used approach is the variational Bayes approximation, in which inference is restricted to a tractable family of distributions. A member of this family is selected by minimizing the Kullback--Leibler divergence from the approximate distribution to the posterior. This optimization yields an upper bound on the free energy and replaces the original inference problem with a tractable variational objective. The quality of the resulting approximation depends strongly on the choice of distribution family. Multivariate Gaussian approximations can retain correlations between variables through their covariance structure, but their direct application is restricted to continuous variables. For discrete variables, or variables subject to constraints incompatible with a Gaussian representation, the standard variational treatment instead relies on mean-field factorizing approximations. These simplify inference by expressing the joint distribution as a product of distributions over individual variables, thereby removing the correlations that may be central to the posterior structure. Although this factorization makes the variational optimization tractable, it typically underestimates fluctuations and can give an overly concentrated account of posterior uncertainty. These limitations motivate the search for approximation methods that retain more of the dependencies present in the original model. Recently, a lot of effort has been devoted to the development of approximation techniques which give an improved performance compared to the variational bound approximation. Thomas Minka's Expectation Propagation (EP) approach (Minka, 2001a,b) seems to provide a general framework from which many of these developments can be re-derived and understood. EP is based on a dynamical picture where factors--their product forming a global tractable approximate distribution--are iteratively optimized. In contrast to the variational bound approach, the optimization proceeds locally by minimizing KL divergences between appropriately defined marginal distributions. Since the resulting algorithm can be formulated in terms of the matching of marginal moments, this would not rule out factorizations where discrete distributions are approximated by multivariate Gaussians. However, such a choice seems to be highly unnatural from the derivation of the EP approximation (by the infinite KL measure) and has to our knowledge not been suggested so far (Minka, private communication). Hence, in practice, the correlations between discrete variables have been mainly treated using tree-based approximations. This includes the celebrated Bethe-Kikuchi approach (Yedidia et al., 2001; Yuille, 2002; Heskes et al., 2003), for EP interpretations see Minka (2001a,b) and Minka and Qi (2004). For a variety of related approximations within statistical physics see Suzuki (1995). However, while tree-type approximations often work well for sparsely connected graphs they become inadequate for inference problems in a dense graph regardless of the type of variables.

Recent developments in data acquisition and computational power have spurred an increased interest in flexible statistical Bayesian models in many areas of science and engineering. Inference in probabilistic models is in many cases intractable; the computational cost of marginalization operations can scale exponentially in the number of variables or require integrals over multivariate non-tractable distributions. In order to treat systems with a large number of variables, it is therefore necessary to use approximate polynomial complexity inference methods. Probably the most prominent and widely developed approximation technique is the socalled variational (or variational Bayes) approximation (see, e.g. Jordan et al., 1999; Attias, 2000; Bishop et al., 2003). In this approach, the true intractable probability distribution is approximated by another one which is optimally chosen within a given, tractable family minimizing the Kullback Leibler (KL) divergence as the measure of dissimilarity between distributions. We will use the name variational bound for this specific method because the approximation results in an upper bound to the free energy (an entropic quantity related to the KL divergence). The alternative approximation methods discussed in this paper can also be derived from the variation of an approximate free energy which is not necessarily a bound. The most important tractable families of distributions in the variational bound approximation are multivariate Gaussians and distributions often in the exponential family which factorize in the marginals of all or for certain disjoint groups of variables (Attias, 2000) (this is often called a mean--field approximation). The use of multivariate Gaussians makes it possible to retain a significant amount of correlation between variables in the approximation. However, their application in the variational bound approximation is limited to distributions of continuous variables which have the entire real space as their natural domain. This is due to the fact that the KL divergence would diverge for distributions with non-matching support. Hence, in a majority of those applications, where random variables with constrained values (such as Boolean ones) appear, variational distributions of the mean field type have to be chosen. Over the last decade, there has been much research on the problem of learning Bayesian networks from data (Heckerman, 1998), and successfully applying it both to density estimation, and to discovering dependency structures among variables. Many real-world domains, however, are very complex, involving thousands of relevant variables. Examples include modeling the dependencies among expression levels (a rough indicator of activity) of all the genes in a cell (Friedman et al., 2000a; Lander, 1999) or among changes in stock prices. Unfortunately, in complex domains, the amount of data is rarely enough to robustly learn a model of the underlying distribution. In the gene expression domain, a typical data set describes thousands of variables, but at most a few hundred instances. In such situations, statistical noise is likely to lead to spurious dependencies, resulting in models that significantly overfit the data. The difficulty is not only statistical. Even when a Bayesian network can be learned over thousands of variables, its complexity makes the resulting structure hard to interpret: dependencies are distributed across a large graph, and it may be unclear which relationships form meaningful patterns. We therefore propose organizing variables in a large domain into sets whose members exhibit similar dependencies and behavioral patterns. This partitioning can make the structure easier to discover and understand by focusing attention on groups of related variables. Such groups have natural interpretations in several domains. In gene expression data, for example, genes may form modules whose activity is coordinated to carry out particular cellular functions. In financial data, stocks within the same sector may respond in similar ways to factors specific to that sector. By identifying these sets, we can describe important regularities at the group level while retaining a principled account of the dependencies among individual variables.

Moreover, if our goal is structure discovery, such domains pose additional challenges. First, due to the small number of instances, we are unlikely to have much confidence in the learned structure (Pe'er et al., 2001). Second, a Bayesian network structure over thousands of variables is typically highly unstructured, and therefore very hard to interpret. In this paper, we propose an approach to address these issues. We start by observing that, in many large domains, the variables can be partitioned into sets so that, to a first approximation, the variables within each set have a similar set of dependencies and therefore exhibit a similar behavior. For example, many genes in a cell are organized into modules, in which sets of genes required for the same biological function or response are co-regulated by the same inputs in order to coordinate their joint activity. As another example, when reasoning about thousands of NASDAQ stocks, entire sectors of stocks often respond together to sector-influencing factors (e.g., oil stocks tend to respond similarly to a war in Iraq).

We start with an example that introduces the main idea of module networks and then provide a formal definition. For concreteness, consider a simple toy example of modeling changes in stock prices. The Bayesian network of Figure 1(a) describes dependencies between different stocks. In this network, each random variable corresponds to the change in price of a single stock. For illustration purposes, we assume that these random variables take one of three values: 'down', 'same' or 'up', denoting the change during a particular trading day. In our example, the stock price of Intel (INTL) depends on that of Microsoft (MSFT). The conditional probability distribution (CPD) shown in the figure indicates that the behavior of Intel's stock is similar to that of Microsoft. That is, if Microsoft's stock goes up, there is a high probability that Intel's stock will also go up and vice versa. Overall, the Bayesian network specifies a CPD for each stock price as a stochastic function of its parents. Thus, in our example, the network specifies a separate behavior for each stock. However, this approach reveals a fundamental limitation when applied to more complex stock market domains. In reality, stock prices exhibit hierarchical dependencies with systematic patterns that individual CPDs fail to capture. For instance, Microsoft's stock movements influence not just one chip manufacturer but a group of them--Intel, Applied Materials, and Motorola--which in turn influence a group of computer manufacturers such as Dell and Hewlett Packard. Within each of these tiers, the relationships follow remarkably similar structural patterns: all chip manufacturers respond to Microsoft in fundamentally the same way, and all computer manufacturers respond to the chip manufacturers similarly. A standard Bayesian network would require specifying an independent CPD for each stock, treating each relationship as isolated from the others, thereby obscuring the underlying regularity that binds these dependencies together. Module networks address this limitation by recognizing and exploiting the repeated structure implicit in such domains. Rather than assigning a unique CPD to each variable, module networks partition variables into modules where all variables within a module share the same set of parents and use the same conditional probability distribution. By grouping Intel, Applied Materials, and Motorola together in a single module, for example, we can describe their shared dependence on Microsoft with a single CPD that applies to all three. Similarly, Dell and Hewlett Packard can share a module defined by their common dependence on the chip manufacturers. This module-based representation dramatically reduces computational complexity--in this stock domain, the number of required CPDs drops from six to three--while capturing the essential structural patterns that Bayesian networks overlook. This principle of representing repeated dependencies through shared modules forms the conceptual foundation of the module network formalism.

The stock domain, however, has higher order structural features that are not explicitly modeled by the Bayesian network. For instance, we can see that the stock price of Microsoft (MSFT) influences the stock price of all of the major chip manufacturers -- Intel (INTL), Applied Materials (AMAT), and Motorola (MOT). In turn, the stock price of computer manufacturers Dell (DELL) and Hewlett Packard (HPQ), are influenced by the stock prices of their chip suppliers -- Intel and Applied Materials. An examination of the CPDs might also reveal that, to a first approximation, the stock price of all chip making companies depends on that of Microsoft and in much the same way. Similarly, the stock price of computer manufacturers that buy their chips from Intel and Applied Materials depends on these chip manufacturers' stock and in much the same way. To model this type of situation, we might divide stock price variables into groups, which we call modules, and require that variables in the same module have the same probabilistic model; that is, all variables in the module have the same set of parents and the same CPD. Our example contains three modules: one containing only Microsoft, a second containing chip manufacturers Intel, Applied Materials, and Motorola, and a third containing computer manufacturers Dell and HP (see Figure 1(b)). In this model, we need only specify three CPDs, one for each module, since all the variables in each module share the same CPD. By comparison, six different CPDs are required for a Bayesian network representation. This notion of a module is the key idea underlying the module network formalism.

To evaluate whether model scores could effectively guide selection of an optimal number of modules, we conducted a systematic study across varying training set sizes and module configurations. We trained models on datasets containing 100 to 500 instances, allowing the learning algorithm to consider up to 50 possible modules. Our investigation revealed a consistent pattern: performance peaked at 10 modules for small sample sizes and plateaued beyond this threshold for larger datasets, suggesting that model scores contained useful information for directing architectural selection. Further analysis of the learned models revealed the structural basis for this performance pattern. Across high-performing configurations, at least 80% of the variables demonstrated consistent assignment to the same 10 modules, indicating a natural clustering of variables at this architecture size. Models that increased the module count beyond 10 exhibited broader dispersal of variable assignments across the module space and corresponding degradation in performance metrics. Object-Oriented Bayesian Networks and module networks represent distinct approaches to structured probabilistic modeling, differentiated fundamentally by their structural constraints. Module networks impose a rigid requirement that all variables within a given class share identical parent sets, a constraint that substantially simplifies the learning problem by reducing the space of possible structures. However, this uniformity requirement carries a significant cost: modifications to the parent set structure of any single variable propagate globally across all variables in its class, amplifying the impact of local structural decisions throughout the entire model. Consequently, existing OOBN learning algorithms, which were designed under different structural assumptions, prove inapplicable to module networks when dealing with complex domains where such rigidity becomes problematic. The Probabilistic Relational Models framework addresses some of these limitations through an alternative mechanism: explicit relational structure that mediates the specification of probabilistic dependencies between objects rather than merely among variables in isolation. Module networks, by contrast, lack this relational scaffolding entirely, constraining their probabilistic modeling capabilities to operate at the level of class-level aggregates rather than capturing fine-grained dependencies between particular objects and their instances. Attempts to bridge this gap, such as the class hierarchy approach proposed by Getoor and colleagues, introduce layers of algorithmic complexity that resist straightforward adaptation to the specialized domains and problem configurations central to the present work. To better relate the PRM approach to module networks, recall the relationship between module networks and clustering, as described in Section 4.2. As we discussed, we can view the module network learning procedure as grouping variables into clusters that share the same probabilistic dependency model. As shown in Figure 5, we are taking the data points in the (variables x instances) matrix, and grouping rows. As we discussed, in other settings, we often group columns (instances). In fact, in many cases, the notion of "variables" and "instances" is somewhat arbitrary. PRMs allow us to define a probabilistic model where the value of a data point depends both on properties of the rows and properties of the column. In particular, we can define a hidden attribute for either rows, columns, or both; the values of this hidden attribute would correspond to a clustering of rows, or columns, or a two-sided clustering of both rows and columns simultaneously (see Segal et al. (2001)).

In OOBNs, objects in the same class must have the same internal structure and parameterization, but can depend on different sets of variables (as specified in the mapping of variables in an object's interface to its actual inputs). By contrast, in a module network, all of the variables in a module (class) must have the same specific parents. This assumption greatly reduces the size and complexity of the hypothesis space, leading to a more robust learning algorithm. On the other hand, this assumption requires that we be careful in making certain steps in the structure search, as they have more global effects than on just one or two variables. Due to these differences, we cannot simply apply an OOBN structure-learning algorithm, such as the one proposed by Langseth and Nielsen (2003), to such complex, high-dimensional domains. In PRMs, the probabilistic dependency structure of the objects in a class is determined by the relational structure of the domain (e.g., the Cost attribute of a particular car object might depend on the Income attribute of the object representing this particular car's owner). In the case of module networks, there is no known relational structure to which probabilistic dependencies can be attached. Without such a relational structure, PRMs only allow dependency models specified at the class level. Thus, we can assert that the objects in one class depend on some aggregate quantity of the objects in another. We cannot, however, state a dependence on a particular object in the other class (without some relationship specified in the model). Getoor et al. (2000) attempt to address this issue using a class hierarchy. Their approach is very different from ours, requiring some fairly complex search steps, and is not easily applied to the types of domains considered in this paper. Even in domains where the modularity assumption is warranted, the module network models we presented here may not be ideal. In particular, the module network models we presented here allow each variable to be assigned to only one module. For instance, in the gene expression domain, this means that each gene is allowed to participate in only a single module. This assumption is not realistic biologically, as biological processes often involve partially overlapping sets of genes, so that many genes participate in more than one process. The framework presented in this paper, by restricting each gene to only one module, cannot represent such overlapping processes with different regulatory mechanisms. Recently (Segal et al., 2003a; Battle et al., 2004), we presented one possible extension to the module network framework presented in this paper, which allows genes to be assigned to several modules. The expression of a gene in a particular array is then modeled as a sum of its expression in each of the modules in which it participates, and each module can potentially have a different set of regulators. Clearly, this approach for "allocating" a variable and its observed signal among different modules is only one possible model, and one which is not appropriate to all settings. Other domains will likely require the development of other approaches. Beyond these representational issues, the module network learning algorithm has two main limitations. First, the number of modules must be specified in advance. This choice determines the granularity at which variables are grouped and thus constrains the models considered during learning. Although our scoring framework provides a possible basis for selecting the number of modules automatically, doing so would require searching over models with different numbers of modules as well as over their assignments and dependency structures. Developing an effective procedure for this selection would reduce the need to fix an important modeling choice before examining the resulting networks. Second, our heuristic search returns a single model, without providing confidence estimates for the structural relationships that it contains. The selected model summarizes the dependencies found by the search, but does not indicate how strongly the data support an individual relationship relative to alternative structures or assignments. Such estimates would be useful when interpreting a learned network, particularly when its dependencies are used to formulate hypotheses for further investigation. Model scoring can help compare candidate networks, but the outcome of a single heuristic search does not by itself characterize uncertainty about their structure. Bootstrap resampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods offer more direct approaches to estimating this uncertainty. Bootstrap resampling could assess the stability of inferred relationships across models learned from resampled data, while Markov Chain Monte Carlo could explore alternative models according to their posterior probabilities. Adapting either approach to module networks, however, requires efficient strategies for exploring the large space of possible assignment functions together with the associated dependency structures. Changes in module membership can affect the interpretation of structural relationships, so confidence estimation must account for uncertainty in both components of the model. Developing sampling strategies that make this exploration computationally practical remains an important challenge for future work. In this paper, we focused on the statistical properties of our method. In a companion biological paper (Segal et al., 2003b), we use the module network learned from the gene expression data described above to predict gene regulation relationships. There, we performed a comprehensive evaluation of the validity of the biological structures reconstructed by our method. By analyzing biological databases and previous experimental results in the literature, we confirmed that many of the regulatory relations that our method automatically inferred are indeed correct. Furthermore, our model provided focused predictions for genes of previously uncharacterized function. We performed wet lab biological experiments that confirmed the three novel predictions we tested. Thus, we have demonstrated that the module network model is robust enough to learn a good approximation of the dependency structure between 2355 genes using only 173 instances. These results show that, by learning a structured probabilistic representation, we identify regulation networks from gene expression data and successfully address one of the central problems in analysis of gene expression data.

In this paper, we addressed this issue only indirectly, through statistical generalization tests on held out data and through the evaluation of our results relative to the to existing annotations (e.g., of stock categories in the stock market domain). In the context of module networks, we also need to construct efficient sampling strategies over assignment functions. Recall that the space of possible assignment functions is huge, and so a priori it is not clear that a simple sampling procedure (e.g., mirroring our search strategy and moving one variable at each step) will mix in reasonable time. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a well-established technique for dimension reduction and classification, and it has been applied successfully in a wide range of domains, including face recognition, text categorization, and gene expression analysis. Its practical success is somewhat surprising given how restrictive its underlying assumptions are. Classical LDA presumes that each class follows a Gaussian distribution and that all classes share a common covariance matrix, conditions that real data often violate. Yet the method frequently performs well even when these assumptions hold only loosely. A common explanation is that simple linear models have low variance, so they are relatively insensitive to noise in the training data and are less prone to overfitting than more flexible nonlinear alternatives. This robustness helps explain why LDA remains a standard baseline despite the availability of far more elaborate classifiers. The classical formulation nevertheless runs into a fundamental difficulty when the data are undersampled, that is, when the number of samples is smaller than the dimensionality of the data. Classical LDA seeks a transformation that maximizes the between-class scatter relative to the within-class scatter, and computing the solution requires inverting the within-class scatter matrix or, in some formulations, the total scatter matrix. When the data are undersampled, these matrices are singular, so the inverse does not exist and the standard criterion cannot be evaluated directly. The problem is far from rare, since high-dimensional settings such as image analysis, microarray studies, and document retrieval routinely produce far fewer samples than features. This singularity problem has motivated researchers to propose a number of extensions of classical LDA, each modifying the formulation or the computation so that a meaningful discriminant transformation can still be obtained. A common way to deal with the singularity problems is to apply an intermediate dimension reduction stage such as PCA to reduce the dimension of the original data before classical LDA is applied. The algorithm is known as PCA+LDA (Belhumeur et al., 1997; Swets and Weng, 1996; Zhao et al., 1999). In this two-stage PCA+LDA algorithm, the discriminant stage is preceded by a dimension reduction stage using PCA. The dimension of the subspace transformed by PCA is chosen such as the "reduced" total scatter matrix in the subspace is nonsingular, so that classical LDA can be applied. A limitation of this approach is that the optimal value of the reduced dimension for PCA is difficult to determine. Moreover, the PCA stage may lose some useful information for discrimination.

Although relying on heavy assumptions which are not true in many applications, LDA has been proven to be effective. This is mainly due to the fact that a simple, linear model is more robust against noise, and most likely will not overfit. Generalization of LDA by fitting Gaussian mixtures to each class has been studied in (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1996). Note that classical discriminant analysis requires the total scatter matrix S t to be nonsingular, which may not hold for undersampled data. The criterion we propose generates a whole family of LDA-based algorithms, depending on how its constraints and optimization are instantiated. In this paper we concentrate on two members of that family. The first is an established technique, uncorrelated LDA (ULDA), which produces features that are statistically uncorrelated with one another. The second is a new algorithm, orthogonal LDA (OLDA), which we propose here. Looking at both through a single criterion lets us compare them on equal footing, and it clarifies how the choice of constraint on the transformation shapes the features that are extracted. Earlier work on ULDA showed that, when the data satisfy an invertibility requirement, it achieves discriminative performance comparable to that of classical LDA. That finding motivated the development of an efficient computational procedure for ULDA, which avoids some of the cost of the standard formulation. A central observation of this paper is that the earlier procedure is not a stand-alone construction. We show that it is one particular instance of our criterion-based framework, so the same criterion that yields ULDA also yields OLDA by a different choice within the family. This connection explains why the earlier algorithm works, and it gives us a principled route to an algorithm with orthogonal discriminant vectors. OLDA is a novel dimension reduction algorithm proposed in this paper. The key property of OLDA is that the discriminant vectors of OLDA are orthogonal to each other, i.e., the transformation matrix of OLDA is orthogonal. There has been some early development on LDA based algorithms with orthogonal transformations. The algorithm is known as Foley-Sammon LDA (FSLDA). FSLDA was first proposed by Foley and Sammon for two-class problems (Foley and Sammon, 1975). It was then extended to the multi-class problems by Duchene and Leclercq (Duchene and Leclerq, 1988). The OLDA algorithm proposed in this paper provides an alternative, but simple and efficient way for computing orthogonal transformations in the framework of LDA.

Among the family of algorithms, we study two specific ones in detail, namely Uncorrelated LDA (ULDA) and Orthogonal LDA (OLDA). ULDA was developed in the past for feature extraction and dimension reduction, whereas OLDA is a novel LDA based algorithm proposed in this paper. ULDA was recently proposed for extracting feature vectors with uncorrelated attributes (Jin et al., 2001a,b). A more recent work (Ye et al., 2004a) showed that classical LDA is equivalent to ULDA, in the sense that both classical LDA and ULDA produce the same transformation matrix when the total scatter matrix is nonsingular. Based on this equivalence, an efficient algorithm was presented in (Ye et al., 2004a) for computing the optimal discriminant vectors of ULDA. Interestingly, the solution in (Ye et al., 2004a) is a special case of the solutions to the proposed criterion in this paper (See Section 4).
