But with the sheep-dog it was otherwise. Being a female, she possessed no such instinct. On the other hand, being a sheep-dog, her instinctive fear of the Wild, and especially of the wolf, was unusually keen. White Fang was to her a wolf, the hereditary marauder who had preyed upon her flocks from the time sheep were first herded and guarded by some dim ancestor of hers. And so, as he abandoned his rush at her and braced himself to avoid the contact, she sprang upon him. He snarled involuntarily as he felt her teeth in his shoulder, but beyond this made no offer to hurt her. He backed away, stiff-legged with self-consciousness, and tried to go around her. He dodged this way and that, and curved and turned, but to no purpose. She remained always between him and the way he wanted to go. "Here, Collie!" called the strange man in the carriage. Weedon Scott laughed. "Never mind, White Fang! It's all right!" he called back, and then the horses leaped forward and the wheels crunched off down the drive. But it was not all right, not to White Fang. The master was going away, and the god had not bidden him stay. He started after the carriage, and at once Collie was before him, bristling, her teeth bared and her body flung across his path. He swerved to the left, out onto the lawn, and she was there; he doubled back toward the drive, and still she was there, matching him turn for turn, never quite closing with him, but never giving ground. He tried the long way round, a wide circle across the grass that should have carried him clear of her, and she cut across the chord of it and met him at the far side, snarling. Always it was the same. Whichever way he turned, she was there to block him, and between whiles he could hear the receding rattle of the wheels. The sound grew fainter. Through a gap he caught a glimpse of the carriage, small now, slipping in among the trees at the bend of the drive, and then it was gone altogether. Something like panic took hold of him. He had played her game long enough, dodging and doubling as though she were a thing to be escaped from instead of fought through. He had no more time for it. He ceased trying to slip past her and drove straight in, as he had driven at many a dog in the old days on the trail and in the fighting-pit at Dawson. He did not snap. He struck her with his shoulder against hers, hard, with the whole weight and speed of his body behind the blow. It was the old trick, and it had never failed him. Collie was lifted clean off her feet. She went over sideways and rolled across the gravel of the drive, legs flailing, the stones spurting out from under her. Twice she tried to get up and went down again, scrabbling for a hold on the loose footing, and all the while she filled the air with her shrill yelping, half pain and half outrage at the indignity that had been done her. White Fang did not wait. The way was clear, and that was all he had wanted. She took after him, never ceasing her outcry. It was the straightaway now, and when it came to real running, White Fang could teach her things. She ran frantically, hysterically, straining to the utmost, advertising the effort she was making with every leap: and all the time White Fang slid smoothly away from her silently, without effort, gliding like a ghost over the ground. As he rounded the house to the porte-cochère, he came upon the carriage. It had stopped, and the master was alighting. At this moment, still running at top speed, White Fang became suddenly aware of an attack from the side. It was a deer-hound rushing upon him. White Fang tried to face it. But he was going too fast, and the hound was too close. It struck him on the side; and such was his forward momentum and the unexpectedness of it, White Fang was hurled to the ground and rolled clear over. He came out of the tangle a spectacle of malignancy, ears flattened back, lips writhing, nose wrinkling, his teeth clipping together as the fangs barely missed the hound's soft throat. The master was running up, but was too far away; and it was Collie that saved the hound's life. Before White Fang could spring in and deliver the fatal stroke, and just as he was in the act of springing in, Collie arrived. She had been out-manoeuvred and out-run, to say nothing of her having been unceremoniously tumbled in the gravel, and her arrival was like that of a tornado--made up of offended dignity, justifiable wrath, and instinctive hatred for this marauder from the Wild. She struck White Fang at right angles in the midst of his spring, and again he was knocked off his feet and rolled over. The master arrived a moment later and caught White Fang by the scruff before he could gather himself for a fresh attack. His voice was low and steady, and his hands were firm, and White Fang, quivering with the rage of battle, let himself be held. Over his shoulder the master called to his father, who had come down from the porch, to get the dogs away. "Call them off, Father," he said. "It's hard on a poor wolf from the Arctic to be knocked flat twice in as many seconds, and in his first minute on new ground. He came all this way to be given a better welcome than that." These people pressed close about the master, laid hands upon him, and clung to his neck, and each time it happened the hair rose along White Fang's back and a growl rumbled in his throat. When they edged too close, the growl came again, low and certain, and they had the good sense to keep their distance. Nor was the welcome any warmer from his own kind. Collie, held fast by the elder Scott, was even less at ease. She had not forgiven his intrusion, and she gave no sign that she ever would. At last the master straightened and turned toward the house, and the whole company began to move with him up the steps. As the wolf drew near, the hound's lip lifted and a growl rolled out of him, and White Fang answered it in kind, his own hair rising and his teeth showing. The two of them stood a few feet apart on the porch, stiff-legged and menacing, each warning the other off, while the people paused in the doorway and looked back at them. "Take Collie inside and leave the two of them to fight it out," suggested Scott's father. "After that they'll be friends." "Then White Fang, to show his friendship, will have to be chief mourner at the funeral," laughed the master. The elder Scott looked incredulously, first at White Fang, then at Dick, and finally at his son. "You mean . . .?" Weedon nodded his head. "I mean just that. You'd have a dead Dick inside one minute--two minutes at the farthest." He turned to White Fang. "Come on, you wolf. It's you that'll have to come inside."

On the other hand, being a sheep-dog, her instinctive fear of the Wild, and especially of the wolf, was unusually keen. White Fang was to her a wolf, the hereditary marauder who had preyed upon her flocks from the time sheep were first herded and guarded by some dim ancestor of hers. And so, as he abandoned his rush at her and braced himself to avoid the contact, she sprang upon him. He snarled involuntarily as he felt her teeth in his shoulder, but beyond this made no offer to hurt her. He backed away, stiff-legged with self-consciousness, and tried to go around her. Weedon Scott laughed. "Never mind, father. It is good discipline. White Fang will have to learn many things, and it's just as well that he begins now. He'll adjust himself all right." Shoulder to shoulder, he struck her squarely. Not only was she overthrown. "In all his life he's only been known once to go off his feet, and here he's been rolled twice in thirty seconds." The carriage had driven away, and other strange gods had appeared from out the house. Some of these stood respectfully at a distance; but two of them, women, perpetrated the hostile act of clutching the master around the neck. White Fang, however, was beginning to tolerate this act. No harm seemed to come of it, while the noises the gods made were certainly not threatening. These gods also made overtures to White Fang, but he warned them off with a snarl, and the master did likewise with word of mouth. At such times White Fang leaned in close against the master's legs and received reassuring pats on the head. The hound, under the command, "Dick! Lie down, sir!" had gone up the steps and lain down to one side of the porch, still growling and keeping a sullen watch on the intruder. Collie had been taken in charge by one of the woman-gods, who held arms around her neck and petted and caressed her; but Collie was very much perplexed and worried, whining and restless, outraged by the permitted presence of this wolf and confident that the gods were making a mistake. All the gods started up the steps to enter the house. White Fang followed closely at the master's heels. Dick, on the porch, growled, and White Fang, on the steps, bristled and growled back. White Fang allowed all the members of the family to pet him and make much of him; but he never gave to them what he gave to the master. No caress of theirs could put the love-croon into his throat, and, try as they would, they could never persuade him into snuggling against them. This expression of abandon and surrender, of absolute trust, he reserved for the master alone. In fact, he never regarded the members of the family in any other light than possessions of the love-master. Also White Fang had early come to differentiate between the family and the servants of the household. The latter were afraid of him, while he merely refrained from attacking them. This because he considered that they were likewise possessions of the master. Between White Fang and them existed a neutrality and no more. They cooked for the master and washed the dishes and did other things just as Matt had done up in the Klondike. They were, in short, appurtenances of the household. Outside the household there was even more for White Fang to learn. The master's domain was wide and complex, yet it had its metes and bounds. The land itself ceased at the county road. Outside was the common domain of all gods--the roads and streets. Then inside other fences were the particular domains of other gods. A myriad laws governed all these things and determined conduct; yet he did not know the speech of the gods, nor was there any way for him to learn save by experience. He obeyed his natural impulses until they ran him counter to some law. When this had been done a few times, he learned the law and after that observed it. But most potent in his education was the cuff of the master's hand, the censure of the master's voice. Because of White Fang's very great love, a cuff from the master hurt him far more than any beating Grey Beaver or Beauty Smith had ever given him. They had hurt only the flesh of him; beneath the flesh the spirit had still raged, splendid and invincible. But with the master the cuff was always too light to hurt the flesh. Yet it went deeper. It was an expression of the master's disapproval, and White Fang's spirit wilted under it. In point of fact, the cuff was rarely administered. The master's voice was sufficient. By it White Fang knew whether he did right or not. By it he trimmed his conduct and adjusted his actions. It was the compass by which he steered and learned to chart the manners of a new land and life. In the Northland, the only domesticated animal was the dog. All other animals lived in the Wild, and were, when not too formidable, lawful spoil for any dog. All his days White Fang had foraged among the live things for food. It did not enter his head that in the Southland it was otherwise. But this he was to learn early in his residence in Santa Clara Valley. Sauntering around the corner of the house in the early morning, he came upon a chicken that had escaped from the chicken-yard. White Fang's natural impulse was to eat it. A couple of bounds, a flash of teeth and a frightened squawk, and he had scooped in the adventurous fowl. It was farm-bred and fat and tender; and White Fang licked his chops and decided that such fare was good. Later that same day, the taste of the first bird still fresh in his memory, White Fang came upon another hen that had slipped her pen and was scratching about in the dust beside the stables. He did not pause to weigh the matter. In the land he came from, a creature that wandered unguarded belonged to whoever was quick enough to claim it, and he was very quick. One of the grooms happened to glance up from his work just as the wolf-dog closed on his prize, and the man snatched up a light buggy-whip from where it hung by the door and ran forward, shouting. The first stroke of the lash cut across White Fang's shoulders. He let the hen drop at once, but not in the way the groom had hoped. A club he would have understood and perhaps respected, for clubs had taught him much in the camps of the Indians; but this thin, stinging thing in the hand of a stranger stirred only fury. He came at the man without a sound, low and straight. The groom flung up an arm to shield his throat, and the teeth meant for his neck sank into his forearm instead and tore it open to the bone. He beat at the grey head, staggered back, tried to put a wall behind him, but each time he lowered his guard the fangs found new flesh, and his sleeve was soon dark and dripping. It might have gone much worse had Collie not arrived. The sheep-dog had always regarded the newcomer as a wolf and a menace to everything she was bred to protect, and here at last was proof of it. She hurled herself into the fight in a rage far beyond anything the groom could muster, snapping and slashing at White Fang's flanks. He would not turn his teeth on her; some law older than his own anger held him back. He tried to shoulder her aside and press on, but she gave him no room, and while she harried him the bleeding man stumbled to the stable and pulled the door shut behind him. Collie kept after the wolf-dog until he broke away entirely and went loping off across the open fields, with her clamour following him all the way to the fences. The master heard the tale that evening, saw the groom's bandaged arm, and was not especially troubled. "He has come out of a country where any bird on the ground is meat," he said. "He'll give up chickens in time, I don't doubt that. But nobody can explain it to him beforehand. He'll only learn it by being caught with one in his mouth." He had watched them for many days before he moved. The chickens belonged to the life of the ranch, and from the shadows of the stables White Fang had studied their ways: how they scratched and quarrelled in the yard by day, how at dusk they filed into the long low house with a sleepy clucking, and how the hired man shut the door upon them and went off to his supper. He noted that the door was always closed, but he noted also the pile of fresh lumber stacked against one end of the building, its top boards reaching almost to the eaves. On a night when the moon was down and the household slept, he went silently to the lumber, climbed it board by board, and drew himself onto the roof. He crossed it softly, his pads making no sound on the shingles, until he found the place where he could drop through to the darkness beneath. Then he was among them. Fifty white Leghorn hens roosted there, and the warm, rank smell of them filled the house. What followed was swift and thorough, the old killing instinct of the Wild loosed in a closed room where nothing could escape, and when he left the way he had come, not one hen remained alive. In the morning the master came out and found them. The hired man had laid the dead hens out upon the porch in a long white row, and the master stood looking at them for a time without speaking. He whistled low, in surprise, and something like admiration crept into his face; it had been a clean piece of work, cunningly planned and boldly done. But the admiration passed, for he knew that such a thing could not be let go, and that if White Fang was to live among tame creatures he must be taught that they were not his to kill. He called the wolf to him. White Fang came at his summons with no sign of guilt upon him. He did not slink nor drop his ears nor drag his tail; he walked with his head up and his body erect, as one who had done a thing worth doing and expected no blame for it. The master's voice, when it came, was harsh with anger, and White Fang felt the change in it at once. Then the master caught him by the scruff and held his nose down against the slain hens, forcing it from one stiffened body to the next, and with each the hand fell upon him in sharp, heavy blows, while the angry words went on above his head.

And it would have gone hard with him had not Collie appeared on the scene. As she had saved Dick's life, she now saved the groom's. She rushed upon White Fang in frenzied wrath. She had been right. She had known better than the blundering gods. All her suspicions were justified. Here was the ancient marauder up to his old tricks again. The groom escaped into the stables, and White Fang backed away before Collie's wicked teeth, or presented his shoulder to them and circled round and round. Two nights later came the act, but on a more generous scale than the master had anticipated. White Fang had observed closely the chicken-yards and the habits of the chickens. In the night-time, after they had gone to roost, he climbed to the top of a pile of newly hauled lumber. From there he gained the roof of a chicken-house, passed over the ridgepole and dropped to the ground inside. A moment later he was inside the house, and the slaughter began. In the morning, when the master came out on to the porch, fifty white Leghorn hens, laid out in a row by the groom, greeted his eyes. He whistled to himself, softly, first with surprise, and then, at the end, with admiration. His eyes were likewise greeted by White Fang, but about the latter there were no signs of shame nor guilt. He carried himself with pride, as though, forsooth, he had achieved a deed praiseworthy and meritorious. There was about him no consciousness of sin. The master's lips tightened as he faced the disagreeable task. Then he talked harshly to the unwitting culprit, and in his voice there was nothing but godlike wrath. Also, he held White Fang's nose down to the slain hens, and at the same time cuffed him soundly.

At first, White Fang could scarcely pass a chicken without feeling the old impulse stir in him. The flutter of wings, the quick retreat of a plump body, the scratching feet among the straw--all invited pursuit. His master took him into the chicken yards and remained beside him, watching for the stiffening of his legs and the sudden intentness of his gaze. Before the leap could come, a sharp command checked it. Again and again White Fang turned from the birds to the man, troubled by a law that protected creatures so plainly made to be hunted. Yet the command was always the same, and his master never allowed a rush to go unchecked. Gradually he ceased to crouch when a chicken crossed his path. He learned to endure their bustling presence, then to look beyond them, until they could peck and flutter about him without drawing so much as a turn of his head. At lunch, the master's son described what had been accomplished, dwelling with satisfaction on White Fang's indifference in the very yards where he had once been so eager to kill. Judge Scott listened, but his expression gave no encouragement. To his mind, obedience under a watchful eye proved little; the restraint might last only as long as the man who enforced it remained within sight. "Once an animal has taken to killing chickens, you cannot cure him of it," he declared. "He has tasted blood, and he will go back to it when he gets the chance." The account of the training had not shaken his conviction. He regarded White Fang's quiet passage among the birds as a temporary submission to authority, and waited for his son to explain why he believed it meant anything more. Weedon Scott waited until the talk around the table had turned to White Fang, then put forward his proposal. He would shut the animal in the chicken-yard for an afternoon and leave the birds there with him. It would give White Fang an opportunity to show that he could obey even when obedience required more than answering his master's call. Weedon spoke quietly, but with an assurance that drew his father's attention. Judge Scott regarded the suggestion with evident misgiving. The chickens, he pointed out, would have no choice in the experiment, and he was unwilling to expose them merely to settle a difference of opinion. A closed yard might make the matter worse: whatever happened, the birds would be confined there with White Fang until someone intervened. Weedon listened without interrupting, acknowledging the objection with a nod, though he showed no inclination to withdraw his proposal. "Then let me bear the expense," he said. "For every chicken White Fang kills, I'll pay you one dollar in gold." He looked across the table at the Judge, making the offer as plainly as he had made the proposal. His father's concern had thus been answered with a definite penalty, and Weedon leaned back, waiting for him to accept the terms. "But you should penalise father, too," interposed Beth. Her sister seconded her, and a chorus of approval arose from around the table. Judge Scott nodded his head in agreement. "All right." Weedon Scott pondered for a moment. "And if, at the end of the afternoon White Fang hasn't harmed a chicken, for every ten minutes of the time he has spent in the yard, you will have to say to him, gravely and with deliberation, just as if you were sitting on the bench and solemnly passing judgment, 'White Fang, you are smarter than I thought.'" From hidden points of vantage the family watched the performance. But it was a fizzle. Locked in the yard and there deserted by the master, White Fang lay down and went to sleep. Once he got up and walked over to the trough for a drink of water. The chickens he calmly ignored. So far as he was concerned they did not exist. At four o'clock he executed a running jump, gained the roof of the chicken-house and leaped to the ground outside, whence he sauntered gravely to the house. He had learned the law. And on the porch, before the delighted family, Judge Scott, face to face with White Fang, said slowly and solemnly, sixteen times, "White Fang, you are smarter than I thought." But it was the multiplicity of laws that befuddled White Fang and often brought him into disgrace. He had to learn that he must not touch the chickens that belonged to other gods. Then there were cats, and rabbits, and turkeys; all these he must let alone. In fact, when he had but partly learned the law, his impression was that he must leave all live things alone. Out in the back-pasture, a quail could flutter up under his nose unharmed. All tense and trembling with eagerness and desire, he mastered his instinct and stood still. He was obeying the will of the gods. And then, one day, again out in the back-pasture, he saw Dick start a jackrabbit and run it. The master himself was looking on and did not interfere. Nay, he encouraged White Fang to join in the chase. And thus he learned that there was no taboo on jackrabbits. In the end he worked out the complete law. Between him and all domestic animals there must be no hostilities. If not amity, at least neutrality must obtain. But the other animals--the squirrels, and quail, and cottontails, were creatures of the Wild who had never yielded allegiance to man. They were the lawful prey of any dog. It was only the tame that the gods protected, and between the tame deadly strife was not permitted. The gods held the power of life and death over their subjects, and the gods were jealous of their power. Life was complex in the Santa Clara Valley after the simplicities of the Northland. And the chief thing demanded by these intricacies of civilisation was control, restraint--a poise of self that was as delicate as the fluttering of gossamer wings and at the same time as rigid as steel. Life had a thousand faces, and White Fang found he must meet them all--thus, when he went to town, in to San Jose, running behind the carriage or loafing about the streets when the carriage stopped. Life flowed past him, deep and wide and varied, continually impinging upon his senses, demanding of him instant and endless adjustments and correspondences, and compelling him, almost always, to suppress his natural impulses. There were butcher-shops where meat hung within reach. This meat he must not touch. There were cats at the houses the master visited that must be let alone. And there were dogs everywhere that snarled at him and that he must not attack. And then, on the crowded sidewalks there were persons innumerable whose attention he attracted. They would stop and look at him, point him out to one another, examine him, talk of him, and, worst of all, pat him. And these perilous contacts from all these strange hands he must endure. They continued in the yards for half an hour. Time and again the impulse surged over White Fang, and each time, as he yielded to it, he was checked by the master's voice. Then there were cats, and rabbits, and turkeys; all these he must let alone. In fact, when he had but partly learned the law, his impression was that he must leave all live things alone. He forgot that in the covenant entered into between him and the gods they were pledged to care for him and defend him. Knowing his deadly method of fighting, the master had never ceased impressing upon White Fang the law that he must not fight. As a result, having learned the lesson well, White Fang was hard put whenever he passed the cross-roads saloon. After the first rush, each time, his snarl kept the three dogs at a distance but they trailed along behind, yelping and bickering and insulting him. This endured for some time. The men at the saloon even urged the dogs on to attack White Fang. One day they openly sicked the dogs on him. The master stopped the carriage. "Go to it," he said to White Fang. White Fang glanced up at his master, uncertain whether he had understood. The three dogs stood before him, bristling and growling, but he had learned that his own desire was not always sufficient warrant for a fight. He waited, his body rigid and his ears turned toward the voice above him. His master pointed at the dogs and repeated the command. The doubt vanished. White Fang sprang forward without a sound. He struck at the nearest, slipped clear of its answering jaws, and turned upon the dog that rushed to its assistance. There was no pause in which either could recover its footing or bring its strength to bear. His movements were swift and exact, each attack followed by an escape so narrow that it seemed part of the same motion. Soon two of his enemies lay still, and he stood beyond them, untouched, looking for the third. That dog had already turned and fled. White Fang followed it across the field, leaving his master and the fallen dogs behind. The fugitive ran with all the urgency of terror, but White Fang steadily closed the distance. It glanced back, swerved, and lost the little advantage it still possessed. He overtook it before it could reach safety, and the chase ended in a brief struggle upon the grass. Men repeated how the strange dog had taken on three opponents and left none alive, and those who heard the story looked more carefully at the quiet animal walking beside his master. His silence now carried a meaning they had failed to see before. As word passed farther through the region, men called their dogs to heel when White Fang approached, held them by their collars, or shut them away until he had gone. Eat them up." White Fang no longer hesitated. He turned and leaped silently among his enemies. All three faced him. The months slipped by, and White Fang grew sleek in the Southland. Food came to him without the asking, and in such plenty that the old gnawing anxiety of the trail, the memory of lean winters and the desperate scramble for a scrap of frozen fish, faded until it was no more than a shadow at the back of his mind. There was no sled to haul, no pack to hold at bay, no blow to dodge. He lay in the sun on the wide porch and dozed, or trotted at the heels of the horse when the master rode abroad, and the days passed in a pleasant monotony that asked nothing of him but that he be content. And he was content. The kindness that surrounded him worked upon him as warmth works upon a frozen stream, loosening what had been locked and hard. The hands that touched him meant no harm, the voices that spoke to him carried no threat, and slowly, in response, he opened and flourished like a plant set at last in good soil. Yet for all his flourishing, he was not as the other dogs about him. They had been born to this soft land and its ways, and they wore its laws lightly, as a thing they had never had to learn. White Fang had learned them hard, one by one, and he kept them more scrupulously than any dog native to the place. The chickens he let alone; the strange dogs on the road he endured; the master's goods and the master's people he guarded with a sober, unbending exactness. Still, there was something in him that the Southland had not reached. It showed in the way he lifted his head at a sudden sound, in the flat, silent watchfulness of his eyes, in the long, gliding gait that was not the gait of a house dog. The Wild was in him yet. It had not died; it had only gone to sleep, and it lay coiled and quiet beneath the gentleness, waiting for whatever might one day wake it. And because of that sleeping thing, the dogs of the place were never quite easy with him, nor he with them. He never chummed with other dogs. Lonely he had lived, so far as his kind was concerned, and lonely he would continue to live. In his puppyhood, under the persecution of Lip-lip and the puppy-pack, and in his fighting days with Beauty Smith, he had acquired a fixed aversion for dogs. The natural course of his life had been diverted, and, recoiling from his kind, he had clung to the human. Besides, all Southland dogs looked upon him with suspicion. He aroused in them their instinctive fear of the Wild, and they greeted him always with snarl and growl and belligerent hatred. He, on the other hand, learned that it was not necessary to use his teeth upon them. His naked fangs and writhing lips were uniformly efficacious, rarely failing to send a bellowing on-rushing dog back on its haunches. But there was one trial in White Fang's life--Collie. She never gave him a moment's peace. She was not so amenable to the law as he. She defied all efforts of the master to make her become friends with White Fang. Ever in his ears was sounding her sharp and nervous snarl. She had never forgiven him the chicken-killing episode, and persistently held to the belief that his intentions were bad. She found him guilty before the act, and treated him accordingly. She became a pest to him, like a policeman following him around the stable and the hounds, and, if he even so much as glanced curiously at a pigeon or chicken, bursting into an outcry of indignation and wrath. His favourite way of ignoring her was to lie down, with his head on his fore-paws, and pretend sleep. This always dumfounded and silenced her. With the exception of Collie, all things went well with White Fang. He had learned control and poise, and he knew the law. He achieved a staidness, and calmness, and philosophic tolerance. He no longer lived in a hostile environment. Danger and hurt and death did not lurk everywhere about him. In time, the unknown, as a thing of terror and menace ever impending, faded away. Life was soft and easy. It flowed along smoothly, and neither fear nor foe lurked by the way. He missed the snow without knowing that he missed it. When the long summer lay heavy on the valley and the sun beat down without mercy, a vague unrest stirred in him, a hunger with no name. He would rise from where he lay in the shade, pace a little, then sink down again, ill at ease and puzzled by his own disquiet. Had he been able to reason about it, he might have traced the feeling to the far white country where he was born, to the cold that had bitten his first days and the frozen silence that had closed around them. But he did not reason about it. He knew only that something was wanting, that at times the softness of this new life chafed him, and that the old wild lands called to him in a voice too faint to be understood. Then the mood would pass, and he would go to look for the master. For it was always to the master that he turned, and it was in his dealings with the master that he found new ways of speaking. Expression had never come easily to him. He could not fawn, nor wriggle, nor fling himself about in the extravagant delight of other dogs. His love was a deep, still thing, and for a long while he had no means of showing it except to press close and lay his head against the master's knee. Then he learned to laugh. The master had a way of teasing him, of poking gentle fun at him in a voice that was half mockery and half caress. At first White Fang resented it. Laughter had always stung him; since his puppyhood among the Indian dogs it had meant ridicule, and he had answered it with rage. But the master's laughter was different, and White Fang could not hold to his anger for long. He would bristle and try to stand on his dignity, and the master would only laugh the harder, until White Fang's stiffness broke. His jaws would part a little, his lips lift in a quizzical curl, and a strange light would come into his eyes that was more love than humour. He had learned to laugh. He learned, too, to play. The master would tumble him over and roll him about, cuffing him and pushing him in a mock attack, and White Fang would answer in kind. He snarled and snapped and flung himself forward with every show of savagery, bristling and growling as though he fought for his life. Yet never once did his teeth close in earnest. His jaws clipped shut on empty air, his rushes stopped short a hair's breadth from the master's skin, and all the fierce strength of him was held in a restraint as fine as any he had ever practised. It was pretence, and both of them knew it. Faster and wilder the romp would go, feints and leaps and furious snarls, until at last they broke off and stood a few feet apart, eyeing each other. Then, as suddenly as a cloud lifts from the sun, the master would begin to laugh, and White Fang would laugh back, and the battle would end with the master's arms around his neck and shoulders. And White Fang, pressed close against him, would croon his love-song, that strange sound that was half growl and half something softer, the only voice he had for all that was in his heart. But nobody else ever romped with White Fang. He did not permit it. He stood on his dignity, and when they attempted it, his warning snarl and bristling mane were anything but playful. That he allowed the master these liberties was no reason that he should be a common dog, loving here and loving there, everybody's property for a romp and good time. He loved with single heart and refused to cheapen himself or his love. The master went out on horseback a great deal, and to accompany him was one of White Fang's chief duties in life. In the Northland he had evidenced his fealty by toiling in the harness; but there were no sleds in the Southland, nor did dogs pack burdens on their backs. So he rendered fealty in the new way, by running with the master's horse. The longest day never played White Fang out. His was the gait of the wolf, smooth, tireless and effortless, and at the end of fifty miles he would come in jauntily ahead of the horse.

He did not finish his sentence. White Fang stood before him, growling fiercely. "Go away! Lie down, sir!" Judge Scott commanded. White Fang turned to the love-master's wife. She screamed with fright as he seized her dress in his teeth and dragged on it till the frail fabric tore away. By this time he had become the centre of interest. He had ceased from his growling and stood, head up, looking into their faces. His throat worked spasmodically, but made no sound, while he struggled with all his body, convulsed with the effort to rid himself of the incommunicable something that strained for utterance. "I do believe he's going mad," said Weedon's mother, drawing her shawl about her shoulders as though the sight of the straining animal had chilled her. "I said it from the first, that this climate would never agree with him. He is a creature of the snow and the ice, and it's too warm for him here. Look at him. He's been out of sorts for days, and now this." Nobody answered her. The dog did not so much as glance in her direction. His eyes moved from face to face, pleading, and the muscles of his lean body rippled and shook as though some great force were wrenching at him from within. He whined once, a thin broken sound, and then the whine was lost in a harsh convulsion of the throat. He tried again. Something rose in him, something that had waited through all the years of the wild and the years of the fight, and it would not come out as a growl, nor as a howl, nor as any cry that he had ever known. Then it broke from him. It was a burst of barking, abrupt and ragged, one sharp note tumbling over another, as if he were hurling every word he had never possessed at the people in the room. He barked until his sides heaved, and when he stopped he stood trembling, still watching them, begging them to understand. It was Weedon's wife who spoke first, and she spoke quietly, with her hand pressed to her breast. "Something has happened to him," she said. "Something has happened to my husband." They were all on their feet now, and White Fang ran down the steps, looking back for them to follow. For the second and last time in his life he had barked and made himself understood. After this event he found a warmer place in the hearts of the Sierra Vista people, and even the groom whose arm he had slashed admitted that he was a wise dog even if he was a wolf. Judge Scott still held to the same opinion, and proved it to everybody's dissatisfaction by measurements and descriptions taken from the encyclopaedia and various works on natural history. The days came and went, streaming their unbroken sunshine over the Santa Clara Valley. But as they grew shorter and White Fang's second winter in the Southland came on, he made a strange discovery. Collie's teeth were no longer sharp. There was a playfulness about her nips and a gentleness that prevented them from really hurting him. He forgot that she had made life a burden to him, and when she disported herself around him he responded solemnly, striving to be playful and becoming no more than ridiculous. One day she led him off on a long chase through the back-pasture land into the woods. It was the afternoon that the master was to ride, and White Fang knew it. The horse stood saddled and waiting at the door. White Fang hesitated. But there was that in him deeper than all the law he had learned, than the customs that had moulded him, than his love for the master, than the very will to live of himself; and when, in the moment of his indecision, Collie nipped him and scampered off, he turned and followed after. The master rode alone that day; and in the woods, side by side, White Fang ran with Collie, as his mother, Kiche, and old One Eye had run long years before in the silent Northland forest.

It was about this time that the newspapers were full of the daring escape of a convict from San Quentin prison. He was a ferocious man. He had been ill-made in the making. He had not been born right, and he had not been helped any by the moulding he had received at the hands of society. The hands of society are harsh, and this man was a striking sample of its handiwork. He was a beast--a human beast, it is true, but nevertheless so terrible a beast that he can best be characterised as carnivorous. Jim Hall had come into the world among the crowded tenements and cold alleys of the San Francisco slums, where a boy learned early that hunger was constant and that kindness, when it came at all, came with a price. Nothing in those lean years had softened him. What little gentleness he might have carried was scraped away by want and by the blows of men stronger than himself, and what remained was a hard knot of defiance that answered every injury with a fiercer one. He had passed through prison gates more than once, and each sentence had only deepened what the first had begun. The keepers of the law believed that pain could reform a man, that enough severity would bend him into obedience. With Jim Hall the method worked backward. Every lash, every dark day in solitary, every curse flung at him through the bars only fed the fury already burning in him, until it seemed that harshness was the one food on which he thrived. It was in the course of his third term behind the walls that he came under the charge of a guard whose cruelty was a match for his own rage. This keeper singled him out from the first and made a careful study of tormenting him. He carried lies about Hall to the warden, invented offenses that had never taken place, and turned each fabrication into a fresh penalty. The credits Hall had slowly accumulated toward an earlier release were stripped from him one after another, so that the gate he had been counting toward receded with every week. Hall endured it in sullen silence for a time, his hatred gathering and thickening. Then one day it broke loose. He threw himself upon his tormentor without weapon or warning, bearing him to the ground and tearing at his throat with his teeth like a wolf pulling down its prey. The strange god paused at the foot of the great staircase and listened, and White Fang was as dead, so without movement was he as he watched and waited. Up that staircase the way led to the love-master and to the love-master's dearest possessions. White Fang bristled, but waited. The strange god's foot lifted. He was beginning the ascent. Then it was that White Fang struck. He gave no warning, with no snarl anticipated his own action. Into the air he lifted his body in the spring that landed him on the strange god's back. White Fang clung with his fore-paws to the man's shoulders, at the same time burying his fangs into the back of the man's neck. He clung on for a moment, long enough to drag the god over backward. Together they crashed to the floor. White Fang leaped clear, and, as the man struggled to rise, was in again with the slashing fangs. Every sleeper in the house at Sierra Vista was jolted upright at once. The din rising from the ground floor seemed too large for one dog and one intruder: a pistol barked, then barked again, and a third time; a man shrieked, a single raw cry that broke off sharply; and woven through all of it came a savage, rolling growl that rose and fell with the struggle. Chairs went over with a clatter, a table toppled, and somewhere glass burst into fragments across the boards. Doors along the upper corridor flew open, and pale faces peered out into the black, nobody quite daring to move toward the stairs. The uproar ended nearly as abruptly as it had begun. It could scarcely have run longer than a few minutes, yet to those listening above it felt far longer. Afterward there was only a hush, and within the hush a single sound that made the women grip each other's arms: a laboured, rasping breath dragging in and out somewhere below in the dark, wet and uneven, like something drawing air through liquid. Then even that grew fainter. Weedon Scott reached for the switch, and light spilled down the steps and across the lower hall. Each holding a revolver, he and the Judge started down slowly, testing every tread, their eyes fixed on the shadows beyond the newel post. Nothing stirred to meet them, and the precaution proved needless. At the foot of the stairs the hall looked as though a storm had torn through it. Splintered chair legs, an upended cabinet and scattered shards lay strewn in every direction, and in the middle of that ruin a man sprawled half on his side, one arm flung across his face as though he had tried at the last to shield it. He did not move. Weedon Scott stooped, drew the arm away, and rolled the body so the features turned toward the light. The throat had been ripped wide open, and no one needed to ask how the stranger had died. The Judge leaned closer, studying the face for a long moment, and recognition settled into his expression. "Jim Hall," said Judge Scott, and father and son looked significantly at each other. Then they turned to White Fang. He, too, was lying on his side. His eyes were closed, but the lids slightly lifted in an effort to look at them as they bent over him, and the tail was perceptibly agitated in a vain effort to wag. Weedon Scott patted him, and his throat rumbled an acknowledging growl. But it was a weak growl at best, and it quickly ceased. His eyelids drooped and went shut, and his whole body seemed to relax and flatten out upon the floor. "He's all in, poor devil," muttered the master. "We'll see about that," asserted the Judge, as he started for the telephone. "Frankly, he has one chance in a thousand," announced the surgeon, after he had worked an hour and a half on White Fang. Dawn was breaking through the windows and dimming the electric lights. With the exception of the children, the whole family was gathered about the surgeon to hear his verdict. "One broken hind-leg," he went on. "Three broken ribs, one at least of which has pierced the lungs. He has lost nearly all the blood in his body. There is a large likelihood of internal injuries. He must have been jumped upon. To say nothing of three bullet holes clear through him. One chance in a thousand is really optimistic. He hasn't a chance in ten thousand." "But he mustn't lose any chance that might be of help to him," Judge Scott exclaimed. "Never mind expense. Put him under the X-ray--anything. Weedon, telegraph at once to San Francisco for Doctor Nichols. No reflection on you, doctor, you understand; but he must have the advantage of every chance." The surgeon smiled indulgently. "I understand, Judge. Every chance he shall have, and I shall do my part toward it." He turned back to the matted form stretched upon the floor and spoke as much to the room as to anyone in it. "He must be nursed as you would nurse a sick child, a human baby that has no way of telling you where it hurts. Keep him quiet. Keep him warm. See that he is not disturbed, and that he takes what nourishment he can. Watch his breathing and watch his temperature, and do not let him tear at the bandages if he comes round enough to try. I shall look in on him again at ten o'clock, and after that as often as the case requires. Everything will depend on the care he gets in these next days." He spoke gravely, and nobody who heard him could mistake how little he expected from that care. Judge Scott proposed at once that a trained nurse be sent for, someone who knew sickrooms and would follow the surgeon's orders exactly. But Beth and Mary would have none of it. They had seen White Fang go down the hall dragging himself toward the man he had killed, and they would not give him over to a stranger. Between them they divided the hours of the day and night, sitting beside him in turn, smoothing the blankets, moistening his parched mouth, and speaking low to him whenever his eyes opened in pain and dull bewilderment. They laughed at the idea that a hired woman could do better, and in the end the Judge gave way. So the girls nursed him, and White Fang, against all the odds the surgeon had laid down when he gave him scarcely one chance in ten thousand, did not die. The latter was not to be censured for his misjudgment. All his life he had tended and operated on the soft humans of civilisation, who lived sheltered lives and had descended out of many sheltered generations. Compared with White Fang, they were frail and flabby, and clutched life without any strength in their grip. White Fang had come straight from the Wild, where the weak perish early and shelter is vouchsafed to none. In neither his father nor his mother was there any weakness, nor in the generations before them. A constitution of iron and the vitality of the Wild were White Fang's inheritance, and he clung to life, the whole of him and every part of him, in spirit and in flesh, with the tenacity that of old belonged to all creatures. He slept long hours and dreamed much, and through his mind passed an unending pageant of Northland visions. All the ghosts of the past arose and were with him. Raa!" when they came to a narrow passage and the team closed together like a fan to go through. He lived again all his days with Beauty Smith and the fights he had fought. A spasm of fear went through him. He reached hastily for a brand to throw at her. But even as he reached, and before his fingers had closed on the missile, she sprang back into safety; and he knew that she was used to having things thrown at her. She had snarled as she sprang away, baring her white fangs to their roots, all her wistfulness vanishing, being replaced by a carnivorous malignity that made him shudder. He glanced at the hand that held the brand, noticing the cunning delicacy of the fingers that gripped it, how they adjusted themselves to all the inequalities of the surface, curling over and under and about the rough wood, and one little finger, too close to the burning portion of the brand, sensitively and automatically writhing back from the hurtful heat to a cooler gripping-place; and in the same instant he seemed to see a vision of those same sensitive and delicate fingers being crushed and torn by the white teeth of the she-wolf. Never had he been so fond of this body of his as now when his tenure of it was so precarious. All night, with burning brands, he fought off the hungry pack. When he dozed despite himself, the whimpering and snarling of the dogs aroused him. Morning came, but for the first time the light of day failed to scatter the wolves. The man waited in vain for them to go. They remained in a circle about him and his fire, displaying an arrogance of possession that shook his courage born of the morning light. He made one desperate attempt to pull out on the trail. But the moment he left the protection of the fire, the boldest wolf leaped for him, but leaped short. He saved himself by springing back, the jaws snapping together a scant six inches from his thigh. The rest of the pack was now up and surging upon him, and a throwing of firebrands right and left was necessary to drive them back to a respectful distance. Even in the daylight he did not dare leave the fire to chop fresh wood. Twenty feet away towered a huge dead spruce. He spent half the day extending his campfire to the tree, at any moment a half dozen burning faggots ready at hand to fling at his enemies. Once at the tree, he studied the surrounding forest in order to fell the tree in the direction of the most firewood. The night was a repetition of the night before, save that the need for sleep was becoming overpowering. The snarling of his dogs was losing its efficacy. Besides, they were snarling all the time, and his benumbed and drowsy senses no longer took note of changing pitch and intensity. He awoke with a start. The she-wolf was less than a yard from him. Mechanically, at short range, without letting go of it, he thrust a brand full into her open and snarling mouth. She sprang away, yelling with pain, and while he took delight in the smell of burning flesh and hair, he watched her shaking her head and growling wrathfully a score of feet away. He took the pine-knot and bound it to his hand, winding the fastening tight enough, he thought, to keep the flame beside him while he slept. It was a poor guard against the weariness that had been gathering for nights. The dogs' snarls blurred into one unbroken sound, and the fire's glow seemed to sink away as his eyes closed. The knot had not been secured well; as he slept, it slipped loose and fell into the snow. In his dream he was at Fort McGurry, seated across from the Factor over a game of cribbage. Outside, wolves circled the fort, their cries rising against the walls, but the cards lay between them and the game went on. Then the siege pressed closer. The door shuddered beneath the wolves' assault, burst inward, and they poured through the opening. He started awake to the same rush and snarling--not in the fort, but around him. The attack was real, and the wolves were upon him. Their teeth had already found him. Pain flared where they bit, and instinct carried him toward the fire. He leaped into it, heedless of the flames, and seized the burning brands. Then he flung hot coals in every direction, scattering them among the wolves as they crowded close. But it could not last long. His face was blistering in the heat, his eyebrows and lashes were singed off, and the heat was becoming unbearable to his feet. With a flaming brand in each hand, he sprang to the edge of the fire. The wolves had been driven back. On every side, wherever the live coals had fallen, the snow was sizzling, and every little while a retiring wolf, with wild leap and snort and snarl, announced that one such live coal had been stepped upon. Flinging his brands at the nearest of his enemies, the man thrust his smouldering mittens into the snow and stamped about to cool his feet. His two dogs were missing, and he well knew that they had served as a course in the protracted meal which had begun days before with Fatty, the last course of which would likely be himself in the days to follow. "You ain't got me yet!" he cried, savagely shaking his fist at the hungry beasts; and at the sound of his voice the whole circle was agitated, there was a general snarl, and the she-wolf slid up close to him across the snow and watched him with hungry wistfulness.

All worked well, but there came a time when he fastened the pine-knot insecurely. As his eyes closed it fell away from his hand. He dreamed. It seemed to him that he was in Fort McGurry. It was warm and comfortable, and he was playing cribbage with the Factor. Also, it seemed to him that the fort was besieged by wolves. They were howling at the very gates, and sometimes he and the Factor paused from the game to listen and laugh at the futile efforts of the wolves to get in. And then, so strange was the dream, there was a crash. The door was burst open. He could see the wolves flooding into the big living-room of the fort. They were leaping straight for him and the Factor. With the bursting open of the door, the noise of their howling had increased tremendously. This howling now bothered him. His dream was merging into something else--he knew not what; but through it all, following him, persisted the howling. And then he awoke to find the howling real. There was a great snarling and yelping. The wolves were rushing him. They were all about him and upon him. The teeth of one had closed upon his arm. Instinctively he leaped into the fire, and as he leaped, he felt the sharp slash of teeth that tore through the flesh of his leg. Then began a fire fight. His stout mittens temporarily protected his hands, and he scooped live coals into the air in all directions, until the campfire took on the semblance of a volcano. But it could not last long. His face was blistering in the heat, his eyebrows and lashes were singed off, and the heat was becoming unbearable to his feet. With a flaming brand in each hand, he sprang to the edge of the fire. The wolves had been driven back. On every side, wherever the live coals had fallen, the snow was sizzling, and every little while a retiring wolf, with wild leap and snort and snarl, announced that one such live coal had been stepped upon. Flinging his brands at the nearest of his enemies, the man thrust his smouldering mittens into the snow and stamped about to cool his feet. His two dogs were missing, and he well knew that they had served as a course in the protracted meal which had begun days before with Fatty, the last course of which would likely be himself in the days to follow. "You ain't got me yet!" he cried, savagely shaking his fist at the hungry beasts; and at the sound of his voice the whole circle was agitated, there was a general snarl, and the she-wolf slid up close to him across the snow and watched him with hungry wistfulness.

He set to work to carry out a new idea that had come to him. He extended the fire into a large circle. Inside this circle he crouched, his sleeping outfit under him as a protection against the melting snow. When he had thus disappeared within his shelter of flame, the whole pack came curiously to the rim of the fire to see what had become of him. Hitherto they had been denied access to the fire, and they now settled down in a close-drawn circle, like so many dogs, blinking and yawning and stretching their lean bodies in the unaccustomed warmth. Then the she-wolf sat down, pointed her nose at a star, and began to howl. One by one the wolves joined her, till the whole pack, on haunches, with noses pointed skyward, was howling its hunger cry. Burning brands made them spring aside, but they no longer sprang back. In vain he strove to drive them back. As he gave up and stumbled inside his circle, a wolf leaped for him, missed, and landed with all four feet in the coals. It cried out with terror, at the same time snarling, and scrambled back to cool its paws in the snow. He crawled close to the fire and sat with his hands held out to the feeble warmth. The wolves had drawn back, but they were still there, silent shapes beyond the circle of flame. He was too tired now to watch them with any care. His shoulders sagged, his head drooped, and the weariness that had been held off by fear settled over him with its full weight. He knew the fire would not last, and that there was nothing more he could do. He fed it the last bits of wood within reach, one at a time, watching each piece catch and then burn down. The flames dwindled, and the cold crept closer. He drew his knees up and wrapped his arms around them, making himself as small as he could. Outside, the wolves waited. He would sleep, he thought, if only for a little while; the thought came without hope or protest, simply because he could no longer keep his eyes open. The men gathered around his slumped form, speaking urgently and shaking him, while the dogs crowded close. He heard them dimly, caught between waking and sleep, as they tried to rouse him.

Their small movements and thin cries held his mate's attention, and she watched him anxiously whenever he drew near them. He travelled miles from the lair, ranging through the timber with his nose alert to every promise of game. Hunger gave purpose to his movements, but experience governed them. There might be prey ahead, yet there might also be a dispute over it, with little to gain from the encounter. It was occupied with the bark, working steadily and showing no concern for the forest about it. One Eye paused where he could observe it. Through all his long experience, no porcupine had ever furnished him a meal. Here was meat within easy reach, apparently absorbed in its own affairs, yet guarded by a covering that made the ordinary methods of pursuit and attack useless. Nevertheless, he advanced cautiously. Living prey did not always behave as a hunter expected, and the moment that seemed least promising could sometimes yield an opening. He had learned to watch before abandoning a possibility, to let movement and circumstance disclose what haste would miss. Keeping his steps light, he drew nearer to the tree, his single eye fixed upon the feeding animal. Then the porcupine became aware of him and ceased its work upon the bark. The porcupine rolled itself into a ball, radiating long, sharp needles in all directions that defied attack. In his youth One Eye had once sniffed too near a similar, apparently inert ball of quills, and had the tail flick out suddenly in his face. One quill he had carried away in his muzzle, where it had remained for weeks, a rankling flame, until it finally worked out. So he lay down, in a comfortable crouching position, his nose fully a foot away, and out of the line of the tail. Thus he waited, keeping perfectly quiet. There was no telling. Something might happen. The porcupine might unroll. There might be opportunity for a deft and ripping thrust of paw into the tender, unguarded belly. But at the end of half an hour he arose, growled wrathfully at the motionless ball, and trotted on. He had waited too often and futilely in the past for porcupines to unroll, to waste any more time. He continued up the right fork. The day wore along, and nothing rewarded his hunt. The urge of his awakened instinct of fatherhood was strong upon him. He must find meat. Each saw the other. As the track led his way, he followed, prepared to meet the maker of it at every turn of the stream. He slid his head around a corner of rock, where began an unusually large bend in the stream, and his quick eyes made out something that sent him crouching swiftly down. It was the maker of the track, a large female lynx. She was crouching as he had crouched once that day, in front of her the tight-rolled ball of quills. If he had been a gliding shadow before, he now became the ghost of such a shadow, as he crept and circled around, and came up well to leeward of the silent, motionless pair. He lay down in the snow, depositing the ptarmigan beside him, and with eyes peering through the needles of a low-growing spruce he watched the play of life before him--the waiting lynx and the waiting porcupine, each intent on life; and, such was the curiousness of the game, the way of life for one lay in the eating of the other, and the way of life for the other lay in being not eaten. While old One Eye, the wolf crouching in the covert, played his part, too, in the game, waiting for some strange freak of Chance, that might help him on the meat-trail which was his way of life. Slowly, cautiously, it was unrolling its ball of impregnable armour. It was agitated by no tremor of anticipation. Slowly, slowly, the bristling ball straightened out and lengthened. One Eye watching, felt a sudden moistness in his mouth and a drooling of saliva, involuntary, excited by the living meat that was spreading itself like a repast before him.

His mate looked at him anxiously. Every little while she emitted a low growl, and at times, when it seemed to her he approached too near, the growl shot up in her throat to a sharp snarl. Old One Eye was feeling the urge of an impulse, that was, in turn, an instinct that had come down to him from all the fathers of wolves. He did not question it, nor puzzle over it. It was there, in the fibre of his being; and it was the most natural thing in the world that he should obey it by turning his back on his new-born family and by trotting out and away on the meat-trail whereby he lived. The porcupine sensed the danger just as the lynx sprang. It had barely time to turn its back and raise its quills before she was upon it, one forepaw reaching to seize the exposed head. Her claws caught nothing; the porcupine twisted beneath her and swept its tail against the descending paw. She snatched the paw back, but the quills came with it, lodged in the tender flesh. For a moment she crouched beside her quarry, holding the wounded foot clear of the ground, her ears flattened and her lips drawn back. The porcupine huddled close, presenting a bristling barrier wherever she moved. Pain drove the lynx into a fiercer attack. With a harsh cry she struck again, thrusting her face toward the porcupine as though she could force a way through its defence. She recoiled almost at once, her nose and face pierced with fresh quills. The porcupine remained curled beneath its armour while she backed away, shaking her head and scraping at her muzzle with her paws. Each effort disturbed the embedded points and brought another cry from her. She sneezed, rubbed her face against the ground, then bounded aside as if the pain were something pursuing her. One Eye watched from a distance as she twisted and leaped, unable either to endure the quills or to tear them free. She sneezed continually, and her stub of a tail was doing its best toward lashing about by giving quick, violent jerks. She quit her antics, and quieted down for a long minute. One Eye watched. The paw, with rigid claws curving like talons, shot under the tender belly and came back with a swift ripping movement. Everything had happened at once--the blow, the counter-blow, the squeal of agony from the porcupine, the big cat's squall of sudden hurt and astonishment. One Eye half arose in his excitement, his ears up, his tail straight out and quivering behind him. The lynx's bad temper got the best of her. She sprang savagely at the thing that had hurt her. Then she fell to backing away and sneezing, her nose bristling with quills like a monstrous pin-cushion. She brushed her nose with her paws, trying to dislodge the fiery darts, thrust it into the snow, and rubbed it against twigs and branches, and all the time leaping about, ahead, sidewise, up and down, in a frenzy of pain and fright. And even he could not repress a start and an involuntary bristling of hair along his back when she suddenly leaped, without warning, straight up in the air, at the same time emitting a long and most terrible squall. Then she sprang away, up the trail, squalling with every leap she made. It was not until her racket had faded away in the distance and died out that One Eye ventured forth. He walked as delicately as though all the snow were carpeted with porcupine quills, erect and ready to pierce the soft pads of his feet. The porcupine met his approach with a furious squealing and a clashing of its long teeth. It had managed to roll up in a ball again, but it was not quite the old compact ball; its muscles were too much torn for that. It had been ripped almost in half, and was still bleeding profusely. One Eye scooped out mouthfuls of the blood-soaked snow, and chewed and tasted and swallowed. This served as a relish, and his hunger increased mightily; but he was too old in the world to forget his caution. He waited. He lay down and waited, while the porcupine grated its teeth and uttered grunts and sobs and occasional sharp little squeals. In a little while, One Eye noticed that the quills were drooping and that a great quivering had set up. The quivering came to an end suddenly. There was a final defiant clash of the long teeth. It had happened more than once, and each time the grey cub watched it with the same steady attention. His father would rise from the warm darkness at the back of the lair, pad toward the place where the light was strongest, and walk straight into it. The white wall took him whole. One moment there was the lean shape, the swing of the tail, the scent of him; the next there was only brightness, and the scent thinning on the air. The cub had tried it himself. He had toddled after the old wolf on unsteady legs and run against the side of the cave where it curved toward the opening, and the earth had not let him through. It had struck him on the nose and turned him back, and he had sat down hard and whimpered. After that he kept away from the walls that hurt. The bright one swallowed his father and gave him back again, smelling of distance and of things killed; the dark ones were hard and did not give way. That was simply how it was. He did not ask why. Questions of that kind were not in him. A man, meeting such a thing, would worry at it, turning it over and demanding a reason and a rule that would fit both the wall that opened and the wall that would not. The cub required nothing of the sort. He knew that some things yielded and some did not, that some walls were for his father and some were for nobody, and the knowing was enough. His mind took each new fact as it came and set it in its place among the others, much as his body took the milk, without inquiring into its source. What mattered to him was the how of a thing, the way it behaved when he met it, and what it would do to his nose or his belly. The reasons behind it lay beyond his reach, and he felt no lack of them. He sorted the world into what hurt and what did not, what fed him and what did not, and lived content within those divisions. Then the feeding began to fail. There was less meat brought into the lair, and at last there was none, and the milk that had flowed so freely from his mother's side grew thin and then ceased altogether. At first the cubs whimpered and cried and nuzzled at her, but crying took strength, and soon they had none to spare. They stopped playing. They stopped crawling toward the light. They lay heaped together in the back of the cave and slept, and the sleep was heavy and long and hard to break, a dull stupor in which hunger was no longer felt as pain but only as a great weight pressing them down. The little flame of life in each of them burned lower. They breathed slowly, stirred seldom, and drifted further from waking each day, while outside the lair the season turned and the land gave up nothing to eat. One Eye was desperate. He ranged far and wide, and slept but little in the lair that had now become cheerless and miserable. The she-wolf, too, left her litter and went out in search of meat. In the first days after the birth of the cubs, One Eye had journeyed several times back to the Indian camp and robbed the rabbit snares; but, with the melting of the snow and the opening of the streams, the Indian camp had moved away, and that source of supply was closed to him. When the grey cub came back to life and again took interest in the far white wall, he found that the population of his world had been reduced. Only one sister remained to him. The rest were gone. As he grew stronger, he found himself compelled to play alone, for the sister no longer lifted her head nor moved about. His little body rounded out with the meat he now ate; but the food had come too late for her. She slept continuously, a tiny skeleton flung round with skin in which the flame flickered lower and lower and at last went out. Then there came a time when the grey cub no longer saw his father appearing and disappearing in the wall nor lying down asleep in the entrance. This had happened at the end of a second and less severe famine. The she-wolf knew why One Eye never came back, but there was no way by which she could tell what she had seen to the grey cub.
